items.title: THOR: A GPU-accelerated and MPI-parallel radiative transfer code
items.abstract: Emission and absorption line features are important diagnostics for the physics underlying extragalactic astronomy. The interpretation of observed signatures involves making comparisons against forward-modeled spectra from galaxy formation simulations as well as more simplified geometries, while including the complex scattering radiative transfer (RT) of resonant emission lines. Here, we present þor, a modern C++ RT code focused initially on resonant emission lines. þor is a high-performance, distributed-memory, multi-target code that uses the message passing interface (MPI) for parallel execution. It runs on CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators, yielding large ∼ 10-50 speed-ups compared to previous CPU-only codes. Our code supports multiple grid-based and grid-less data structures, enabling comparisons across different hydrodynamical codes as well as toy model geometries. We demonstrate its science capabilities with a number of example use cases across scales: (i) Lyman-alpha RT on simple shell-like gas distributions; (ii) Lyman-alpha RT applied to a high-resolution, high-redshift (z ∼ 6) cosmological hydrodynamical galaxy formation simulation; (iii) magnesium-II halos, namely, scattering and emission from the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of a z ≃ 1 galaxy drawn from a cosmological magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulation; (iv) the large-scale cosmic web in gas emission, a 6144^3 volume element RT scaling calculation; and (v) synthetic absorption spectra of the Lyman-alpha forest. We employed extensive verification and benchmarking to validate our approach and its computational efficiency. x

items.title: Loop quantum gravity black holes surrounded by quintessence
items.abstract: Quantum gravity corrections act on the near-horizon geometry of a black hole (BH), while dark energy acts on its asymptotic region, and how the two imprints combine is still poorly understood. We study a static, spherically symmetric BH of Loop Quantum Gravity (LQG) surrounded by a quintessence field. The metric function carries the LQG parameters [Formula: see text] and the quintessence parameters [Formula: see text], and for suitable values it has three horizons, a structure found neither in pure LQG BHs nor in classical quintessence BHs. We analyze null and timelike geodesics, photon spheres and the shadow seen by a static observer placed between the event and the cosmological horizons. Sixth-order WKB quasinormal modes (QNMs) of scalar and electromagnetic fields confirm stability over the ranges examined. The quantum term behaves as a short-range repulsive correction: it shrinks the photon sphere and the shadow, raises the QNM oscillation frequency and lowers the light deflection. Quintessence works the other way on the photon sphere, the ringing frequency and the bending. With the Gauss–Bonnet method, we obtain a weak deflection angle valid for [Formula: see text], which we check against direct numerical integration, and in which quintessence dominates at large impact parameters and the LQG terms at small ones.

items.title: Photometric classification of supernovae detected by the Zwicky Transient Facility using noise augmentation
items.abstract: Modern time-domain surveys, such as the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), detect far more extragalactic transients than can be spectroscopically classified. Photometric classification offers a scalable alternative, enabling the identification of larger, fainter, and higher-redshift supernova (SN) samples suitable for applications such as Type Ia SN (SN Ia) cosmology. We present a feature-based photometric classifier for SNe detected by ZTF, with the primary goal of constructing a photometric SN Ia sample for cosmological analyses. Our approach utilises the autoencoder architecture from the model to capture the intrinsic diversity of SN light curves. We trained the model on a spectroscopically classified ZTF SN sample, incorporating a realistic redshift and augmentation procedure that simulates the flux uncertainties of fainter sources. This enables the model to generalise to noisier, higher-redshift populations. Light curve features were used to train a gradient-boosted decision tree classifier, implemented in both binary (SN Ia vs non-Ia) and multi-class configurations. We validated our classifier on independent, fainter ZTF data with and without augmentation. To evaluate real-time performance, we also applied our classifier to live ZTF alerts and conducted a spectroscopic classification survey within the ePESSTO+ collaboration. ParSNIP We found that redshift and noise augmentation significantly improves classification performance, particularly for fainter sources. Our binary classifier achieves an SN Ia recall of $(98.1 ± 0.4)%$, averaged across five train–test splits. SN Ia recall exceeds 98% for events with more than 10 detections and a peak apparent magnitude of up to 20, remaining above 96% up to a magnitude of 20.5. Overall, 95% of the sources were correctly classified in both binary and multi-class modes. In our live classification survey, we correctly identified the class for 78% of the targets, including rare events such as superluminous SNe, despite a median of only nine detections per object. Our classifier performs efficiently on real ZTF data, including faint and noisy light curves. Applied to the full ZTF transient sample, it will enable the construction of a large photometric SN Ia dataset for cosmology. It also provides a practical tool for real-time spectroscopic target prioritisation, which will be essential for large-scale surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time.

items.title: Cross-simulator transfer with foundation-model summaries: Toward robust SKA-era reionization inference
items.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) for parameter estimation is vulnerable to model misspecification: neural summaries and density estimators trained on a specific forward model typically fail when applied to data drawn from another model or from real observations, and no training simulator can capture the full observational pipeline of a real measurement exactly. We show that a self-supervised vision transformer (ViT), pretrained label-free on a fast approximate simulator, produces transferable data summaries that generalize across simulators. Without retraining, it can be reused as a frozen encoder to infer astrophysical parameters from a completely different simulator that explicitly resolves radiative transfer and on which it was never trained. As a concrete use case in 21cm cosmology, SKATR, a ViT pretrained with a self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), serves as a foundation model for reionization inference from upcoming Square Kilometre Array (SKA) measurements: SKATR was pretrained once on 67k low-cost, noiseless semi-numerical 21cmFAST light cones, frozen, and applied to hydrodynamical Loreli II light cones, where a lightweight conditional flow matching (CFM) head infers five astrophysical parameters. The encoder is never shown Loreli data, its parameters, or any noise. In our comparison, SKATR yields the most precise and best-calibrated posteriors across all five parameters, matching the accuracy of the fully supervised in-domain baseline while requiring 2.6 fewer radiative-transfer simulations. Under realistic SKA AA* noise, only SKATR remains simultaneously accurate, informative, and calibrated, outperforming even a supervised baseline retrained from scratch on noisy data. Self-supervised pretraining on computationally efficient semi-numerical simulations is therefore a viable route to calibrated, simulator-, and noise-agnostic reionization inference for the SKA-era.

items.title: Low-Cost Visual Art in Stroke Neurorehabilitation: A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Each stroke survivor's path to recovery is highly individualized, often needing support and collaboration from an interdisciplinary team of experts. This scoping review aims to explore how low-cost visual art is used as an intervention in stroke neurorehabilitation beyond traditional therapy alone. Medline, CINAHL, Embase, Scopus, PubMed, and DOAJ databases were searched using keywords: art, art communication, art therapy, stroke, and neuroplasticity. Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer; full texts by two reviewers, with conflicts resolved by a third. 42 papers were included and mapped across three themes: communication, stroke therapy, and neuroplasticity. Visual art supported self-expression and patient-clinician communication, particularly for patients with language or visuospatial deficits, while art-based assessments were used to identify cognitive-perceptual impairments. Low-cost therapeutic interventions, including drawing, painting, and other group art programs, were associated with improvements in quality of life, mood, self-efficacy, social connectedness, and fine motor or speech outcomes. However, visual arts-based research directly linking to neuroplastic changes remains limited. Visual art can be applied as low-cost and accessible interventions, although further research on the relationship between visual art, neuroplasticity, and clinical implementation is needed.

items.title: Cerebellar-Extracerebellar Relations: Editorial Overview of Current Knowledge, Open Questions, Technical Limitations, and the Where-What-How Method.
items.abstract: The cerebellum contributes to neurological function by influencing activity in other parts of the nervous system. This statement, apparently simple, underscores the inherent complexity of cerebellar neuroscience, because complex cerebellar-extracerebellar relations are central in the study of the cerebellum. To study the cerebellum means to study how the cerebellum relates to the brain, as much as studying the visual system means studying how the visual system relates to light. As far as we know, there is no direct behavioral output stemming from isolated cerebellar activity, unlike in primary motor cortex, and no cognitively accessible content stemming from isolated cerebellar activity, unlike in cerebral associative cortex. Extracerebellar relations are not extra credit for cerebellar neuroscience; they are a central element of what cerebellar neuroscience is. We discuss (i) open questions in cerebellar-extracerebellar relations; (ii) technical challenges related to these questions, with an emphasis on human research, including issues highlighted in the present special issue; and (iii) the Where-What-How method as a framework to organize the analysis of cerebellar-extracerebellar relations. An example of this framework is that right arm dysmetria can be decomposed into where function is affected (right arm, rather than left arm or right leg); what function is affected (motor function, rather than language or emotion regulation); and how function is affected (deficits in precision and coordination, rather than in speed or initiation). Open questions in the study of cerebellar-extracerebellar relations, and methodological limitations that apply to these questions, can be organized following the Where-What-How method.

items.title: Clozapine beyond schizophrenia: an umbrella systematic review of the off-label uses of clozapine in managing psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions.
items.abstract: To systematically appraise the literature for systematic reviews on the off-label uses of clozapine for psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions beyond psychotic disorders. Systematic searches of Medline, PsychInfo, CINAHL, and Cochrane Database were performed on February 8th, 2025, using the search terms "clozapine" AND "systematic review". Systematic reviews investigating clozapine as an intervention for conditions aside from schizophrenia (or related psychotic disorders) were included in this review. Risk of bias was assessed using the AMSTAR 2 assessment tool. The search yielded 571 studies after removal of duplicates, with 20 studies being suitable for systematic review. Six meta-analyses were found to meet the inclusion criteria demonstrating clozapine's efficacy in managing Parkinson's psychosis (SMD = -4.23; 95% CI = -6.53, -1.93), tardive dyskinesia (SMD = - 2.56, p = 0.02), insomnia (OR = 0.45, p < 0.01), substance use disorder (OR = 0.10, p < 0.00001), and in reducing suicidality (OR = 0.229, p < 0.0001) and mortality (RR = 0.43, 95% CI = 0.34-0.55). Additionally, systematic reviews were found meeting the inclusion criteria demonstrating that clozapine was efficacious in managing treatment-resistant bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, catatonia, psychogenic polydipsia, essential tremor, behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), neurodevelopmental disorders, violence and aggression, and aggression in children. Confidence in the quality of evidence was assessed to be high in 7, moderate in 3, low in 3, and critically low in 7 reviews. Clozapine is potentially efficacious in the off-label management of a wide range of psychiatric and neurological conditions beyond treatment-resistant schizophrenia. There is evidence justifying re-evaluation of clinical guidelines for Parkinson's psychosis.

items.title: Reducing the burden of cervical cancer in Zambia in the next 40 years: impact of enhanced screening efforts.
items.abstract: Zambia bears one of the world's highest cervical cancer burdens, driven by high human papillomavirus (HPV) prevalence, gaps in vaccination and screening, and the intersecting human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) epidemic. In this study we assess the potential impact of scaling up HPV screening alongside vaccination efforts, based on a community outreach plan designed by ICAP Columbia and Zambia's Ministry of Health. The plan targets Zambia's rural communities and promotes self-collection of samples, on-site HPV testing, and same-day treatment when eligible, with referral to hub sites for severe cases. To estimate the expanded screening's impact, we developed an individual-based model capturing HPV transmission through age-structured sexual partnership, and subsequent progression from infection to cervical lesions and cervical cancer. The model was calibrated to Zambia's demographic profile, 2022 HPV prevalence, 2020 cervical cancer incidence. We compared five 40-year scenarios: no intervention, vaccination only (girls 9-14 years); vaccination plus visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA)-based screening targeted towards women living with HIV, and scenarios extending screening to all women ( ~ 200,000 vs ~400,000 tests/year with 5% annual increase). Outcomes were cervical cancer incidence, percent reduction across intervention scenarios, and cumulative cases averted. Uncertainty was quantified via repeated stochastic simulations with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs). Sensitivity analyses examined alternative HIV incidence trajectories and reduced screening accessibility. By 2060, HPV vaccination alone reduces cervical cancer incidence by 47% (95% CI: 39%-55%) compared to current rates but has limited effect in the first 20 years. Adding population screening accelerates impact: under ~400,000 tests/year, incidence falls 64% (95% CI: 56%-70%) by year 20 and 97% (95% CI: 96%-98%) by year 40, averting ~35,000 cases by 2040 and ~183,000 by 2060 and reaching the World Health Organization elimination threshold by 2060. Exploratory analyses suggest additional long-term benefit from vaccinating boys, especially when vaccination coverage is suboptimal. In Zambia, vaccination alone will not meaningfully reduce cervical cancer burden in the near term, and pairing vaccination with a community-based HPV-screening/treatment could prevent tens of thousands of cancer cases within two decades and place elimination within reach.

items.title: Proceedings from the 2025 precision public health transdisciplinary conference: capacity building.
items.abstract: The 2025 Precision Public Health Transdisciplinary Conference brought together over 150 attendees from five continents to discuss innovative research and advances in precision health and promote sharing of insights, with an emphasis on capacity-building in different contexts of precision public health, including non-Western settings and settings with constrained resources. The conference was hosted by the Precision Public Health Network and held virtually on 19-20 November 2025, featuring 11 invited speakers with expertise across key areas of precision public health and genomic medicine, and 20 oral and poster presentations selected from submitted abstracts. This report summarises the conference proceedings and key emerging themes, including the need to strengthen capacity through robust, inclusive data systems that reflect population diversity; meaningful community involvement in genomic medicine; integration of clinical, genomic and national health datasets; and evidence-based incorporation of innovative tools such as artificial intelligence (AI) to support analysis and decision‑making.

items.title: Surveillance of selected infectious agents in captive felids from Polish zoological gardens - preliminary study.
items.abstract: Infectious diseases threaten the health and welfare of captive nondomestic felids, yet data on the occurrence of infectious agents in zoological collections remain limited. The aim of this study was to investigate the exposure to selected feline viral pathogens together with Toxoplasma gondii in captive white lion, Amur (Siberian) tiger, white Bengal tiger, Eurasian lynx, cheetah, and sand cat maintained in two Polish zoological gardens using molecular and serological methods. Serum samples and nasal swabs were collected for analysis. Serological testing was performed for feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), feline leukemia virus (FeLV), and T. gondii, while real-time PCR assays were used to detect feline calicivirus (FCV), feline herpesvirus type 1 (FHV-1), feline leukemia virus (FeLV), and feline coronavirus (FCoV). Nasal swabs were also used for conventional bacteriological examinations. Feline calicivirus RNA was detected in nasal swabs from one white lion and white Bengal tiger, whereas all tested animals were negative for FHV-1, FCoV, and FeLV by real-time PCR. Serological analysis revealed: (i) no evidence of FIV infection; (ii) antibodies against T. gondii in two animals; and (iii) FeLV seropositivity in one white lion despite a negative PCR result. Staphylococcus aureus and Acinetobacter beijerinckii were detected in the sample of white Bengal tiger, as well as Staphylococcus haemolyticus and Psychrobacter maritimus cultured in the sample of white lion. These isolates were distinguished by their low resistance to antimicrobials: : ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, cephalothin, tetracycline and oxytetracycline (A. beijerinckii), clindamycin (S. aureus), as well as streptomycin (P. maritimus). These findings contribute to knowledge of infectious diseases in zoo-housed felids in Central Europe and highlight integrated molecular and serological surveillance for health monitoring and disease management in zoological collections.

items.title: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies in Latin America: clinical diversity, diagnostic challenges, and unmet needs.
items.abstract: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) are a heterogeneous group of rare, systemic autoimmune diseases that remain understudied in Latin America despite the region's ethnic admixture, socioeconomic heterogeneity, and unequal access to rheumatologic care. This narrative review synthesizes the literature on IIM from Latin American centers, integrating single- and multicenter cohorts, national registries, and collaborative networks. Dermatomyositis is the most frequently reported subtype in most national series, although this may partly reflect differences in patient selection and classification, and regional autoantibody profiles show distinctive features, including a high frequency of anti-Mi-2 in Mexican cohorts and among Colombian patients in a multinational survey and emerging data on anti-MDA5-associated dermatomyositis in Latin American cohorts that diverge phenotypically from Asian cohorts. Anti-synthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion body myositis, and juvenile dermatomyositis are characterized mainly through Brazilian series, complemented by Argentine data and multinational collaborations, alongside multicenter data on myositis-associated interstitial lung disease from Argentina, Chile, and Mexico. The COVID-19 pandemic further complicated regional care, prompting pharmacovigilance and vaccine-safety collaborations, including a Brazilian interventional trial of an inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. We highlight neglected dimensions of regional IIM care, including reproductive health. Persistent obstacles include diagnostic delay, restricted access to myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibody panels, heterogeneous availability of muscle MRI and biopsy, and inequitable access to immunosuppressive and biologic therapies across public and private health systems. We highlight priority actions, including expansion of multinational registries, harmonization of diagnostic algorithms, and investment in translational research reflecting the admixed ancestry of Latin American populations, which may help reduce diagnostic delay and improve long-term outcomes.

items.title: Profiling antibiotic resistance genes, virulence factors, and carbohydrate-active enzymes using metagenomics: implications for Plateau Wetland ecological health.
items.abstract: This study employs metagenomic analysis to systematically characterize the diversity and abundance of CAZymes, ARGs, and VFs in water and soil samples collected from the Napahai Plateau Wetland. Significant differences in α-diversity were observed across the sample types, with VFs exhibiting the most pronounced variation. PCoA revealed distinct clustering of water and soil samples based on the abundance profiles of ARGs and VFs, whereas CAZymes displayed relatively uniform distribution across both environments. Among CAZymes, GH and GT were the most prevalent, with PL and AA enriched in water, and CBM and GH more abundant in soil. ARGs associated with aminoglycoside and sulfonamide resistance were more prevalent in water, whereas soil samples exhibited a higher abundance of genes such as acrR and vanI. Additionally, VFs related to exotoxins and motility were significantly more abundant in aquatic environments, indicating a potentially heightened pathogenic potential in these settings. Environmental variables, including pH, TN, TP, and metal ions (Zn, Mg), were significantly correlated with CAZymes and VFs abundance. For ARGs, these correlations are likely indirect and mediated by shifts in microbial community composition and abundance. Notably, a positive correlation among CAZymes, ARGs, and VFs suggested their co-enrichment, likely driven by microbial adaptation to ecological stressors such as antibiotic pollution. These findings highlight the critical role of plateau wetlands as reservoirs and potential dissemination hubs for antibiotic resistance and microbial virulence, with important implications for ecosystem health and public health surveillance amidst global environmental change.

items.title: A hypothesis-generating integration of single-cell and bulk transcriptomics nominates SPP1-CD44 innate-adaptive crosstalk in ocular hypertension.
items.abstract: Neuroinflammation accompanies retinal ganglion cell (RGC) loss in glaucoma, but the immune states elicited by intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation and the crosstalk among them remain incompletely characterized. We performed a hypothesis-generating re-analysis integrating single-cell and bulk transcriptomes from four public cohorts. Among 30,063 CD45 + immune cells from the microbead ocular hypertension (OHT) model (GSE293358), the retinal homeostatic-microglia compartment was relatively depleted under OHT. In contrast, MHCII+ macrophage/APC and lymphocyte compartments, including γδ T, NK, and T cells, were relatively expanded, whereas DAM-like microglia showed a non-significant upward trend. These changes reflect composition within the CD45 + fraction and should not be interpreted as absolute changes in cell number. Diffusion pseudotime organized microglia along an inferred homeostatic→DAM→interferon/MHCII transcriptional continuum, with module scores showing directional concordance in an independent bulk time-course cohort (retina DAM Δ=+1.00, nominal p = 0.044; two pooled libraries per group, exploratory). In sorted Müller glia, expression of the microglia-restraining ligand Cx3cl1 was markedly reduced (log2FC = - 5.30; nominal p = 0.010, with no gene passing FDR correction in this n = 3-per-group cohort). Cell-cell communication inference further predicted an OHT-associated SPP1→CD44 ligand-receptor interaction from activated myeloid cells to lymphocytes. Together, these findings nominate candidate hypotheses involving immune-state reorganization and ligand-receptor signaling in OHT; we present them as parallel, compartmentalized responses and do not claim a validated causal cascade. Exploratory Mendelian randomization and compound-reversal analyses (Figs. S1 and S2 in Online Resource 1) did not provide definitive causal or therapeutic evidence. All proposed mechanisms are inferred from transcriptomic data and require protein-level, spatial, and functional validation.

items.title: FAP-targeted 211 At radiotherapy remodels the tumor microenvironment and is associated with enhanced anti-PD-L1 efficacy.
items.abstract: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP)‑positive cancer‑associated fibroblasts contribute to immune exclusion and resistance to checkpoint blockade in the tumor microenvironment (TME). This study evaluated whether 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr, a FAP‑targeted alpha‑emitting radiopharmaceutical, could remodel the TME and enhance responsiveness to PD-L1 blockade. Given the complex and immune-excluded microenvironment of lung cancer, we analyzed public datasets to define the clinical and immune context of FAP in this malignancy. 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr was synthesized and characterized for radiochemical purity, stability, FAP‑specific uptake, DNA damage, and PD‑L1 induction. Biodistribution, PET/CT imaging, therapeutic efficacy, histology, immune remodeling, and systemic cytokine profiles (MSD platform) were assessed in LLC/3T3‑FAP tumor‑bearing mice treated with saline, 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr, TPP-1 (a PD-L1-blocking peptide), or combination. FAP was enriched in stromal regions and correlated with advanced stage, reduced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, and immunosuppressive signatures. 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr showed > 95% radiochemical purity, FAP‑dependent uptake, induced γ‑H2AX foci, and upregulated PD‑L1 in vitro. Tumor uptake peaked at 5.63 ± 0.72%ID/g (1 h) and remained 4.53 ± 2.13%ID/g at 24 h. Combination therapy exhibited the most potent tumor growth inhibition, reduced 18F‑FDG uptake, increased PD-L1-specific 68​Ga-TPP-1 uptake, decreased proliferation and angiogenesis, and enhanced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration and granzyme B expression. At the immunological level, MSD‑based cytokine analysis revealed that combination therapy induced more extensive alterations in systemic immune modulation than either monotherapy, whereas 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr alone shifted the profile toward pro‑inflammation. No overt organ histopathology or sustained body-weight loss was observed during the assessment period (8 days), while treatment-associated haematological changes (reduced WBC and RBC counts) were detected. In the engineered LLC/3T3-FAP model, 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr selectively targets FAP-rich tumor stroma, induces DNA damage and adaptive PD-L1 upregulation, and is associated with a shift of the immune-excluded TME toward a state that is more responsive to PD-L1 blockade. These findings suggest that FAP-targeted alpha radiotherapy may be a promising strategy for TME remodeling and immunotherapy sensitization in preclinical NSCLC models, and support further investigation toward clinical translation in more physiologically relevant systems.

items.title: Clinical characteristics, genetics, and long-term outcomes in children with very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease: a Turkish cohort.
items.abstract: Very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease (VEO-IBD) is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity, a higher prevalence of monogenic disease, and an increased risk of an aggressive disease course. We evaluated clinical, genetic, and nutritional profiles and long-term outcomes in VEO-IBD and identified predictors of disease severity. This retrospective longitudinal cohort study included 49 children with VEO-IBD followed at a tertiary center between 2015 and 2025. Patients were stratified into infantile-onset (< 2 years) and non-infantile-onset (2-5 years) groups to compare clinical characteristics, nutritional status, biologic-free survival, and predictors of aggressive disease. Median age at diagnosis was 3.25 years (median follow-up: 56.6 months); 57.1% had ulcerative colitis, 32.7% Crohn disease, and 10.2% IBD-unclassified. Genetic testing was performed in 57.1% of patients and identified monogenic disease in 21.4% of those tested. Infantile-onset patients had higher rates of identifiable genetic variants (88.9% vs. 47.4%, p = 0.049) and baseline stunting (33.3% vs. 5.6%, p = 0.047). Biologic-free survival did not differ by onset age (p = 0.719). Crohn disease (OR 11.82, 95% CI 1.32-106.22) and moderate-to-severe baseline disease activity (OR 21.55, 95% CI 2.29-202.70) independently predicted an aggressive course, whereas age at onset and monogenic disease were not independent predictors of an aggressive disease course. Infantile-onset VEO-IBD was associated with more genetic abnormalities and baseline stunting. These findings support early molecular genetic evaluation in infants. Long-term disease severity was primarily determined by disease phenotype and baseline disease activity rather than age at onset or monogenic disease. • Very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease is characterized by marked clinical and genetic heterogeneity. • Monogenic disease is more frequently identified in children with very early disease onset. • Infantile-onset VEO-IBD was associated with a higher frequency of stunting at diagnosis. • Disease phenotype and baseline disease activity, rather than age at onset or monogenic disease, independently predicted an aggressive disease course.

items.title: Consumers' perceptions of environmental sustainability labelling and dual front-of-pack labelling on packaged foods: an exploratory qualitative study.
items.abstract: Little is known about how consumers understand the concept of food sustainability and how they process combinations of nutrition and sustainability information provided on food products. This study aimed to explore consumers' awareness and perceptions of sustainability information on food packaging, the importance they place on sustainability in food choices and their suggestions for implementing dual labelling systems that provide both nutrition and sustainability information. Qualitative study using focus group discussions analysed through thematic analysis. Twelve online focus groups were conducted with participants from three Australian states: New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland. (n 112) discussed their perceptions of sustainability labelling and appropriate methods of displaying dual labelling on food packages. Three key themes emerged: (i) low salience of sustainability during food purchase decisions; (ii) barriers to sustainability label use were scepticism, misinterpretation, and lack of trust due to label proliferation and lack of standardisation; and (iii) suggested approaches to labelling included the introduction of evidence-based sustainability labels endorsed by trusted organisations presented in simplified formats, with nutrition and sustainability information displayed separately. Participants reported limited engagement with sustainability labelling, often prioritising cost and healthiness. Trust and comprehension issues were commonly cited as barriers to label effectiveness. Participants viewed clear, credible and standardised labelling, presented separately from nutrition information, as potentially useful for improving consumer understanding and use of sustainability information on packaged foods.

items.title: Association Between Social Isolation and Stroke Risk among Survivors Following the Great East Japan Earthquake: A Prospective Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Evidence linking social isolation (SI) with incident stroke remains limited, especially regarding post-disaster populations and potential sex-based differences. We examined sex-based differences in the association between SI and incident stroke among Great East Japan Earthquake (GEJE) survivors. This prospective cohort study included 27,379 GEJE survivors. SI was assessed at baseline using the Lubben Social Network Scale. Incident stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic) was identified using the population-based Iwate Stroke Registry. Three sequential, sex-stratified Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for age, BMI, systolic blood pressure, HbA1c, LDL, HDL, estimated glomerular filtration rate, drinking and smoking status, exercise habit, marital status, living arrangement, educational attainment, employment status, psychological distress (K6), and housing damage. 208 men and 156 women developed stroke during follow-up (mean follow-up: 5.99 years). SI was significantly associated with an increased risk of stroke in men (HR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.06-1.92), but not in women (HR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.62-1.40; p for interaction = 0.005). The association was observed mainly for ischemic stroke in men (HR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.07-2.12). Subgroup analyses by housing damage showed a stronger association among men without direct housing damage than among men with housing damage (adjusted HR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.02-1.90 vs. 1.19; 95% CI, 0.68-1.91). In post-disaster populations, SI is significantly associated with incident stroke in men but not women. Socially isolated men in disaster-affected areas represent a priority group for public health interventions to reduce stroke risk.

items.title: "It's their house": unintended consequences of healthcare privatization in US Correctional facilities.
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to intend to examine correctional healthcare workers' different experiences and challenges in private versus public settings across the US. While quantitative research consistently demonstrates that privatized correctional healthcare produces worse health outcomes, this study sought to identify mechanisms responsible. Design/methodology/approach The author conducted semi-structured interviews with correctional healthcare workers in jails and prisons across the US in facilities with private (n = 19) and public (n = 27) healthcare. Findings Healthcare workers in correctional facilities with private healthcare reported less autonomy and authority when negotiating with custody staff and readily acquiesced to appeals of "safety and security." Additionally, the turnover of private healthcare companies resulted in administrative and policy turnover, leading to compromised ethical standards and procedures. Originality/value The study supplements quantitative research that documents higher mortality in privatized settings. By interviewing frontline healthcare workers, the study provides insight into how contracting care alters workplace dynamics above and beyond simple "cost-cutting" explanations.

items.title: Predisposition of galaxy clusters to producing exotic hyperbolic umbilic lensing configurations
items.abstract: Strong gravitational lensing is a powerful tool for investigating the universe's large-scale structure and understanding the properties of dark matter and dark energy. The magnification and distortion of distant background sources by cluster lenses have enabled detailed studies of both lens and source populations, making these systems promising probes for precision cosmology. While classical strong-lenses are well understood, much remains to be explored for hyperbolic-umbilic (HU) exotic lenses, which produce unique telescopic effects and uncommon images with potentially very high magnifications. Identifying and quantifying these objects, along with characterising their geometric configurations, could have broad implications for studies of galaxy clusters and lensed galaxy populations. z<10 ). items.title: Cosmic CORALS: Timing the Universe with high-z star clusters
items.abstract: In this work, we explore the potential of anchoring the age--redshift relation across cosmic time by probing the oldest star clusters at high redshifts, now observed thanks to the Space Telescope in strongly lensed fields. As a case study, we consider one of the highest-redshift systems observed, the Cosmic Gems arc at z=9.625. We performed image deconvolution of multi-band JWST imaging, identifying a total of 20 point sources along the arc. We derived the stellar ages through a cosmology-independent spectral energy distribution fitting framework, ensuring that these measurements can be used as unbiased cosmological anchors. By combining these high-z systems with state-of-the-art local globular cluster ages, we performed a joint Bayesian fit to the age--redshift relation in a flat Λ cold dark matter model, measuring H_0=70^ James Webb +27 _ -16 km -1 Mpc^ -1 and Ω_m=0.33^ +0.37 _ -0.21 . While these constraints are still loose, we show that the slope of the degeneracy, a power law in the Ω_m - H_0 plane, is highly dependent on the redshift of the sources, becoming shallower as redshift increases. Leveraging this geometric rotation, we present forecasts showing that a future sample of ∼ 300 lensed proto-globular clusters well distributed up to z ≈ 10 could tighten the statistical precision to 4% on H_0 and 11% on Ω_m; this is competitive with and independent of methods currently in use. The present work, therefore, represents a new avenue in cosmology and comes at a timely moment, when JWST is observing high-redshift lensed star clusters routinely and and the Space Telescope are uncovering new strong lensing fields, and close to the start of operation of the ESO Extremely Large Telescope. items.title: The X-ray catalogue of FGK stars within 10 pc: The coronal temperature-brightness relation explained with the RTV scaling law
items.abstract: A comprehensive measurement of stellar X-ray emission has important implications for our understanding of stellar dynamos, exoplanet atmosphere loss, and evaporation of protoplanetary disks. However, the samples discussed in the literature are often biased and the X-ray properties reported in published catalogues are often not homogeneously derived. We present a volume-limited catalogue of X-ray detections of the FGK-type main-sequence stars within 10,pc, which properly accounts for stellar multiplicity and considers the instrumental effect of optical loading of the X-ray detectors. The FGK,10pc sample derives from a recent Gaia -based catalogue of all stars in a sky volume of 10,pc around the Sun from which we extract all stars of spectral type F, G, and K. To build the X-ray catalogue, we retrieved and analysed all observations from SRG (Spectrum Roentgen Gamma)/eROSITA and XMM-Newton for stars in the FGK,10pc sample, and we cross-matched the sample with ROSAT catalogues. After accounting for optical loading, flares, and multiplicity, we fitted thermal plasma models to the X-ray spectra to derive X-ray fluxes and coronal temperatures. The FGK,10pc sample comprises 60 stars and has an X-ray completeness of 95%. We present a detailed investigation of the relation between coronal temperature and X-ray surface flux and we find the result to be consistent with the ranges covered by different types of coronal magnetic structures observed on the Sun. The lower end of the temperature-brightness relation is defined by the Maunder minimum star HD,166620 and three other stars whose positions identify them as possible Maunder minimum candidates. We identify systematic differences between the temperature-brightness law derived from XMM-Newton and eROSITA data that we attribute to their different instrumental response functions. For the first time, we study the impact of variability, both short-term flaring and long-term activity cycles, on the evolution of coronal temperature along with X-ray brightness. With the exception of three stars, a remarkably small scatter is observed in the temperature-brightness relation across the whole FGK,10pc sample. A natural explanation of the empirical kT-F_!̊m X relation is provided by the Rosner-Tucker-Vaiana (RTV) scaling laws defined for solar hydrostatic magnetic loops. The small spread of the observed relation indicates a universal scaling between the length and filling factor of coronal loops. Three observed outliers to the relation are stars that deviate from this invariance of the ratio of loop length to filling factor for an unknown reason.

items.title: The Pristine Survey. XXX. Mapping substructures in the inner and outer halo with blue horizontal branch stars
items.abstract: Blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars serve as good standard candles and kinematic tracers of the Milky Way halo. The halo displays various overdensities and kinematical substructures of different shapes and sizes. Our objective is to investigate the substructure in three dimensions and the bulk motion of the halo up to distances well exceeding the limit of the parallaxes. Gaia We selected BHB stars in the łeft(u-CaHK̊ight) _ 0-$(g-r) _ 0$ colour-colour diagram with a hierarchical Bayesian mixture model of three populations: BHB stars, blue straggler stars, and outliers. Using CaHK photometry derived from XP spectra and the Pristine survey, we provide both a shallow and a deep catalogue of BHB stars of 7,057 and 8,824 stars, respectively, where the deep catalogue is restricted to the deeper Pristine footprint compared to the shallower with XP. Using the shallow catalogue, we trace to larger distances 6D substructures identified earlier within a 2.5 kpc from the Sun, including accepted populations; namely, Gaia-Enceladus, Thamnos, Helmi streams, Sequoia, and other smaller halo substructures such as ED-3, ED-4, and ED-6. The deep catalogue provides reliable distance measurements for a more detailed 3D mapping of the Sagittarius stream and of the Pisces Overdensity. We add new candidate BHB stars with line-of-sight velocities to existing catalogues and confirm previously reported differences between the northern and southern Galactic hemispheres, likely due to the infall of the Large Magellanic Cloud. Gaia Gaia This research demonstrates that probabilistic photometric classification can effectively identify distant candidate BHB stars, and can provide catalogues of these stars that enhance our understanding of the 3D and 6D structures in the halo of the Milky Way.

items.title: The spatial structure of solar magnetoconvection at scales up to 60 Mm.
items.abstract: While convective motions at the scale of granules on the solar surface are well understood, those of mesogranular and supergranulation are not. At still larger scales, the lack of giant cells is a major mystery. We aim to slightly improve understanding of the radial and horizontal flows associated with mesogranular scales and supergranulation. We performed a deep MURaM small-scale dynamo simulation, extending from 50 Mm below the solar surface and with a horizontal size of 60 Mm and sufficient resolution to begin to properly resolve the magnetic bright points in intergranular lanes. We determined the structure of the convective modes from the simulations at different scales, and compared the power spectra to those which have been previously observed. At all scales that are resolved by the simulation, the simulated flows agree with the amplitude implied by Doppler measurements and local correlation tracking measurements. The power in the vertical Doppler velocities at supergranular and larger scales is shown to be affected by density perturbations near the surface. The structure of the modes at depth is simple, as expected from previous studies, except the horizontal forcing scale scales as H_̊ho^2/3 instead of H̊ho. The simulations reproduce the observations up to scales of 60 Mm. Within the simulated range, l>=70, no excess power associated with the convective conundrum is detected.

items.title: ALMA detection of continuum emission from GQ Lup B
items.abstract: GQ Lup B is a massive (10-40 M_ Jup ) companion orbiting the young T-Tauri star GQ Lup A at a projected distance of ∼110 au (0.7''). It lies outside the circumprimary disk in the submillimeter continuum , but its ∼,63^̧irc inclined orbit intersects the primary's gas disk twice per period. We report a 5.8σ detection of continuum emission at the location of GQ Lup B, obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 0.89 mm (band 7). We associate this emission with a dusty disk around the companion, already detected by VLT/NACO and JWST/MIRI in the mid-infrared. To date, this is the third disk observed at millimeter wavelengths around a companion spanning the brown dwarf and planetary mass regimes , following PDS 70 c, a gas giant embedded in the parent circumstellar disk, and SR 12 c, a planetary mass companion at 1200 au from the primary. We retrieve a point source with a peak intensity of 54.5 , co-spatial with GRAVITY astrometry. The emission is spatially unresolved, Jy, beam^ -1 placing an upper limit of 2.3 au on the source radius (from a synthesized beam of ∼,29 disks. mas). For comparison, this is smaller than 1/3 of the Hill radius (3-5 au for GQ Lup B, depending on the assumed mass), the theoretical upper limit for circumplanetary Assuming optically thin thermal emission from millimeter-sized grains in a disk-like structure , we infer a mass of 0.0032 M_⊕, while the optically thick limit yields an emission radius of 0.2 au. Assuming a gas-to-dust ratio of 100, our results indicate a very low disk-mass-to-accretion-rate ratio, on the order of sim10^4 yr, analogously to the highest accretors in the stellar mass regime. In the case of GQ Lup B, this can be explained by its periodic crossing of the circumprimary disk, which could deliver a substantial amount of gas to the companion's disk over a long timescale.

items.title: Precise deep-learning reconstruction of galaxy cluster mass maps and substructures from optical observations
items.abstract: Accurately mapping the total mass distribution within galaxy clusters, including dark matter, is fundamental to understanding structure formation and constraining cosmological parameters. Standard mass mapping relies almost exclusively on gravitational lensing, which often yields smooth distributions based on analytical profiles, thereby missing critical internal substructures. We introduce a complementary, simulation-based inference approach to reconstruct detailed galaxy cluster mass maps and resolve internal substructures directly from optical imaging. We trained deep learning models on realistic hydro-simulated galaxy clusters to interpret observed cluster images. This framework was then applied to observations of real galaxy clusters obtained by the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) as part of the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble (CLASH) program. The reconstructed mass maps successfully reproduce the overall shapes and radial mass profiles of the CLASH clusters, showing strong agreement with independent gravitational lensing measurements. Using the subhalos derived from these reconstructed maps, we find that their mass functions exhibit a power-law behavior broadly consistent with predictions from numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that combining optical imaging with deep learning provides a scalable, physically meaningful approach to mapping cluster masses. This framework opens a new avenue for utilizing upcoming wide-field imaging surveys to systematically study dark matter substructures, complementing traditional lensing techniques across much larger samples. Furthermore, the model is inherently flexible and can integrate multiwavelength data, such as X-ray and Sunyaev-Zeldovich observations, to further improve total mass predictions.

items.title: Properties of chromium and manganese in Tycho's supernova remnant with XRISM/Resolve
items.abstract: The X-ray emission of young supernova remnants (SNRs) gives access to the composition and spatial distribution of elements ejected in supernovae. The emission from the ejecta provides crucial insights into the explosion mechanism, especially for Fe-group elements formed in the innermost layers of the star. The objective of this paper is to provide constraints on the supernova progenitor and explosion mechanism of Tycho's type Ia supernova remnant by studying the properties of Cr and Mn. We analyzed /Resolve high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy observations of five regions of Tychos's supernova remnant, which were performed during the performance-verification phase and the AO1 phase. Gaussian line modeling was first used to determine the spatial distribution and intensity of Cr and Mn Kα lines. We then modeled the emission of the Cr, Mn and Fe plasma in each pointing with two nonequilibrium ionization shock models to reproduce both the front- and rear-emitting sides of the shocked ejecta shell. Mass ratios of Cr/Fe, Mn/Fe, and Mn/Cr are compared with expectations from different Type Ia supernova models from 1D and 3D numerical simulations. XRISM The unprecedented spectral resolution of /Resolve allows us to detect significant emission lines of Cr and Mn in different regions of Tycho's supernova remnant, even on small scales, providing a much more precise spatial distribution of Cr and Mn with respect to previous measurements. Significant Cr and Mn emission lines are observed in the Fe-bright northeastern-to-southeastern emitting rim; some are observed in the center region, but none in the southern region. The observed mass ratios of Mn/Fe, Cr/Fe, and Mn/Cr, are consistent with 1D delayed detonation models of near-Chandrasekhar-mass Type Ia supernovae and 1D pure-detonation models of 1 M_⊙ sub-Chandrasekhar-mass progenitors. In both cases, the observations imply supersolar zero-age main-sequence progenitor metallicities. XRISM Overall, the best agreement is found for models with metallicities too high to be realistic for Tycho's location. This points to additional sources of neutronization such as carbon simmering for a Chandrasekhar-mass progenitor. For sub-Chandrasekhar-mass, double-detonation models with a white-dwarf mass lower than 1M_⊙ are suggested.

items.title: Associations between multiple early risk factors and cognitive functioning at time of diagnosis in adolescents and adults with first-episode psychosis.
items.abstract: First-episode psychosis (FEP) is associated with widespread cognitive impairments. Several early risk factors for psychosis have been identified, and some studies suggest associations between early risk factors and cognition, yet the literature is sparse in psychosis populations. Clinical cohorts of adolescent and adult patients with FEP and healthy controls (HC) were linked with register-based information (N = 276). Gestational age, Apgar scores, birth weight and length, parental age, and season of birth were extracted from the Danish medical birth registry. Cognition was assessed at time of diagnosis using BACS, CANTAB, and WAIS-III/WISC-IV. Missing data was imputed using MICE. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) was used to examine patterns of associations. Post hoc analyses explored group differences according to diagnosis, age, and sex. CCA resulted in two significant patterns of associations. CCA1 was stable across imputations (r = 0.44, p = .036, pmin = .017, pmax = .055) and constituted by a risk profile of lower maternal age, lower birth length, being small for gestational age, and lower birth weight and a cognitive profile of lower estimated IQ and poorer working memory, mental flexibility, processing speed, verbal fluency, and motor latency. The pattern was more expressed in FEP compared to HC and in adults compared to adolescents. CCA2 was more unstable across imputations (r = 0.38, p = .033, pmin = .003, pmax = .168) and constituted by a broad pattern of minor loadings. Cognitive functioning later in life is associated with multiple early risk factors, underscoring the complexity of developmental processes and the importance of the early developmental context in shaping cognitive trajectories.

items.title: The invisible insult: replication-independent neurotoxicity of viral and bacterial factors in post-infectious neurological syndromes.
items.abstract: Post-viral neurological syndromes, including Neuro-PASC (long COVID), HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders, and flavivirus-associated encephalopathies, present a paradox: neurological dysfunction persists despite minimal or absent viral replication in the central nervous system (CNS), challenging the replication-dependent models of neuropathogenesis. This review synthesizes evidence for a "protein-as-pathogen" framework in which viral proteins, independent of intact virus or active replication, act as neurotoxic effectors: they breach the blood-brain barrier, activate neuroinflammatory cascades, induce neuronal death, and seed chronic proteinopathies. The same principle extends to bacterial factors such as lipopolysaccharide and curli, which converge on these pathways and point to a CNS vulnerability independent of pathogen class. We treat this as a complement to replication- and reservoir-based pathogenesis, not a replacement. We performed a comprehensive analysis of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (S1) as a paradigmatic case study, then extended this framework through comparative analysis of human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) gp120, flavivirus proteins (NS1, capsid, NS2A), and influenza A proteins (M1, NS1, nucleoprotein). Despite distinct viral origins and structural properties, these proteins exploit conserved host vulnerabilities. Toll-like receptor (TLR) 4 emerges as a convergent hub for microglial activation, with downstream NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome assembly amplifying neuroinflammation through interleukin (IL)-1β release. Mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by membrane depolarization, reactive oxygen species production, and impaired mitophagy, links acute protein exposure to chronic oxidative stress and proteinopathic seeding. Neuronal death pathways show virus-specific divergence: S1 induces necroptosis via NRP1/RIPK1, gp120 triggers apoptosis through CXCR4/CCR5 acting in concert with microglia-derived neurotoxins, and ZIKV envelope protein activates PARP-1-dependent parthanatos. All proteins converge on IL-1β-mediated inflammatory neuronal killing and complement-dependent synaptic elimination that persists beyond detectable viral clearance. The protein-as-pathogen framework reveals mechanistic unity across superficially disparate post-viral and post-bacterial syndromes and identifies druggable convergent pathways, including TLR4, NLRP3, complement, and mitochondrial targets, amenable to therapeutic intervention with existing compounds. This framework has direct implications for diagnosis (protein biomarkers), prognosis (determinants of protein persistence), and treatment (protein-targeted versus downstream anti-inflammatory strategies) of post-viral neurological disease.

items.title: Inequalities in quitting smoking and use of support among women by age and socioeconomic position: a population study in England.
items.abstract: Mid-life may be a particularly challenging period to quit smoking among women, especially those from less advantaged socioeconomic groups. Differences in quit attempt characteristics, use of evidence-based support, and nicotine dependence may contribute to lower quit success, but their relative importance remains unclear. We analysed data from 7,791 women in the Smoking Toolkit Study (England, 2013-2026) who attempted to stop smoking in the past year. Age was categorised as younger (16-44 years), mid-life (45-60 years), and older (> 60 years), and social grade as more (ABC1) or less advantaged (C2DE). Logistic regression models examined differences in quit attempt characteristics (planned vs. unplanned, abrupt vs. gradual), use of evidence-based support (e-cigarettes, prescription nicotine replacement therapy, non-nicotine pharmacotherapy, face-to-face behavioural support), and quit success, adjusted for survey year and relevant covariates. Mid-life women had the lowest quit success (18.1%) compared with younger (22.3%) and older women (20.6%), with the lowest quit success observed among less advantaged mid-life women (15.8% vs. 25.2% among more advantaged younger women; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 0.56, 95%CI 0.45-0.69). Yet, mid-life women were among the most likely to use evidence-based support (more advantaged: 45.8%; less advantaged: 47.4%), comparable to younger less advantaged women (46.4%) and higher than other groups (36.9-40.0%). Adjustment for quit attempt characteristics and use of evidence-based support had minimal impact on age-related differences in quit success. However, adjustment for nicotine dependence attenuated the lower odds of success in mid-life women. In fully adjusted models with younger more advantaged women as the reference category, less advantaged mid-life women had the lowest odds of quitting (aOR = 0.75, 95%CI 0.58-0.98), older more advantaged women had higher odds (aOR = 1.36, 95%CI 1.02-1.82), and differences for other groups were not evident (aORs 0.93-1.16). Less advantaged mid-life women are the least likely to be successful in their attempts to stop smoking, despite relatively high uptake of evidence-based support. Higher nicotine dependence partly explains this disparity, but other factors also likely contribute and warrant further investigation.

items.title: Consciousness, complexity, and clinical implications.
items.abstract: Consciousness remains one of science's most challenging problems because it cannot be exhaustively characterized as a single function, computation, or behavior; it also refers to the presence and organization of subjective experience. This position paper integrates clinical neurology, neurophysiology, psychiatry, psychoanalysis, embodied cognition, moral neuroscience, theoretical physics, philosophy of mind, and neurotechnology. We argue that, despite major advances in identifying neural correlates, computational models, and behavioral markers, contemporary consciousness research has not resolved the explanatory gap between objective description and subjective experience. We propose that claims about consciousness at neurophysiological, embodied, cognitive, social, and ontological levels should be coordinated through explicit cross-level constraints rather than merged into a single unitary theory. These domains have different evidential roles and are not all constituents of consciousness. Perturbational measures of cortical complexity, including the Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) and its state-transition variant (PCIst), support assessment of preserved conscious capacity in studied human populations. They do not independently determine a clinical diagnosis or phenomenal content. Evidence from aphasia, sleep, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness also demonstrates dissociations among language, wakefulness, behavioral responsiveness, and conscious experience. Perspectives from embodied simulation, mind-object identity, quantum information, and the philosophy of physics are treated here as heuristic stress tests rather than as mechanistic accounts; they keep open foundational questions concerning subjectivity, representation, and the role of the observer. We advocate constrained pluralism, a methodological framework in which consciousness is conceptualized as an integrated, embodied, relational, and temporally extended process. Such an approach provides a coherent foundation for future research while strengthening the dialogue between neuroscience, clinical practice, philosophy, and neuroethics.

items.title: MoCA deficits and white matter in Huntington's disease.
items.abstract: This study explored the relationship between the Montreal Cognitive Assessment's (MoCA) subdomains and white matter changes in Huntington's disease (HD). Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) were measured using Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) in 22 early-stage symptomatic HD patients and 20 healthy controls. Tract-Based Spatial Statistics was used to compare the two groups and to correlate patients' FA and MD values with their performance on MoCA subdomains. Among all MoCA subdomains, only visuospatial performance was associated with white matter integrity in the corpus callosum, corona radiata, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, supporting the utility of identifying regional imaging correlates of specific cognitive performance through the combination of DTI analysis and brief screening tools in early-stage patients.

items.title: ACC hyperactivity and synaptic remodeling underlie sensory hypersensitivity in Adnp-haploinsufficient mice.
items.abstract: Pathogenic variants in the transcriptional regulator ADNP cause a frequent autism syndrome marked by pronounced tactile and pain hypersensitivity, yet the responsible cortical circuits are poorly defined. Here we show that Adnp-haploinsufficient (Adnp-HT) mice exhibit mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity together with enhanced shock-related defensive responding. Caudal conditional Adnp deletion did not reproduce these phenotypes, arguing against a dominant peripheral or spinal contribution. c-Fos mapping and ultrahigh-field fMRI revealed stimulus-evoked hyperresponsiveness across a distributed sensory-affective network that included the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and recordings from naive mice identified increased intrinsic excitability and altered synaptic transmission in ACC pyramidal neurons. Global chemogenetic inhibition of ACC excitatory neurons only partially normalized mechanical and paw-heat hypersensitivity but increased shock-related freezing, whereas inhibition of electric-foot-shock-activated (FosTRAP2) ACC ensembles normalized mechanical and paw-heat responses and attenuated baseline and early shock-related freezing. Multiomic profiling, MERFISH, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing converged on synaptic and ion-channel programs in layer 2/3 and layer 5 excitatory neurons. These results identify the ACC as a major, but not exclusive, cortical contributor within a broader network and support cell-type- and ensemble-resolved approaches to ADNP-linked sensory abnormalities.

items.title: Untangling the motives for avoiding contraception among women who underwent elective termination of pregnancy in Belgrade (Serbia).
items.abstract: Unwanted pregnancies and induced abortions are the key health issues in Serbia. Empirical evidence suggests that the use of widely accessible contraception methods among Serbian women is low. The purpose of this study was to investigate the reasons for not using contraception as well as factors that might impact those reasons among women who have had an induced abortion. Women who sought abortion at the Clinic for Obstetrics and Gynaecology, University Clinical Center of Serbia from 2022 to 2024 were enrolled in this cross-sectional study. They responded to an anonymous questionnaire examining their demographic data, lifestyle and habits, medical history, and reasons for not using contraceptives prior to this pregnancy. Responses of 433 women aged 16 to 49 years (mean age 32.0 ± 6.7 years) were analysed. The most common reasons for avoiding contraception were being afraid to take hormones (22.6%) and not knowing how to count the cycle days (22.4%). Majority of women (28.4%) had multiple reasons not to use contraception while 28.2% could not specify the reason. Being afraid of hormonal contraception was associated with having recurrent abortions. Belonging to national minorities and having chronic illnesses was associated with not knowing how to count the cycle days. The fact that women did not use contraception because it is expensive was associated with having lower salary and vigorous physical activity intensity at work. Being bothered to take the contraception regularly was associated with being an atheist and having gynaecological illnesses. Women who thought that they could not get pregnant easily were more likely from national minorities, not married or partnered and had previous Caesarean Sections. It is of paramount importance to improve counselling on contraception throughout the reproductive period to optimise family planning for Serbian women.

items.title: Endophytic fungi shape tree epigenomes and enhance thermotolerance under climate warming.
items.abstract: Background Rising global temperatures threaten the survival and regeneration of temperate and boreal forests. Yet how microbial symbioses contribute to tree heat-resilience remains unclear. Results Here, we integrated field ecological surveys with controlled multi-omics analyses and found that soil fungal diversity declined, accompanied by enrichment of potentially beneficial taxa along regional variation in max temperature of the warmest month (BIO5). Inoculation with representative endophytes significantly promoted birch (Betula platyphylla) growth and photosynthetic performance under non-stress conditions. Furthermore, endophytic fungi enhance thermal tolerance in birch by establishing a transcriptional chromatin state at heat-responsive genes that facilitates their activation under heat stress. Integrative network analyses identified regulatory networks linking fungal symbiosis to thermotolerance pathways. Conclusion These findings connect macroecological patterns to molecular mechanisms, uncovering an epigenetic basis for microbe-mediated heat adaptation in trees and highlighting symbiotic fungi as both key partners and practical means to strengthen forest resilience under climate warming. items.title: Assessment of phenotypic variability of F 1 hybrids of winter rapeseed and their parental forms using multivariate statistical methods.
items.abstract: The effect of genotype, environment (year) and their interaction is one of the main target in breeding programs and play important role in the final expression of quality traits and seed yield of winter oilseed rape. In this study, phenotypic traits, yield and yield components and also biochemical traits of 72 hybrids and their parental forms were investigated. Plant material were tested in the field experiments in a randomized complete block design with three replications during two growing seasons. Field observations were recorded on beginning and length of flowering, seed yield and its structure: the number of branches and siliques per plant, the silique length, the number of seeds per silique, the thousand seed weight and biochemical traits: oil content, saturated (palmitic, stearic) and unsaturated fatty acids (oleic, linoleic, linolenic) and eicosenic acid in the seed oil and glucosinolates (GLS) content (alkenyl, indolyl, total glucosinolates and total alkenyl GLS content), protein and fibre (ADF, NDF) content (26 traits). The use of multivariate statistical methods allowed for the simultaneous characterization and grouping of tested genotypes in terms of 26 traits. Two-way multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) revealed significant effects of both genotype (G) and environment (E-year) as well as the G×E interaction regarding all analyzed traits, except oleic acid and indolyl glucosinolate content. Graphic images of the distribution of hybrids and their parental forms in the space of the two canonical variates showed a great variation between the plant materials, both in terms of yield, structure of yield as well as oil content and all biochemical traits.

items.title: Prenatal smoking exposure and postnatal affluence: a developmental mismatch associated with adiposity among children and adolescents.
items.abstract: The developmental origins of health and disease framework posits that a mismatch between prenatal and postnatal environments may lead to maladaptation such as increased obesity risk. This study examined whether exposure to maternal smoking during pregnancy followed by an affluent postnatal environment was associated with adiposity and whether this exposure context modified the association between protein intake and adiposity. Analyses included 12,660 children and adolescents (1,727 exposed and 10,933 unexposed to maternal smoking during pregnancy) aged 6-15 years from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2003-2018. Body roundness index (BRI) was used as an anthropometric indicator of adiposity, and the protein-to-energy ratio (PER) was derived from dietary recalls. Among children from low-income and high-income families, those exposed to maternal smoking had higher BRI than those unexposed, whereas no significant difference was observed among children from middle-income families. The association between the PER and BRI also differed across combined smoking exposure-income groups. The exposed/high-income group showed the largest positive association between the PER and BRI (b = 10.74, p = 0.008), which was significantly stronger than that in the unexposed/high-income group (Holm-adjusted p = 0.031). These findings suggest that the association between prenatal smoking exposure and adiposity varies nonlinearly across postnatal family socioeconomic contexts. Children exposed to prenatal smoking and living in high-income families showed a particularly strong association between dietary protein and adiposity.

items.title: Front-of-package warning labels and fruit and vegetable consumption: a difference-in-differences analysis in Mexico and the United States.
items.abstract: In 2020, Mexico implemented front-of-package warning labels (FoPWL) to identify packaged foods high in critical nutrients. Evidence suggests indirect dietary benefits following implementation; however, potential effects on fruits and vegetables (FV) consumption remain understudied. This study assessed trends in consumption and efforts to increase FV intake in Mexico before and after FoPWL implementation, against trends in the United States (U.S.), where no comparable policy was introduced. Secondary analysis of five waves (2018-2022) from the International Food Policy Study, a repeat cross-sectional online survey of adults (18-100 years), using a difference-in-differences design. Self-reported daily FV consumption and efforts to eat more FV were compared across countries and policy periods: initial (2019-2020), early (2019-2021) and full (2019-2022), relative to the pre-policy period (2018-2019). Mexico and the U.S. Respondents (Mexico: 16 509; U.S.: 15 290) were recruited through the Nielsen Consumer Insights Global Panel. Compared to the pre-policy trend, Mexico FV consumption increased across all post-policy periods, with greater increases than the U.S. during early implementation (adjusted rate ratios (aRR) = 1·38, 95 % CI:1·11-1·71). By the full implementation period, FV intake had increased in both countries (Mexico: aRR = 1·53, 95 % CI: 1·21-1·93; U.S.: aRR = 1·29, 95 % CI: 1·07-1·55). Efforts to eat more FV remained stable in Mexico but declined in the U.S. by the full implementation period (aOR = 1·07, 95 % CI: 1·02-1·12). FV intake increased in Mexico following FoPWL implementation; concurrent increases in the U.S. suggest that broader contextual factors, in addition to FoPWL, likely contributed to these changes.

items.title: AI-assisted development of a rule-based pipeline for pre-examination screening in clinical neuropsychology: An exploratory method-development study.
items.abstract: We present an exploratory, method-development study of a framework for rule-based pre-examination screening. The study is exploratory: no clinical endpoint, success threshold, or control condition was pre-specified. Demonstrated on retrospectively analyzed irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) data, the pipeline produces a structured analysis with cross-domain pattern detection and audience-tailored reports. A large language model was used as a coding assistant to draft scoring logic, cross-domain rules, and Python code. The deployed pipeline executes these fixed rules deterministically; no model inference occurs when patient data are processed. The pipeline processes five instruments (Bergen Insomnia Scale, Conners' Continuous Performance Test, Chalder Fatigue Scale, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status). For each patient, it generates an eight-step processing sequence, visualizations, and clinician-gated reports. Analyses used data from 105 adults (65 IBS, 40 controls) from the Bergen Brain-Gut-Microbiota study. The tool flagged findings above threshold in sleep (50%), fatigue (40%), anxiety (35%), and attention (30%), with multi-domain flags in 60%. Cross-domain rules linked co-occurring findings to candidate mechanisms drawn from published literature. Two case illustrations demonstrated the rule-based summaries alongside clinician interpretation that went beyond the rules. The framework is a transparent support tool rather than an autonomous reasoning system: every output traces to a stated rule, and the contribution of artificial intelligence lies in development, not deployment: it augments rather than replaces clinical judgment. Because the analysis is exploratory and single-cohort, the findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective, comparative validation.

items.title: Primary Language as a sociocultural predictor of cognitive dispersion: Cross-racial/ethnic findings from the HABS-HD study.
items.abstract: Research on cognitive test score dispersion and Alzheimer's Disease-related cognitive impairment has been conducted predominantly among Non-Hispanic White (NHW) samples. This study examined (1) baseline dispersion differences across Non-Hispanic Blacks (NHBs), Mexican Americans (MAs), and NHW older adults and cognitive status after controlling for age, sex, education, primary language, and MMSE and (2) primary language as an independent predictor of cognitive dispersion within the MA subsample. Participants from the Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities study (HABS-HD; N = 4,140; Mage = 65.08 years, SD = 8.66; 61.52% female, 29.37% NHB, 36.18% MA, and 34.44% NHW) underwent test administration in their primary language (English/Spanish). Cognitive status showed a large, significant main effect on dispersion (CN < MCI ≈ Dementia; partial η2 = .144), consistent across all three racial/ethnic groups (EthnicityxCognitive Status interaction p = .113), with a non-significant main effect of ethnicity (p = .135). There was a significant main effect of primary language on dispersion (p < .001, η2 = .01), with Spanish-speaking MAs demonstrating uniquely elevated ISD compared to NHWs, NHBs, and English-speaking MAs (p < .001). The language effect persisted across progressively conservative covariate specifications and strengthened on residualized ISD. Normative sensitivity analysis restricting comparisons to English-speaking MAs and NHWs found that English-speaking MAs still showed significantly higher ISD than NHWs, with the effect strengthening on residualized ISD (p-values = < .001-.006). These findings support ISD as a marker of cognitive impairment and identify primary language as a novel, independent sociocultural predictor of dispersion.

items.title: Thriving in training: a mixed-methods acceptability and feasibility study of a tailored acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) intervention to support trainee psychological professional wellbeing.
items.abstract: The wellbeing of psychological therapy trainees (PTTs) has important implications for practitioner mental health, clinical effectiveness, and service delivery. This study was designed to assess the acceptability and feasibility of a tailored acceptance and commitment therapy wellbeing intervention for PTTs. The intervention was co-constructed with trainees, and designed to fill gaps in the literature by detailing a clear theory of change, and approaching wellbeing in trainees in a theoretically informed manner. A convergent-parallel, mixed-methods approach was used. Quantitative data on recruitment, retention and data completion were considered alongside qualitative data from post-intervention interviews. To explore preliminary evidence of clinical utility, standardised measures of psychological flexibility, stress, psychological distress, wellbeing and resilience were completed at three time points. Reliable change scores were calculated and effect sizes estimated. The intervention was highly acceptable to trainees. Pre-determined benchmarks of feasibility were partially met. Recruitment was strong (63 starters over 2-month period) and retention was satisfactory (79%). Data collection fell below required thresholds (52.7% at T2 and 29.7% at T3). Tentative evidence was identified that this intervention may be useful in this population and setting, and that it may work through theorised pathways of change (supporting wellbeing through increasing psychological flexibility). The intervention was found to be highly acceptable to trainees, and feasible to deliver in the setting of a UK university. Progression to further pilot testing to assess the feasibility of randomisation to different treatment arms is supported. Important learning was generated here to support the design of such testing.
