items.title: Measuring the behavioural manifestations of generalised anxiety in adolescents: applying network psychometrics to the Worry Behaviors Inventory.
items.abstract: Research into Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) has historically focused on its cognitive and somatic elements, whilst behavioural manifestations have been overlooked. The development of the Worry Behaviors Inventory (WBI; Mahoney et al., 2016) addressed this gap, but this scale has not yet been validated for use with adolescents. This study evaluated the WBI's psychometric properties in a community population of 13- to 18-year-olds. Four hundred and forty-five young people completed the WBI. Data were randomly split into two samples; exploratory graph analysis (EGA) was applied to the first, and the emergent structure was subsequently confirmed with factor analysis (CFA). Convergent and divergent validity, measurement invariance across gender and age, and the sensitivity and specificity of the WBI in distinguishing low and moderate/severe generalised anxiety, were assessed. EGA identified a uni-dimensional structure with high consistency, and this was partly supported by CFA. However, pre-registered exploratory analyses revealed that the two-factor structure of the WBI (i.e. the original model identified in adult populations), also provided good fit to the data. Convergent validity was demonstrated, whilst evidence for divergent validity and measurement invariance was mixed. This study established the psychometric properties of the WBI with adolescents, providing empirical support for both uni- and correlated two-factor models. Implications for theory, practice, and further research are discussed - in particular, the scope for co-developing an adapted version of the WBI with input from young people with lived experience, which better aligns with the unique psychosocial context of adolescence.

items.title: Where to start? Impact of module ordering in acceptance and commitment therapy for young adults experiencing paranoia and low mood.
items.abstract: Paranoia is common in young adults and often occurs alongside low mood. Brief transdiagnostic interventions may therefore be useful for students who do not meet criteria for specialist psychosis services but experience distressing suspicious thoughts. This single-case experimental study evaluated a six-session Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) intervention and explored whether the order of ACT modules differentially impacted therapy effects. Ten UK university students aged 18-25 with elevated paranoia and mild to moderate depressive symptoms completed daily visual analogue measures of paranoia, affect and ACT processes during baseline, intervention and 2-week follow-up. Participants were randomised to receive either ACT-ENGAGE sessions first (values and committed action) followed by ACT-OPEN sessions (mindfulness, defusion and acceptance), or the reverse order. Standardised measures of paranoia, mood and psychological flexibility were completed at baseline, pre-intervention, post-intervention and follow-up. Daily data showed significant reductions in state paranoia, negative affect and improvements in openness and valued action for the ACT-ENGAGE-first condition only. Standardised paranoia scores improved reliably in both conditions, while depression improved more clearly in the ACT-ENGAGE-first condition. Findings provide preliminary evidence that a brief ACT intervention may benefit students experiencing paranoia and low mood, and suggest that beginning with values and committed action may strengthen clinical impact.

items.title: A pilot single-case experimental evaluation of virtual reality-integrated work-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for patients experiencing burnout.
items.abstract: Burnout is a major cause of long-term sickness absence. Work-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (W-CBT) is a promising approach, but in vivo workplace exposure is difficult to arrange during sick leave, leaving few preparatory options before gradual work resumption. This pilot study evaluated the preliminary effectiveness of a 9-session W-CBT protocol integrating graded virtual reality (VR) exposures to interpersonal return to work (RTW) challenges, for workers on sick leave due to burnout. In a single-case experimental design (A-B-A), four participants (two women, two men; mean age = 49.5 years, range 40-56; mean sick-leave duration = 7.5 months) completed a 9-session intervention combining psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, behavioural activation, and VR exposures (sessions 2-8) with in vivo assignments. Outcomes were assessed at 14 time points and analysed through visual inspection and non-overlap (Tau-U) indices benchmarked against Parker et al. (2011). Responses were heterogeneous. Three participants showed visible improvements in RTW self-efficacy, expectations and confidence communicating with managers and colleagues during the intervention, with Tau-U values in the medium-to-strong range for most primary outcomes; gains were partially maintained at follow-up. RTW-related anxiety fluctuated and re-elevated in two participants. The fourth participant showed smaller, partial changes and no burnout reduction. Secondary outcomes (distress, negative affect, and ruminations) improved for three participants but were largely stable for the fourth. Attrition was 20%; no adverse events occurred. VR-integrated W-CBT may support RTW readiness for a subset of patients; findings are preliminary. Larger trials are needed to identify who benefits most.

items.title: Revisiting Atkinson-Shiffrin: A Neural-Cognitive Framework for Working Memory.
items.abstract: Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) is widely misconstrued as a fixed boxes-and-arrows model, yet it offered a flexible framework for formal memory theories. We update that framework to clarify today's fragmented working-memory field. First, linking to Complementary Learning Systems, recent durable (long-term) storage corresponds to pattern-separated hippocampal indexing supporting gradual cortical learning, whereas transient (short-term) storage reflects overlapping cortical codes supporting rapid comparison and integration without requiring hippocampal retrieval. Second, like long-term memory, working memory involves cue-dependent retrieval. Capacity limits arise from interference among overlapping cortical representations. Third, background modeling processes operate continuously without goal-directed retrieval, shaping perception, encoding, and retrieval. Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) ranks among the most cited papers in memory research, yet it is widely misconstrued as a fixed boxes-and-arrows model with three structural components—a sensory register, short-term store (STS), and long-term store (LTS)—plus control processes. In fact, the chapter offered a general framework for formal, testable models. We argue that an updated version of this long-misunderstood framework can lend coherence to today’s fragmented working-memory literature. Linking Atkinson–Shiffrin to Complementary Learning Systems (CLS), we suggest that LTS encompasses both rapidly formed, pattern-separated episodic codes in the hippocampal system and the consolidated neocortical representations they gradually help shape. By contrast, STS corresponds to transient, overlapping cortical codes that support immediate task-relevant comparison and integration without requiring hippocampal retrieval but are highly vulnerable to interference. Thus, the STS–LTS distinction reflects differences in neural coding and hippocampal involvement, not elapsed time or separate stores. This linkage also implies that working memory is not a unitary mechanism. Working-memory tasks tap cortical and hippocampal coding to varying degrees, with the label applied mainly to tasks depending on overlapping cortical codes (i.e., STS). Interference models and temporal-context models from cognitive science converge on this view. Capacity limits arise because overlapping cortical codes create representational interference (reducing fidelity) and retrieval competition (reducing accessibility). On this account, both STS and LTS involve cue-dependent retrieval that reinstates stored representations. Finally, background modeling processes—priors, schemas, and predictive inferences—continuously shape encoding, retrieval, and consolidation without goal-directed control or retrieval of a specific memory.

items.title: Human appearance preferences as emergent properties of generalised learning.
items.abstract: The tendency to find some individuals or personal features more visually or aesthetically appealing than others (appearance preferences) is a widespread human experience. The underlying causes of why some people or features in particular are considered attractive has been variably conceptualised as being the product of cultural power structures, a by-product of broader cognitive processes, and a reflection of 'innate' appearance preferences and processes shaped by sexual selection. Evolutionary-adaptationist and cognitive processing perspectives both prompted the development of a large literature attempting to understand why some specific traits are considered attractive. More recently, however, questions have emerged regarding the validity of the proposed 'adaptive' benefits of some of these traits within an evolutionary framework. Simultaneously, cross-cultural research has demonstrated that while some underlying cognitive processes may be similar across populations, specific appearance preferences are more variable than some 'functional' adaptationist hypotheses predict. The current paper outlines what key challenges exist for an approach to appearance preferences that focuses on specific functional mating adaptations, and how cognitive and cultural processes may provide a more robust explanation of current cross- and intra-cultural data without a requirement for sexual selection to have played a role. It then argues that a large portion of human appearance preferences - including those previously thought to be human universals - may in fact be a by-product of broader perceptual and learning processes interacting with cultural-evolutionary feedback. Finally, new predictions, and remaining challenges to this integrated cognitive-cultural model, are put forward for further consideration.

items.title: Exercise to Enhance Mitophagy in Parkinson's Disease - A Narrative Review.
items.abstract: Mitophagy is a central mechanism in mitochondrial quality control and essential for neuronal health. It is impaired in Parkinson's disease (PD) and mutations of a number of genes associated with mitophagy cause familial PD. Recent advances in the development of novel treatment strategies for PD include phase I clinical trials for selective mitophagy enhancers. Next to pharmacological approaches, specific lifestyles, such as regular physical exercise, can promote mitophagy and thereby mitochondrial health and may be safer than pharmacological approaches and associated with many other health benefits. Here we explore, whether the well-known benefits of exercise for PD brain may be mediated by improved mitophagy. We put the potential benefits of mitophagy in the context of other exercise-induced, brain-health promoting mechanisms with relevance for PD and summarize the available literature investigating the role of mitophagy in therapeutic effects of exercise in models of PD. While the potential of exercise to promote mitophagy and brain health is well established, little direct evidence exists that implicates mitophagy as mediator of beneficial effects of exercise on PD symptoms and progression. Based on the identified knowledge gaps, we reflect on how this interaction may be studied in the future.

items.title: Study design to assess women's and children's mortality and child health 13-15 years after exposure to a successful community-based participatory women's group intervention in rural Bangladesh.
items.abstract: Between 2009 and 2011, a cluster-randomised trial of a Participatory Women's Groups (PWGs) intervention using Participatory Learning and Action (PLA) significantly reduced neonatal mortality. A follow-up in 2013 revealed growth differences in surviving children from highly exposed mothers in intervention groups compared to those from control. Currently, the long-term association between PWG interventions and survival of children, their mothers and younger siblings, as well as broader child health outcomes, remains largely unexplored. We describe the design of a 2024 study following up 18,940 eligible women whose pregnancies were registered during our 2009-2011 trial and their 18,107 liveborn children born within this timeframe. We gathered women's survival status and reproductive history since the intervention ended, including the number of subsequent births and the survival status of these children. For children who were alive at 4 weeks as per the 2009-2011 trial records, we recorded current survival status. For those who died after the age of 4 weeks up to the present survey, we used verbal autopsy to identify probable cause of death. Moreover, nested within our larger follow-up sample, we conducted a cross-sectional survey of growth and health outcomes in a sample of 3,835 children born during the 2009-2011 trial across intervention and control clusters. Intention-to-treat analyses will compare survival between trial arms according to original allocation. Analysis of growth and health outcomes will involve two separate comparisons: children in the high-exposure group versus those in the unexposed group and children in the variable-exposure group versus those in the unexposed group.

items.title: Rethinking global health partnerships for the post‑2030 in Timor‑Leste.
items.abstract: Global health partnerships have contributed significantly to health-system development in low- and middle-income countries, yet more partnerships do not necessarily translate into sustainable health-system resilience. This commentary discusses this tension through the concept of partnership density, defined as the concentration and interaction of multiple external partners, financing streams, programmes, technical-assistance arrangements and implementation structures within a national health system. Using Timor-Leste as an illustrative case and drawing on published evidence, policy assessments, and contextual experience, we discuss how partnership density can create opportunities for health-system strengthening while also posing risks of fragmentation, institutional substitution, financing dependence, and inequities in knowledge production. The analysis is situated within contemporary debates on country ownership, decolonising global health and the Lusaka Agenda, including its emphasis on health-system strengthening, sustainable financing, equity, coherence and locally relevant knowledge and innovation. Drawing on scholarship on institutional agency and epistemic equity, including the work of Abimbola and others, we propose four principles for governing partnership-dense health systems: locally led governance and shared decision-making; integrated health-system strengthening; equitable knowledge production; and predictable, flexible and sustainable financing. Timor-Leste illustrates both the substantial gains that sustained partnerships can support and the unfinished institutional agenda that remains. We propose that the post-2030 global health architecture should move beyond counting partnerships or measuring individual programme performance towards assessing whether the collective partnership portfolio strengthens national institutions, reduces transaction costs and builds durable capacity.

items.title: Internship Experience Is Associated With More Positive Implicit but Not Explicit Attitudes Toward Older Adults Among Gerontology Students.
items.abstract: ObjectivesTo examine whether explicit and implicit attitudes toward older adults are dissociated among undergraduate gerontology students, and whether these attitudes differ between students with and without supervised internship experience.MethodsCross-sectional, between-groups survey of 94 undergraduate gerontology students at one public university in Türkiye (mean [M] age = 22.06 years, standard deviation [SD] = 2.38; 56.4% female), February-May 2025. Explicit attitudes were measured with Kogan's Attitude toward Older People Scale (KAOPS), implicit attitudes with a Single-Category Implicit Association Test (SC-IAT) D-score. Students without internship experience (n = 46) were compared with final-year students who had completed the 14-week internship (n = 48), using t-tests (Bonferroni α = .0042) and multivariable linear regression.ResultsExplicit attitudes were well above the scale midpoint (M = 134.19, SD = 15.29; t(93) = 9.63, p < .001), whereas implicit attitudes were neutral (D = -0.04, SD = 0.42), and the two were uncorrelated (r = .20). Explicit attitudes did not differ by internship experience (t(92) = 0.67, p = .50); implicit attitudes did (t(92) = 5.35, p < .001, d = 1.10). Internship experience remained associated with implicit attitudes after adjustment (B = 0.31, 95% CI [0.16, 0.47], p < .001; R2 = .51), whereas the explicit model was null.ConclusionConsciously endorsed positive attitudes operated independently of automatic associations. Students with placement experience showed more positive implicit attitudes, but internship status was fully confounded with academic year and age, so the difference cannot be attributed to the internship itself. The findings are preliminary and require longitudinal confirmation.

items.title: Integrating bioethnography into sleep research: generating better measures, hypotheses, and interpretations.
items.abstract: Sleep research increasingly uses actigraphy, biomarkers, and structured surveys to quantify sleep duration and quality across populations. Yet researchers often interpret these measures without sufficient attention to the social, relational, and structural contexts surrounding sleep. This report presents bioethnography as a complementary methodological approach integrating sustained ethnographic engagement with epidemiological research. The report situates bioethnography alongside developmental-cultural, social-ecological, biocultural, and clinically oriented ecological approaches to sleep and identifies bioethnography's specific contribution: an iterative research architecture allowing ethnographic findings to reshape hypotheses, measurements, analyses, and interpretations of biological data. Drawing on a bioethnographic study of sleep among midlife women enrolled in a long-standing cohort in Mexico City, the report demonstrates how open-ended inquiry generates new hypotheses, reveals unmeasured social processes shaping sleep, and refines the interpretation of quantitative sleep metrics. By situating biological data within lived experience, bioethnography produces 'better numbers': more valid, interpretable findings responsive to population-specific realities. The report discusses the approach's strengths and limitations and outlines practical strategies for integrating bioethnography into sleep research. Bioethnography does not replace established ecological or biosocial frameworks; rather, the approach offers a way to operationalize a shared commitment to understanding sleep as a biological process embedded in social life.

items.title: Building and Sustaining the Disease Intervention Workforce: A Rapid Scoping Review-Informed Framework.
items.abstract: The disease intervention (DI) workforce is essential for preventing and controlling infectious diseases, yet variability in roles and training hampers workforce stability and effectiveness. Certification may help standardize competencies, but its implementation requires understanding workforce barriers, benefits, and feasible solutions. This project aimed to identify factors that influence DI workforce certification and develop a framework to inform certification pathways. We conducted a rapid scoping review following an a priori protocol and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. We searched PubMed, MEDLINE Complete, Scopus, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar for US-based sources published during 2014-2025. Two independent reviewers screened records and extracted data using pilot-tested tools; disagreements were resolved through consensus, with a third reviewer consulted as needed. We inductively coded benefits, barriers, and solutions; mapped them to Public Health Accreditation Board certification objectives; and refined themes by consensus into a multidomain framework. Thirty-five sources met the inclusion criteria. Analysis identified benefits (n = 37), barriers (n = 40), and solutions (n = 27) distributed across organizational, workforce, and community domains. Benefits aligned with standardized competencies, stronger career pathways, and enhanced service capacity. Barriers included workforce shortages, limited training infrastructure, inconsistent expectations, and challenges in meeting broad community needs. Solutions emphasized academic-practice partnerships, regionally adaptable training, employer support, and strategies to improve workforce stability and preparedness. The findings highlight multiple determinants that may shape DI workforce certification. The resulting framework offers an initial structure for guiding certification standards and strategies to strengthen and sustain a DI workforce that is prepared for current and future infectious disease threats.

items.title: Use of X (Twitter) by Official Institutions in Disaster Risk Communication: The Case of Kahramanmaraş, Hatay, and Adıyaman Provinces.
items.abstract: This study aimed to examine the thematic distribution of disaster risk communication posts shared by selected official institutions on X (Twitter) in Kahramanmaraş, Hatay, and Adıyaman following the February 6, 2023 earthquakes. A descriptive quantitative content analysis of 905 disaster-related posts published between February 6, 2023, and March 21, 2025, was conducted. Publicly accessible posts from purposively selected official institutional accounts were manually screened and classified by dominant communicative purpose. Frequencies and percentages were used to summarize the 4 reported themes and their distribution across provinces. Kahramanmaraş and Hatay each accounted for 310 posts (34.3%), and Adıyaman for 285 (31.5%). Information provision accounted for 330 posts (36.5%), aid coordination for 290 (32.0%), psychosocial support for 145 (16.0%), and combating disinformation for 140 (15.5%). Information provision was most frequent in Kahramanmaraş (40.3%) and Hatay (35.5%), whereas aid coordination was most frequent in Adıyaman (36.8%). Information provision and aid coordination predominated in the examined posts. Province-level thematic patterns differed descriptively, but the findings do not establish communication effectiveness or audience response.

items.title: Clinical implications of changes in taste and smell in older people.
items.abstract: Malnutrition in older people is a significant but often hidden public health issue associated with multimorbidity, frailty and increased healthcare use. Changes in taste and smell experienced by older people can reduce their enjoyment of food, appetite and oral intake, thereby affecting their nutritional status and functional ability. Changes in taste and smell become more common with age and can be caused by normal physiological processes associated with ageing, but also by certain health conditions, medicines and treatments. This article outlines the importance of early recognition and management of taste and smell changes as part of routine nutritional care for older people. Effective care should involve clinical assessment and history taking, nutritional screening and person-centred enquiry about appetite, food preferences, oral health, swallowing, mood and social circumstances. According to each patient's presentation and needs, this should be followed by an individualised care plan prioritising food-first strategies, treatment of reversible causes and multidisciplinary and specialist support as needed.

items.title: HspBp1 Promotes Tau Pathology and Cognitive Impairments by Inhibiting STUB1(CHIP)-Mediated Tau Ubiquitination.
items.abstract: Tau pathology is a core neuropathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), increasing evidence indicates that disruption of protein quality control contributes to Tau accumulation. However, the upstream modulators that impair Tau clearance are poorly defined. Heat shock protein 70-binding protein 1 (HspBp1), a co-chaperone of the E3 ubiquitin ligase STUB1 (CHIP), has been implicated in proteostasis regulation, but its role in Tau pathology remains unknown. We found that HspBp1 was selectively expressed in hippocampal neurons and markedly upregulated in the hippocampus of aged AD mice. Neuron-specific overexpression of HspBp1 exacerbated Tau and Tau hyperphosphorylation, synaptic and dendritic degeneration and cognitive impairments, whereas HspBp1 downregulation significantly attenuated Tau-induced neuropathology and cognitive deficits. Mechanistically, HspBp1 reduced STUB1 levels and disrupted STUB1-Tau interactions, leading to decreased Tau ubiquitination and impaired proteasomal degradation. Consequently, Tau accumulated and underwent pathological hyperphosphorylation. Importantly, restoration of STUB1 expression largely abolished HspBp1-induced Tau accumulation, synaptic dysfunction and cognitive deficits. Meanwhile, upregulation of STUB1 improves Tau pathology and cognitive impairments in P301S mice. These findings support HspBp1 as an age-associated modulator that promotes Tau pathology by suppressing STUB1-mediated Tau ubiquitination and degradation. Targeting the HspBp1-STUB1 axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for AD.

items.title: From Emerging Vectors to Missed Fevers: Why Fragile Health Systems Need Integrated Fever-Vector Preparedness.
items.abstract: Climate change, urbanization, population mobility, and expanding mosquito vectors are reshaping infectious-disease risks in fragile health systems, where surveillance, diagnosis, and response often remain fragmented. This Policy Analysis argues that preparedness should move beyond isolated pathogen- or vector-specific programs toward an integrated fever-vector model. Undifferentiated fever should serve as the clinical entry point linking environmental intelligence, entomological surveillance, sentinel fever surveillance, tiered laboratory testing, and public health response. Such integration could improve recognition of arboviral infections overlooked in malaria-centered systems, support earlier outbreak detection, and guide targeted vector control and diagnostic preparedness. Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa illustrate the urgency of this shift because climate shocks, displacement, weak laboratory systems, and emerging urban vector-borne risks increasingly converge. The priority is not a more technologically complex system, but a connected and sustainable preparedness architecture capable of linking emerging vectors with febrile illnesses presenting in routine care.

For the purposes of this special issue, we again brought together a panel of experts to discuss the contemporary financialisation of healthcare in the United States, its consequences for practitioners and policymakers, and possible courses of action to safeguard the public good. items.title: Spatial trends in multiple micronutrient supplementation effects on low birth weight and infant wasting in rural Bangladesh: a secondary geospatial analysis of the JiVitA-3 randomised controlled trial.
items.abstract: To examine spatial patterns in low birth weight (LBW) and infant wasting across the JiVitA-3 study area and assess whether the effects of antenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) vary along the same geographic gradients as socio-economic status and dietary diversity. We conducted a secondary analysis of the JiVitA-3 cluster randomised trial comparing MMS to iron-folic acid (IFA). Outcomes included LBW (<2500 g) and thin mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) at birth (<9 cm), 1 month (<11 cm) and 3, 6 and 12 months (<11·5 cm). Spatial intensity surfaces of LBW and thin MUAC relative to normal values were estimated. Generalised estimating equation Poisson regression models assessed MMS v. IFA effects, adjusting for socio-economic status, maternal dietary diversity, education, parity, BMI and gestational age. Geographic effect modification by longitude was evaluated using natural cubic splines. Modeled relative risks were smoothed and mapped. Rural northwest Bangladesh. 21 975 singleton live births within geolocated households. LBW and infant wasting exhibited a clear east-west gradient, with higher risk in the more rural east. MMS reduced risk of LBW (RR 0·86, 95 % CI: 0·83, 0·90) and thin MUAC at birth (RR 0·90, 0·84-0·97), 1 month (RR 0·89, 0·86-0·92) and 3 months (RR 0·86, 0·80-0·94), but not at 6 or 12 months. Spatial effect modification was present for LBW (Wald interaction coefficient p value <0·001) and thin birth MUAC (p = 0·016). Outcomes and modelled relative risks had visually concordant spatial patterning. While LBW and infant wasting varied geographically, the protective effect of MMS was uniform across space, supporting universal distribution. Additional interventions are needed beyond infancy.

items.title: The effect of Nutri-Score and healthy food label on consumers' food choice.
items.abstract: To compare the effects of the Nutri-Score and healthy food label (HFL) front-of-pack (FOP) nutrition labels on packaged food selections in a Turkish online supermarket setting. Experimental online supermarket study. Data were collected online in Türkiye. Participants completed three online shopping tasks 1 week apart using identical food products presented with a control label, Nutri-Score and HFL, respectively. 168 adults aged 18-50 years participated in the study. Significant overall differences across labelling conditions were observed for the number of selected products, total Food Standards Agency (FSA) score, with higher scores indicating lower nutritional quality and the nutritional composition of selected products (all p < 0·05). Compared with the control condition, participants selected fewer products under HFL (mean difference (MD) 7·54, 95 % CI 4·49, 10·60) and had lower total FSA scores (MD 175·00, 95 % CI 111·07, 238·93). HFL was also associated with lower carbohydrate (MD 228·66 g, 95 % CI 128·67, 328·64), sugar (MD 130·14 g, 95 % CI 76·64, 183·63) and salt (MD 3·08 g, 95 % CI 1·54, 4·62) contents than the control condition. Compared with Nutri-Score, HFL was associated with lower FSA scores and lower carbohydrate, sugar, saturated fat and salt contents. The findings suggest that FOP labelling, particularly HFL, may influence packaged food selections towards products with lower FSA scores and lower carbohydrate, sugar, saturated fat and salt content. Given the fixed order of label exposure and the absence of randomisation, further randomised studies with larger samples are needed to confirm these findings among Turkish consumers.

items.title: Politics and vaccine hesitancy: evidence from the Canadian vaccine behaviours, attitudes and perspectives (VBAP) survey.
items.abstract: Vaccine hesitancy is increasing worldwide when immune-based technologies are poised to advance remarkable scientific breakthroughs with potential to transform healthcare and public health. While many factors have contributed to vaccine hesitancy over time, strained social and political tensions stemming from the COVID-19 pandemic have resulted in decreased vaccine uptake and the resurgence of vaccine-preventable diseases worldwide. There has thus been substantial research on the dynamic between political identity and vaccine hesitancy. However, limited relevant research has been conducted on this dynamic in Canada, where pandemic vaccine requirements triggered political protests. Since the pandemic emergency's end, online vaccine misinformation has remained a major challenge while unprecedented political tensions with the United States have emerged. Using four waves of the Canadian Vaccine Behaviours, Attitudes and Perspectives (VBAP) Survey (December 2024 to March 2026), this paper analyses the complex associations between political alignment, trust in media, and vaccine hesitancy. This paper demonstrates associations between political alignment, vaccine perspectives and uptake, and influential media ecosystems. We conclude that addressing vaccine hesitancy for future pandemic preparedness must critically assess the implementation and communication of pandemic policies, and increase not only surveillance but engagement with online media ecosystems.

items.title: Understanding the barriers and facilitators to dementia risk reduction through dietary change amongst British South Asians: a focus group study.
items.abstract: To explore the barriers and facilitators to dietary change for dementia risk reduction among British South Asian adults and to identify factors that may influence their ability and willingness to make dietary changes to inform the development of culturally adapted interventions. A qualitative study which used focus groups for data collection. This method was selected to capitalise on pre-existing social relationships within community settings, encouraging open discussion. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using template analysis incorporating a deductive and inductive approach. Five focus-groups held in community and religious settings, recruited through community gatekeepers and patient and public involvement activities. Thirty-eight British South Asian adults (mean age = 55 years (sd = 15·1); 68 % female; 58 % unemployed) were purposively recruited through community gatekeepers and pre-existing single-sex community groups across five focus groups, selected to represent a range of perspectives within the community. Findings highlighted a lack of awareness and understanding of concepts around diet and dementia, as well as feelings of shame and stigma associated with the disease. Key barriers were identified as: practical elements including cost, convenience and accessibility; cultural insensitivity of dietary messaging; language/interpretation; and perceived inability to break longstanding habits. Facilitators included recognition of health consequences; culturally sensitive advice and childhood experiences. Broader influences on dietary behaviours included healthcare experiences, religious beliefs/practices, peer influence and generational differences). These findings provide a foundation for developing culturally relevant strategies to support and sustain dietary change amongst South Asians, in the context of dementia risk reduction.

items.title: Epidemiology and Mechanisms of Gastric Cancer in Cold Regions: Multifactorial Interactions and Region-Specific Biomarkers.
items.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a leading global malignancy with distinct epidemiological patterns across geographical zones. This review comprehensively analyzed the epidemiological patterns, biomarker profiles, and molecular mechanisms of GC in cold regions, offering an innovative perspective on the interplay between environmental, genetic, and microbiological factors. Cold geographic zones, including high-latitude and high-altitude areas, exhibit a disproportionately high GC incidence attributable to chronic cold exposure, high-salt dietary habits, vitamin D deficiency, and high prevalence of Helicobacter pylori infection with enhanced virulence genotypes such as CagA+ /VacA+ /OipA+. The study identifies and categorizes novel region-specific biomarkers - including virulence factors, epigenetic regulators (e.g. CDH1, methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), miR-21), and metabolic markers like short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) - and delineates their roles in dysregulating key pathways including Wnt/β-catenin signalling and hypoxia-induced angiogenesis. A significant contribution lies in establishing a multifactorial mechanistic framework that links cold climate stressors with gastric carcinogenesis through immune modulation, oxidative stress, and gut microbiota alterations. These insights facilitate the development of targeted prevention protocols and climate-adapted therapeutic interventions for high-risk populations in cold regions.

items.title: From Playgrounds to Projectiles: Epidemiological Pediatric Gunshot Injuries in United States.
items.abstract: Firearms are the leading cause of death among US children. This study characterizes demographic, psychiatric, and contextual factors associated with pediatric firearm injuries and mortality using the largest trauma cohort to date. Children 18 years or younger with firearm-related injuries were identified in the Trauma Quality Improvement Program (TQIP) database (2017 to 2022). Injuries were categorized by intent, location, and body region using ICD-10 codes. Demographic, mental health, and clinical characteristics were analyzed using the χ2 test. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of in-hospital mortality. Occurrence of firearm injuries over time was also investigated. Among 45,432 injured children, 77.8% were between 15 and 18 years of age; 84.3% were male, and 58.0% were non-Hispanic Black. Medicaid was the most common payer (60.2%). Assault accounted for 70.6% of injuries, followed by unintentional (17.8%) and self-inflicted (4.3%) mechanisms. Overall mortality was 11.8%. The most significant factors associated with mortality on multivariate regression were head injury (OR: 8.78; P<0.001), self-inflicted intent (OR: 6.87; P<0.001), thorax injury (OR: 4.98; P<0.001), and self-pay insurance status (OR: 4.18; P<0.001). Psychiatric comorbidities including mental health diagnoses, ADHD, and alcohol use disorder were each independently associated with decreased odds of mortality (P<0.001). Overall firearm injuries increased over the study period. Non-Hispanic White firearm injuries significantly decreased (19.5% to 13.3%; P<0.001), while non-Hispanic Black injuries simultaneously increased (54.9% to 60.3%; P<0.001). Pediatric firearm injuries represent a multifaceted public health emergency. Injury location and intent are the strongest clinical predictors of mortality, while insurance status and race reflect potential structural disparities. Reducing the burden of pediatric firearm injuries requires coordinated efforts across clinical, legislative, and community domains.

items.title: Association between adherence to EAT-Lancet reference diet and incidence of overweight and obesity in a prospective cohort study of Chinese adults.
items.abstract: The EAT-Lancet reference diet (ELD) was proposed by the EAT-Lancet Commission to promote human well-being. However, the association between adherence to ELD and obesity incidence in Chinese adults remains unclear. This study utilised data from the China Health and Nutrition Survey (1997-2015) and included 10 557 adults to examine the risk of overweight and 14 764 adults to examine the risk of obesity in association with adherence to ELD. ELD adherence was assessed via Planetary Health Diet (PHD) score. Cox regression models were used to analyse the correlation between adherence to ELD and incidence of overweight (24 ≤ BMI < 28 kg/m2) and obesity (BMI ≥ 28 kg/m2). After median follow-ups of 8.8 and 9.9 years, 3478 and 1757 participants, respectively, experienced incident overweight and obesity. Compared with the lowest quartile (Q1) of PHD score, participants in the highest quartile (Q4) were associated with lower incidence of overweight (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.41; 95 % CI: 0.37, 0.46; P-trend < 0.001) and obesity (HR = 0.39; 95 % CI: 0.34, 0.45; P-trend < 0.001). Dose-response analysis revealed a significant inverse association between the Planetary Health Diet (PHD) score and the incidence of overweight and obesity. Subgroup analyses demonstrated this inverse association was more pronounced among rural residents and individuals with low physical activity. Higher adherence to ELD was significantly associated with lower incidence of overweight and obesity in Chinese adults, especially among rural residents and those with low physical activity levels. Promoting this sustainable dietary pattern could be a relevant strategy to address obesity-related public health challenges in China.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable intake and dementia risk in community-dwelling Japanese people aged 40-74 years: a 13-year cohort study.
items.abstract: Cruciferous vegetables containing isothiocyanates and indoles have been suggested to be associated with a reduced risk of dementia, but supporting evidence is scarce. The present cohort study aimed to determine whether cruciferous vegetable intake is associated with dementia risk in middle-aged and older adults. Participants were 13 203 Japanese people aged 40-74 years. Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire. The predictor was cruciferous vegetable intake, and the outcome was newly diagnosed dementia using the Long-Term Care Insurance database. Covariates included age, sex, marital status, education level, occupation, BMI, total physical activity, smoking, alcohol consumption, coffee/green tea consumption, energy-adjusted non-cruciferous vegetable, fruit, dairy products, and fish intake and disease history. Information on food intake was obtained with a validated FFQ, with adjustments made for energy using the residual method. Hazard ratios (HR) were calculated using a Cox proportional hazards model. The mean age of participants was 59·1 years (sd 9·3). During a mean follow-up of 13·3 years, 1048 cases of dementia were observed. Lower cruciferous vegetable intake was associated with a higher dementia risk (P for trend = 0·0127), with an increased risk in the lowest intake quartile (HR = 1·28, 95 % CI: 1·04-1·59) than in the highest quartile (reference) after adjustment for covariates, including non-cruciferous vegetable intake. This association tended to be stronger in the younger subgroup of <65 years (HR = 1·91, 95 % CI: 1·24-2·94) than in the older subgroup of ≥65 years (P for interaction = 0·0856). In conclusion, lower cruciferous vegetable intake is associated with an increased risk of dementia in middle-aged and older people.

items.title: Complementary-feeding patterns, dietary diversity and linear growth among children aged 6-23 months in forty low- and middle-income countries.
items.abstract: Dietary diversity is widely used to assess complementary-feeding quality, but it may not fully reflect variation in diet composition relevant to child growth. We aimed to identify complementary-feeding patterns across forty low- and middle-income countries, examine their correspondence with minimum dietary diversity (MDD) and assess their associations with child linear growth. We analysed nationally representative Demographic and Health Surveys conducted between 2015 and 2024. Latent class analysis of the eight WHO/UNICEF food groups identified feeding patterns among 165 348 children aged 6-23 months. MDD was defined as consumption of at least five of the eight food groups during the previous 24 h. Associations with length-for-age z-score (LAZ) and stunting were assessed using linear regression and modified Poisson regression with robust se, respectively. Four patterns emerged: Diverse (8·8 %), Dairy-oriented (27·5 %), Plant-forward (34·3 %) and Breastmilk-dominant (29·4 %), with prevalence varying across countries. Overall, 24·3 % met MDD. Among those who did not, 38·8 % were Breastmilk-dominant, 37·9 % Plant-forward and 23·3 % Dairy-oriented. Compared with Diverse, Plant-forward and Breastmilk-dominant patterns were associated with lower LAZ and higher stunting prevalence. Dairy-oriented did not differ detectably in either outcome despite lower MDD attainment. These findings indicate that MDD non-attainment encompasses distinct dietary compositions with different growth associations. Pattern-based assessment could complement MDD monitoring by distinguishing the forms of complementary feeding underlying low dietary diversity.

items.title: Interaction between 3-SNP genetic risk score and lifestyle risk score on cardiovascular risk factors and the risk of lifetime ASCVD among overweight and obese women.
items.abstract: Interaction between genetic variations and lifestyle risk factors has been shown to be associated with atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD). This study for the first time sought to investigate this interaction on cardiovascular risk factors and the lifetime ASCVD risk in Iranian obese and overweight women. This study consisted of 256 overweight or obese women. The genetic risk score (GRS) included three genetic variations (CAV-1 rs3807992, CRY-1 rs2287161 and MC4R rs17782313), and each of them was genotyped using PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism. Lifestyle risk score (LRS) consisting of dietary behaviour, physical activity, sleep quality, socio-economic status and waist-to-stature ratio was used to assess lifestyle risk factors associated with ASCVD, and the Bonferroni correction was also applied for multiple comparisons. Following Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons using a family-wise approach (α = 0·0028 for interaction analyses), the interaction between high LRS and high GRS was not significantly associated with any assessed cardiovascular risk factor or lifetime ASCVD risk. The nominal P-values for these interactions were 0·040 (CRI-II), 0·038 (CHOLINDEX), 0·018 (TyG-BMI), 0·041 (TAG), 0·041 (AIP), 0·067 (HDL), 0·075 (LDL) and 0·077 (ASCVD lifetime risk), all of which exceeded the Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold. In this exploratory, hypothesis-generating study, uncorrected analyses suggested preliminary nominally significant interactions. However, after adjusting for multiple comparisons, no definitive evidence of GRS × LRS interactions was observed. These findings require replication in larger, prospective cohorts.

items.title: Molecular characterisation of norovirus GII.4 Sydney [P16] among children with acute gastroenteritis in Sabah of Malaysian Borneo.
items.abstract: Norovirus (NoV) is a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis (AGE), especially in children under 5 years old, with significant morbidity in middle-income countries like Malaysia. This study aimed to detect and characterise the NoV among children with acute gastroenteritis in 2019 to 2020. Stool samples from 124 children with watery diarrhoea were extracted and analysed using RT-PCR, nucleotide sequencing, and phylogenetic analyses. NoV was detected in 27/124 (21.8%) samples, with GII (81.5%) being the predominant genogroup, followed by GI (18.5%). Phylogenetic analysis revealed GII.4[P16] as the most common strain, followed by GII.6[P7]. GII.4 Sydney 2012 strains showed high nucleotide identity to the reference strains from different geographical regions. GII.6 strains showed limited changes compared to earlier studies but warrant attention due to their increasing global presence. Children aged 0-23 months had higher odds (6.7 times) of NoV infection, likely due to behavioural factors and lack of immunity. This study observed an increase in NoV proportion from 17.7% in 2018-2019 to 21.8% in 2019-2020 and changes in predominant genotypes. These findings emphasise the importance of continuous surveillance to track NoV genetic diversity and guide vaccine development, particularly in middle-income countries with high AGE morbidity but low mortality. Future studies should focus on broader geographic coverage and longer surveillance periods to better understand NoV epidemiology in Malaysia.

items.title: Understanding sustainable employment in autistic individuals: insights from a qualitative study.
items.abstract: Employment outcomes for autistic adults are often conceptualized in terms of access and performance, with less attention to long-term sustainability. This study aimed to explore how autistic adults experience work and to identify the factors that support or hinder sustainable employment. We conducted a qualitative study with 19 autistic participants (mean age = 25.21 years) using a focus group (n = 9) and semi-structured interviews (n = 10). We analyzed data using an analytical pluralism approach, combining functional thematic analysis with an interpretative layer based on a triangulation matrix of barriers and facilitators. Themes were developed through an iterative analytical process, with discrepancies discussed and resolved by consensus among the research team. Sustainability -defined as the ability to maintain employment without excessive cognitive, emotional, or physical cost- emerged as the central organizing principle across participants. We identified four functional work profiles (adjusted, strategic, context-vulnerable, and interest-dependent), reflecting different configurations of executive functioning, emotional regulation, and environmental interaction. Workplace context was a key determinant of sustainability, with role clarity, predictability, sensory conditions, and communication acting as facilitators, and multitasking, interruptions, time pressure, and structural hiring barriers acting as obstacles. Control emerged as a transversal compensatory mechanism with differential emotional costs. Motivation was not a stable trait but an emergent outcome of environmental fit. Employment outcomes in autism are best understood as the result of dynamic interactions between individuals and their environments. Sustainability, rather than performance alone, should be considered a primary outcome in employment research and practice. The findings also suggest that four functional profiles may help describe person-environment variability, providing a potential analytical framework to inform the development of an intervention aimed at promoting long-term, sustainable employment. items.title: Socioeconomic gradients in frailty and contribution of lifestyle behaviours from midlife to older age: evidence from 31 countries.
items.abstract: Evidence on the association between socioeconomic status (SES) and frailty trajectories is limited and inconsistent, and the mechanisms underlying inequalities in frailty progression remain unclear. Cross-country comparative evidence is also scarce. Four harmonised cohort studies (HRS, ELSA, SHARE, and CHARLS) were pooled to construct a multinational cohort spanning 31 countries. Frailty was assessed using frailty index (FI, scaled to 100). Mixed effects models were used to estimate trajectories across SES groups (low, lower-middle, upper-middle, and high) among adults aged ≥ 50. Marginal effects, calculated as differences in FI between SES groups, were derived at age of 50, 60, 70, and 80 years to quantify SES gradients over time. Country-specific gradients were estimated using SES fixed effects and country-level random effects. Proportions of the SES gradients accounted for by different lifestyle behaviours (smoking, heavy drinking, physical inactivity, and social inactivity) were calculated. 71,703 participants were included, of whom 50·0% females with a mean age of 63·8 (9·4) years. Compared to the low SES group, the lower-middle, upper-middle, and high SES groups had 2·47 (95% CI: -3·19 to -1·75), 5·06 (95% CI: -5·96 to -4·16), and 6·85 (95% CI: -8·08 to -5·62) points lower FI at the age of 50 years, respectively. These differences widened by 2.03, 4.04, and 5.39 points from age 50 to 80 years, respectively. England and the USA showed higher SES gradients in FI at age 50. Lifestyle behaviours jointly accounted for 12·6%-15·7% of the SES gradient in frailty at age 50 years, increasing to 20·7%-21·8% three decades later. Over the same period, the contribution of social inactivity rose modestly (10·4%-10·8% to 10·7%-14·4%), whereas that of physical inactivity increased markedly (2·1%-4·0% to 10·6%-12·9%). There are substantial socioeconomic gradients in frailty among middle-aged and older people, widening with age, with cross-country variations. Lifestyle behaviours increasingly explained these gradients, accounting for over one-fifth by age 80, with social inactivity and physical inactivity as key contributors. Early interventions targeting socioeconomically disadvantaged groups and the promotion of healthier lifestyles are needed.

items.title: Adherence to the MIND diet and psychoneurological symptoms, inflammation, and brain volumes in postmenopausal breast cancer survivors: a cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: Examine the association between adherence to the MIND diet and psychoneurological symptoms, inflammatory markers, and brain volumes of postmenopausal breast cancer (BC) survivors. This cross-sectional study included an analytical sample of 21 BC survivors, 3-12 months postchemotherapy. Dietary data were collected via electronic food frequency questionnaire. Psychoneurological symptoms (cognitive impairment, fatigue, sleep disturbance, depression, and anxiety) were self-reported using validated questionnaires. Serum inflammatory biomarkers were measured using ELISA. Magnetic resonance imaging assessed brain volumes. Multivariate regressions assessed associations of log-MIND diet adherence with symptom burden (primary), individual symptoms, inflammation, and brain volumes (secondary), and binary MIND recommendations with symptoms, inflammation, and brain volumes (exploratory). Analyses were adjusted for false discovery rate using Benjamini-Hochberg method (p_adj < 0.05). Lower symptom burden was associated with higher berry intake (OR = 0.123, p = 0.001, p_adj = 0.015). While lower depression scores were associated with higher other vegetable intake (β = - 0.868, p = 0.001, p_adj = 0.017). Several nominally significant (p < 0.05, p_adj ≥ 0.05) results were observed between lower symptom burden and adherence to the MIND diet, greater intakes of green leafy vegetables, other vegetables, and beans and legumes. Lower anxiety, depression, fatigue, and sleep disturbance scores were nominally associated with higher intakes of berries, cheese, and other vegetables. Lower inflammatory marker concentrations were nominally associated with higher intake of berries and other vegetables as well as lower intake of butter and margarine. Larger subcortical gray matter volumes were nominally associated with consuming berries within the recommended amount (≥ 5 servings/week). Adherence to the MIND diet, specifically higher berry intake, was associated with lower psychoneurological symptom burden among postmenopausal BC survivors. Recommended intake of MIND diet components was also associated with individual symptoms, inflammation, and brain volumes. Further research is needed to confirm these findings.

items.title: Microplastics as an emerging environmental toxicant: mechanistic alteration in central appetite and obesity.
items.abstract: The hypothalamus is a key central processing hub of appetite regulation. It senses nutrient signals from peripheral hormones, such as ghrelin, leptin, and adipokines, and integrates these signals via feedback mechanisms (AgRP/NPY and POMC/CART) to maintain energy homeostasis. Plastic pollution is rapidly emerging as a significant public health concern worldwide. MPs are a plastic product, and they are increasingly recognised as a pervasive pollutant due to their presence in daily life essentials. Experimental data indicate that MPs can accumulate in the brain, including the hippocampus, hypothalamus, and other regions, where they disrupt neurons, trigger glial activation, induce receptor resistance, and impair mitochondrial function, thereby altering neuroendocrine signalling. This review highlights the potential impact of MPs on neuroendocrine regulation of appetite, focusing on the hypothalamus, a region involved in central appetite regulation. We further summarize the preliminary evidence from human tissue samples, including stool, lungs, and the decedent's brain as well as human health risks associated with MPs. Additionally, this review discusses the key gap in research areas, which will provide future perspective on the underlying mechanism of health risks.

items.title: NR1I2 rs3732356 polymorphism and anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury in eastern Chinese patients: A preliminary study.
items.abstract: Genetic factors may underlie anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury (ATLI), the most common and severe adverse reaction in tuberculosis treatment. We aimed to assess whether the risk of ATLI might be influenced by nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group I member 2 (NR1I2) gene polymorphisms. A 1:4 individual matched case-control study was performed using 224 ATLI cases and 896 controls. Five single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of the NR1I2 gene were analyzed. A multiple conditional logistic regression model was used to estimate the association between genotypes and ATLI risk by the odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with liver disease history and smoking as covariates. Interaction and age-stratified analyses were conducted to investigate gene-age interactions in ATLI risk and genetic associations with ATLI across age groups. No significant associations between the five NR1I2 SNPs and ATLI were observed in the overall analysis. Statistically significant interactions were absent on either the multiplicative or additive scale. In exploratory subgroup analyses, rs3732356 was associated with lower ATLI risk in patients aged under 60 years in the dominant model (OR = 0.540, 95%CI: 0.312-0.933, p = 0.027) and additive model (OR = 0.607, 95%CI: 0.390-0.946, p = 0.027). Peak total bilirubin (TBil) was significantly higher in patients with TG genotype of rs3732356 than in those with TT or GG (16.8 μmol/L vs. 14.3 μmol/L vs. 12.5 μmol/L, respectively, p = 0.007). Despite a preliminary age-stratified signal for rs3732356, we found no overall association and no significant effect modification by age, which warrants validation in larger studies.

items.title: The reduced hospital costs of periprosthetic joint infection patients with successful initial treatment : two-year estimations using activity-based costing.
items.abstract: This study aimed to 1) estimate the two-year hospital costs of treating periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) patients by outcomes of treatment success or treatment failure; 2) compare costs between patients with treatment success or treatment failure, stratified by PJI presentation and initial treatment type; and 3) estimate the cost burden for the study cohort and the projected Australian PJI cost burden of PJI patients by treatment success outcomes. A total of 212 hip and 287 knee patients from the Prosthetic joint Infection in Australia and New Zealand Observational (PIANO) study were included. Patients were grouped by treatment success outcomes, treatment type, and timing of PJI presentation (early acute, late acute, or chronic) at two-year follow-up. Hospital costs were calculated using activity-based costing. For hips, the mean cost of 67 patients with treatment failure was AUD $85,179 (SD 72,030), which was 1.44-fold higher than of 145 successfully treated patients ($59,234 (SD 45,581)). Of successfully treated hip patients, those who underwent additional surgeries ($70,257 (SD 38,481)) had 1.25-fold higher mean costs than patients with successful initial treatment ($56,238 (SD 42,929)). For knees, the mean cost of 133 patients with treatment failure ($89,073 (SD 64,707)) was 1.72-fold higher than 154 patients with successful treatment ($51,785 (SD 31,449)). Of successfully treated knee patients, those who underwent additional surgery ($85,326 (SD 44,885)) had 1.88-fold higher mean costs than patients with successful initial treatment ($45,284 (SD 23,286)). Treatment failure outcomes for patients initially treated with two-stage revision total hip arthroplasty, two-stage revision total knee arthroplasty, single-stage revision total knee arthroplasty, and extensive knee debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) cost 1.78, 1.94, 1.74, and 1.79-fold higher, respectively, compared with successfully treated patients with the same initial treatment (p < 0.05). At two-year follow-up, PJI patients with successful initial treatment had reduced hospital costs, highlighting the importance of strategies that aim to 'get it right the first time'. Patients with treatment failure account for approximately $131 million (51%) of the estimated $254 million annual Australian burden of hip and knee PJI.

items.title: Behavioral Psychology of Homo Sapiens: An Interdisciplinary Review of Evolution, Cognition, Emotion and Culture
items.abstract: Human behavior is best understood as a product of several interacting systems rather than as the outcome of a single psychological or biological cause. This narrative review brings together perspectives from evolutionary psychology, cognitive science, developmental research, social psychology, and cultural evolution to examine how human behavioral capacities are expressed across contexts. The review focuses on cognition and decision-making, emotion, social learning, cooperation, competition, cultural transmission, and behavioral variation. The literature indicates that evolutionary history provides important biological foundations, but these foundations do not specify a single behavioral outcome. Developmental experience, social relationships, institutions, cultural practices, and immediate environmental conditions influence how psychological capacities are expressed. Evidence concerning cultural evolution is particularly relevant because socially transmitted information can shape learning processes and contribute to the development of human cognitive mechanisms. Emotion similarly appears to involve an interaction between affective processes and culturally acquired concepts and expectations. Human cooperation provides another illustration of this multilevel interaction, with kinship, reciprocity, reputation, norms, punishment, institutions, and cultural transmission contributing in different circumstances. The review also considers the generalizability problem in psychology, especially the heavy representation of Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic populations in behavioral research. Overall, the literature supports an integrative framework in which biological inheritance, development, cognition, emotion, social interaction, and culture operate as mutually influencing components of human behavior.

items.title: MidasTUI: Instant Tangible User Interfaces for Wearable Displays using Everyday Objects
items.abstract: While wearable displays can bring digital workspaces anywhere, interaction remains limited by mid-air gestures that lack tactile feedback and induce fatigue, or controllers that are cumbersome to carry. We present MidasTUI, a system that instantly transforms arbitrary everyday objects into opportunistic tangible user interfaces through brief interaction demonstrations. For example, a user can slide an earbud case across a table as a mouse, enabling opportunistic interaction without carrying a dedicated input device. MidasTUI detects when a user is holding and moving an object using the wearable display camera and a Transformer-based temporal classifier. It then infers the intended input modality (e.g., slider, mouse, keypad) from hand movement and maps the tracked hand-object interaction to an application function. Our evaluations demonstrate reliable cross-object and cross-user generalization. A comparative user study further shows that grounding interaction in everyday objects reduces physical burden and improves perceived usability and control relative to mid-air interaction.

items.title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
items.abstract: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

items.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
items.abstract: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

items.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
items.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

items.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
items.abstract: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

items.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
items.abstract: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios. Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

items.title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
items.abstract: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. Experiments on a diverse set of tabular datasets show that our method outperforms standard decision trees and achieves performance on par with ensemble methods, while producing shallow trees that retain or even improve predictive accuracy.

items.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
items.abstract: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

items.title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
items.abstract: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.

items.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.
