items.title: Behavioral Cardiovascular Health Metrics in Adolescence: Evidence From a Cross-Sectional Analysis of the 2022-2023 COMPASS-Québec Cohort Supporting the Relevance of Including Recreational Screen Time.
items.abstract: Purpose The American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 defines cardiovascular health (CVH) through four behavior factors (physical activity, diet, sleep, and nicotine exposure) and four biological factors, but it excludes recreational screen time, a prevalent sedentary behavior increasingly linked to adolescent cardiometabolic risk. We examined whether adding recreational screen time to a behavioral CVH score changes population-level estimates and their sociodemographic and school-level patterning. Methods We analyzed cross-sectional 2022 to 2023 COMPASS-Québec data from 17,882 adolescents (ages 11-19 years). The following two behavioral CVH scores were compared: a four-component score (physical activity, diet quality, sleep health, and nicotine exposure) and a five-component score that additionally included recreational screen time. Linear mixed-effects models with school random intercepts examined associations for each score with grade, gender identity, ethnicity, material deprivation, and school type. Results Mean behavioral CVH was 74.3 (standard deviation 19.7) for the four-component score and 64.5 (standard deviation 18.6) for the five-component score, a 9.8-point reduction when recreational screen time was included. In both models, higher grade, greater material deprivation, racialized identity, and public rural school attendance were associated with lower behavioral CVH; boys scored higher than girls, gender diverse adolescents scored lower, and students in private schools scored higher. Discussion Including recreational screen time lowered population level behavioral CVH estimates without changing the social gradients, indicating that frameworks that exclude it may underestimate adolescent vulnerability. A more behaviorally complete approach could strengthen surveillance, improve intervention targeting, and better support school-based strategies to promote CVH equitably.

items.title: Reimagining professionalism in medicine: uncertainty, disability, and the limits of normative competencies.
items.abstract: Background Professionalism remains central to how medical education evaluates competence and shapes professional identity formation. Throughout training, learners encounter uncertainty regarding who they should become and how to demonstrate competence. Although intended to promote ethical practice and public trust, prevailing models of professionalism can reinforce normative assumptions shaping how learners experience and respond to uncertainty. These assumptions may be particularly consequential for disabled learners and clinicians whose experiences challenge normative expectations. Thus, despite growing attention to disability-related inequities in medical education, the professional norms through which competence and legitimacy are judged warrant greater critical examination. Materials and methods We conducted a critical narrative review and conceptual synthesis of empirical, historical, theoretical, and humanities-based scholarship published between 1990 and 2026. Four transitions in medical training (admissions, pre-clinical education, clinical rotations, and residency) were selected a priori as an organizing framework. Drawing on scholarship in uncertainty tolerance, critical disability studies, and disability justice, we examined how professional expectations are constructed and negotiated across these stages. Results Across the four transitions, our analysis reveals how professional expectations shape learners' experiences of uncertainty. These stages illustrate how professional norms acquire authority through educational practices and the hidden curriculum. Our synthesis also identifies an underexamined dimension of this process: how educators' and institutions' responses to uncertainty may reinforce or challenge ableist assumptions about professional competence. Conclusion Reimagining professionalism requires examining how medical education defines competence and judges responses to uncertainty. Bringing uncertainty tolerance into conversation with critical disability studies and the principles of disability justice, our synthesis advances three complementary pedagogical commitments: cultivating critical awareness of professional assumptions, recognizing diverse expressions of competence, and extending uncertainty tolerance to educational institutions. Together, these commitments offer a framework for challenging ableist norms through epistemic humility, flexibility, and courage while supporting more inclusive approaches to professional identity formation.

items.title: Assessing the Roles of Two Community-Based Health Professionals in Japan: Public Health Nurses and Community Pharmacists.
items.abstract: Community-based health professionals play important roles in public health systems but are often less visible than hospital-based providers. In Japan, the roles of public health nurses and community pharmacists have evolved in response to population aging and changing health system needs. We conducted a case study of these two professions. We drew on published literature, policy documents, and government statistics and examined their basic characteristics, historical development, and current work environments to assess their roles in community health systems in Japan. Public health nurses have traditionally focused on community-based prevention and health promotion, while community pharmacists have been oriented toward dispensing and medication management. In recent decades, both professions have experienced role expansion, with public health nurses taking on greater coordination and administrative responsibilities and community pharmacists increasingly expected to contribute to community-based care. However, both groups face challenges, including role ambiguity, workforce constraints, and limited recognition by other professionals and the public. Gaps also remain between policy expectations and practice, particularly in workload, professional positioning, and education. Strengthening Japan's community health system will require policy support and targeted investment in these two community-based health professions, especially for leadership development and interprofessional collaboration.

items.title: Mental health assessment and access to gender-affirming hormone therapy: perspectives of healthcare professionals in Brazil.
items.abstract: In Brazil, access to gender-affirming hormone therapy remains contested, particularly regarding the role of mental health assessment in clinical decision-making. This qualitative study explored how healthcare professionals make decisions concerning gender-affirming hormone access for trans and gender diverse people in Brazil. We interviewed nine healthcare professionals experienced in the care of trans and gender diverse people. Participants described the ways in which mental health assessment could contribute to shared decision-making, clinical support, and institutional protection, rather than as a means of pathologisation or a determinant of eligibility for gender-affirming hormone therapy. These rationalities legitimised different arrangements of power in clinical care, shaping who could make decisions, who was held responsible, and how much autonomy patients could exercise. Our findings suggest that debates surrounding mental health assessment extend beyond whether assessment should be required to encompass the purposes it might serve as part of gender-affirming care. By demonstrating how a variety of professional rationalities influence access to gender-affirming hormone therapy, this study contributes to international discussion on informed consent, institutional regulation, and healthcare equity. These issues have gained renewed relevance in Brazil following the Brazilian Federal Council of Medicine's Resolution No. 2,427/2025, which introduced new restrictions on access to gender-affirming hormone therapy.

items.title: Radiosynoviorthesis in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Background Although radiosynoviorthesis (RSO) has been used to treat rheumatoid arthritis (RA) for over 70 years, its precise role within contemporary RA treatment algorithms remains variable, particularly in the era of biologic and targeted synthetic therapies. This systematic review evaluated the efficacy and safety of RSO in RA through randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Methods MEDLINE and Embase were systematically searched for RCTs assessing RSO in RA up to January 1, 2026. Eligible studies were summarized according to efficacy and safety outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration's tool. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251174356). Results Sixteen RCTs including 834 RA patients were identified. Most studies (N.=10) focused on treatment of the knee joint, and the most frequently used radiopharmaceutical was [ 90 Y]yttrium (N.=9 trials, either as a single radiopharmaceutical [N.=6] or alongside another radionuclide [N.=3]). In seven trials, RSO was administered in combination with corticosteroids. RSO was most commonly compared with intra-articular corticosteroid injections (N.=10) and placebo (saline) injections (N.=3). Of the corticosteroid trials, three reported greater efficacy for RSO, one showed superiority of RSO plus corticosteroids over RSO alone, and six found no significant differences between RSO and corticosteroids. All three placebo-controlled trials demonstrated superior outcomes with RSO. Adverse events associated with RSO were generally mild, transient, and manageable. Conclusions Available RCTs suggest that RSO is an effective and well-tolerated treatment option for RA. However, the limited number of high-quality trials and the variability of findings underscore the need for further robust, large-scale studies to define its role in clinical practice.

items.title: Research on the spatial decomposition and determinants of Body Mass Index among Chinese residents.
items.abstract: Purpose: To analyze the spatial decomposition and determinants of Chinese residents BMI, and to provide more targeted recommendations for physical health policy based on BMIs spatial characteristics. Methods: Data were sourced from the CGSS from which the height and weight data of 78,663 individuals were extracted and included in the study the China Statistical Yearbook, the China Urban Statistical Yearbook, and provincial sports statistical yearbooks, and analyzed using spatial correlation and a spatial Durbin two-way fixed-effects model. Results: BMI among Chinese residents exhibits significant spatial autocorrelation. Local Morans I reveals marked regional heterogeneity: Beijing, Tianjin, Hebei, and Shandong display highhigh clustering, Jiangxi and Chongqing show highlow clustering, while other provinces are not significant. The spatial Durbin fixed-effects model identifies public sports resources (EPS) and urbanization rate (Urb) as key drivers. Direct effects show that local EPS significantly inhibits BMI, whereas local Urb promotes it. Spatial spillover analysis indicates that rising local EPS generates a strong negative spillover on surrounding areas, with intensity far exceeding its direct effect; local urbanization has significant positive spillovers, driving neighboring development. Total effects confirm that both factors exert broad regional linkages. Spatial heterogeneity analysis shows that EPS significantly reduces local BMI in eastern and western regions (direct effects: -1.803 and -0.748; negative spillovers: -1.699 and -1.406), but has a positive effect in the central region (1.988). All regional spatial autocorrelation coefficients (rho) are significantly negative. Conclusions: Based on the first law of geography and differences across regions in terms of the availability of public sports facilities, dietary patterns, economic development, and urbanization rates, this study examines the spatial spillover effects of the BMI among Chinese residents, as well as its driving factors and heterogeneity, and proposes specific policy recommendations accordingly.

items.title: Gambling Harms: Locating the harm from gambling alongside substance addiction using Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis.
items.abstract: Introduction Gambling harm has previously been treated differently from substance addiction in policy and regulation, despite emerging evidence of comparable population-level harm. However, direct comparison between gambling - a behavioural addiction - and substance addictions is difficult. Current understandings of harm can rely heavily on physical functioning and do not reflect the holistic harms associated with gambling. We aim to (1) compare harms from gambling alongside substances; (2) characterise the contribution of different harm components; and (3) assess the robustness of these rankings. Methods Using Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA), we systematically compared gambling harms at three risk levels (low, medium, and high) with high-risk use of alcohol, cocaine, and cannabis. A purposively sampled expert panel comprising lived experience, research, treatment, and policy/advocacy perspectives was convened, each member having backgrounds in at least two of the harms assessed. The panel assessed harm to self and others across seven components: mental wellbeing, physical wellbeing, finances, ethical lapses, work/study and meaningful activities, close relationships, and social relationships. Results The model ranked high-risk gambling (harm score 0-100: 94.8) and high-risk alcohol (94.7) as essentially equally harmful, followed by high-risk cocaine (86.9). While substance addictions produced greater physical wellbeing harm in the model, gambling caused disproportionate financial harm and comparable relationship harm. Notably, harm to others equalled harm to self across all options. Rankings remained stable across plausible parameter variations in sensitivity testing. Conclusion These findings converge with independent evidence from health utility studies and holistic harm frameworks, demonstrating that high-risk gambling produces comparable harm to high-risk alcohol when assessed through a public health lens rather than purely physiological criteria. The substantial financial and relationship harms associated with gambling suggest harm reduction must address these domains specifically. This work provides policymakers with systematic evidence supporting regulatory alignment between gambling and alcohol, and demonstrates MCDA's utility for assessing behavioural addiction harms.

items.title: Between borders and identities: categories and activism by immigrant transfeminine and travesti individuals in France during the HIV epidemic.
items.abstract: This paper examines the role of transfeminine and travesti (TT) individuals in HIV prevention in Marseille and Paris between 1988 and 1997. Initially included in outreach programmes targeting male sex workers, TT communities became key players in developing community-led research and interventions, rooted in migrant activism. Combining long-term ethnography within Prévention Action Santé Travail pour les Transgenres (PASTT), France's first TT-led organisation, archival research, and interviews, this study analyses how the male sex work categories shaped the inclusion and representation of TT individuals in mainstream public health. Focusing on three projects in Paris and Marseille, the paper explores the cognitive and historical dimensions of HIV-related involvements and activities. It reveals how migrant TT communities developed autonomous prevention strategies, asserted rights, and produced new forms of knowledge. The paper contributes to the historicisation of cisnormativity and informs archival practices aimed at preserving TT memories. It also underscores how material conditions and sex work have shaped gendered experiences, positioning them as foundational to trans history.

items.title: Advances in Chikungunya Fever Prevention and Control: Antiviral Therapeutics, Vaccine Development and Integrated Intervention Strategies.
items.abstract: Chikungunya fever (CHIKF) is an acute mosquito-borne disease caused by chikungunya virus (CHIKV). Driven by globalization, climate change and expanding vector habitats, its geographic range continues to widen; in 2025 it produced the largest outbreak ever recorded in China, with more than 25,800 locally transmitted cases across all 21 prefecture-level cities of Guangdong. Beyond acute fever, rash and arthralgia, a substantial proportion of patients develop chronic arthritis, which accounts for much of the disease burden. This review summarizes the etiological features, life cycle, epidemiology and ongoing evolution of CHIKV, and critically evaluates progress in antiviral drugs and vaccines, together with vector control, microbiome-based approaches and One Health governance. No specific antiviral has yet been approved: compounds targeting viral entry, RNA capping, protease activity and genome replication inhibit CHIKV selectively in cell culture but remain at preclinical or early clinical stages, and host-directed agents are further constrained by host toxicity. Two vaccines are now licensed-the live-attenuated vaccine Ixchiq, whose use has been progressively restricted following post-marketing safety signals, and the virus-like particle vaccine Vimkunya-while inactivated, chimeric, viral-vectored and mRNA candidates remain earlier in development. For all countermeasures, whether the envelope substitutions carried by recently emerged strains, including E2-L210Q and E2-I211 T within the immunodominant domain B, will erode protection remains experimentally unresolved. Collectively, CHIKV control still faces the absence of approved antivirals, incompletely defined long-term vaccine safety and breadth, and ongoing vector population expansion. Future work should prioritize broad-spectrum antivirals and next-generation vaccines, promote multidisciplinary collaboration, and strengthen integrated governance under the One Health framework. items.title: Molecular Discordance Between Primary Non-Small Cell Lung Cancers and Brain Metastases: Associations With Intracranial Outcomes.
items.abstract: Background and objectives In an era of molecular-guided systemic oncologic therapies, a proportion of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) brain metastases (BMs) have demonstrated molecularly discordant profiles for anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) biomarkers compared with the primary tumor. However, its effect on outcomes remains unclear. We investigated the association between molecular discordance for these actionable markers and clinical outcomes in patients with NSCLC BM. Methods We performed a single-institution retrospective analysis screening 476 patients who underwent treatment for a NSCLC BM from January 2012 to December 2025, with 40 patients having molecular profiling for the primary lung and BM lesions. Patient molecular profiles were categorized as concordant or discordant based on comparison of the ALK, EGFR, and KRAS mutational statuses at both tumor sites. Descriptive statistics, univariate comparisons, Kaplan-Meier survival, and Fine-Gray competing risk analyses were performed between the concordant and discordant cohorts. Multiple comparison using false discovery rate was performed for survival-related outcomes. Results ALK, EGFR, or KRAS molecular discordance occurred in 32.5% (13/40) of observed cases. Although nonsignificant, the concordant cohort had a higher rate of distant brain failure (DBF) (63.0% vs 30.8%, P = .056); conversely, the discordant cohort had a higher rate of local recurrence (38.5% vs 18.5%, P = .17). The discordant cohort had a lower subdistribution hazard of DBF than the concordant cohort (subdistribution hazard ratio: 0.34, 95% CI: 0.13-0.91, P = .032). However, this significant difference did not persist after false discovery rate-adjusted analysis. Significant differences in time to intracranial progression, time to local recurrence, and overall survival were not observed between the 2 cohorts. Conclusion Molecular discordance was observed in >30% of analyzed cases, and the subdistribution hazard of DBF differed significantly between the 2 cohorts. This rate of discordance may warrant further investigation on whether increased BM profiling could help refine current approaches to NSCLC BM management.

items.title: Nonlinear joint associations of admission neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and blood urea nitrogen with in-hospital acute kidney injury in cirrhosis with acute variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
items.abstract: Objectives Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common following acute variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with cirrhosis. This study assessed the nonlinear individual and joint associations of admission neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) with in-hospital AKI. Materials and methods This multicentre retrospective cohort study included 953 patients with cirrhosis and acute variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The primary centre constituted the derivation cohort ( n = 667), and the other two hospitals constituted the validation cohort ( n = 286), without patient overlap between the two cohorts. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses assessed nonlinear associations in the derivation cohort, with spline specifications applied unchanged to the validation cohort. A four-group NLR-BUN matrix based on derivation cohort cutpoints was evaluated as a secondary exploratory analysis and applied unchanged to the validation cohort. Results In-hospital AKI occurred in 168 patients (25.2%) in the derivation cohort and 71 patients (24.8%) in the validation cohort. Median time to AKI was 4 days (IQR, 3-6). Both admission NLR and BUN showed significant nonlinear associations with AKI. Jointly modelled as continuous spline terms, both retained evidence of nonlinear associations, and the RCS fitted better than the corresponding linear model (likelihood-ratio p = 0.001). Joint nonlinearity remained significant in validation ( p = 0.046). Conclusions Admission NLR and BUN were nonlinearly associated with in-hospital AKI. The continuous joint association constituted the primary evidence, whereas the data-derived NLR-BUN matrix should be considered exploratory. The retrospective design and validation restricted to the participating centres limit the broader clinical generalizability of the findings.

items.title: Intratumoral Peptostreptococcus stomatis promotes the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma through the integrin α6/β4-ERBB2-MAPK pathway.
items.abstract: The intratumoral microbiome is increasingly implicated in the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), yet its compositional features and functional contributions remain incompletely defined. Here, through an integrated meta-analysis of nine public 16S rRNA sequencing data sets encompassing 578 samples, we revealed a significantly dysbiotic intratumoral microbiota in OSCC, characterized by reduced α-diversity and distinct β-diversity. Machine learning confirmed the diagnostic potential of this microbial signature, achieving an average cross-validation area under the curve of 0.83. Among the tumor-enriched taxa, Peptostreptococcus stomatis was consistently identified, and its intratumoral enrichment was validated by fluorescent in situ hybridization in clinical specimens. Functionally, P. stomatis enhances OSCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro and accelerates tumor growth in a mouse xenograft model. Mechanistically, we demonstrated that P. stomatis directly adheres to OSCC cells and activates the integrin α6/β4-ERBB2-MAPK signaling axis. Genetic ablation of Erbb2 abrogated P. stomatis -induced malignant phenotypes in vitro and tumor growth in vivo , establishing ERBB2 as an essential mediator of this oncogenic pathway. Collectively, our findings establish P. stomatis as a functionally significant driver of OSCC progression, unveiling the bacterium and its host interaction interface as promising targets for microbiome-based diagnostics and therapeutic intervention.IMPORTANCEThe role of the intratumoral microbiome in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains poorly defined. Through a large-scale meta-analysis of 578 samples, we reveal a consistent microbial dysbiosis in OSCC and establish Peptostreptococcus stomatis as a functionally significant driver of tumor progression. We demonstrate that P. stomatis directly activates the integrin α6/β4-ERBB2-MAPK signaling axis, and that genetic ablation of ERBB2 abrogates its oncogenic effects. These findings position P. stomatis and its host interaction interface as promising targets for microbiome-based diagnostics and therapeutic intervention in OSCC.

items.title: Polyamine metabolism as a drug target in clinically relevant fungi.
items.abstract: SUMMARYThe global increase in the incidence of invasive fungal diseases and concurrent rise of antifungal resistance is a growing public health concern. In addition, persistent challenges in the development of novel antifungal agents underscore the need to identify alternative therapeutic targets. To meet these challenges of global concern, polyamine synthesis/transport inhibitors may potentially be used as therapeutic agents against mycoses. Polyamines play essential roles in fungal growth, stress responses, and virulence, rendering their metabolic pathways attractive candidates for therapeutic intervention. A deeper understanding of the contribution of polyamine metabolism to fungal biology and pathogenicity is therefore critical to rationally translate polyamine-targeted approaches into clinical practice. This article reviews the theoretical basis and tested application of targeting polyamine metabolism as an antifungal strategy and provides perspectives into an as yet underexplored aspect of virulence among clinically relevant fungi.

items.title: The critical role of academic institutions in addressing chemical pollution.
items.abstract: Academic institutions and universities have for centuries greatly benefited society through education and the generation of new knowledge and technological advances. These benefits extend across multiple fields, from arts and humanities to sciences and engineering. Here, we highlight the pivotal role independent academic science, along with government-based science and monitoring, plays in safeguarding the planet from chemical pollution. This role has evolved as academic research is the feedstock of innovative and independent research and knowledge, which has served as the basis for many national regulatory policies and Multilateral Environmental Agreements (MEAs). This is, in part, due to the mandate of academic institutions to conduct curiosity- and issue-driven inquiry, in this case directed towards discovering and understanding the breadth of the challenges threatening human and ecosystem health and exploring the multitude of innovative solutions. Independent academic research will continue its role of developing new knowledge, innovative insights, and evidence-based solutions to support the newly formed Intergovernmental Science-Policy Panel on Chemicals, Waste, and Pollution (ISP-CWP), the Global Framework on Chemicals, and other fora. We argue that the contributions of independent academic science need support now, more than ever, by safeguarding academic freedom and recognizing the need for curiosity- and issue-driven inquiry. Academics need to engage with the public to illustrate the benefits that accrue from independent academic and government-based science, as a trusted source, countering misleading narratives, and to provide evidence upon which sound decisions to protect the public good can be made.

items.title: Geographic and Socioeconomic Disparities in Stage at Diagnosis and Nodal Burden Among Patients With HPV-Era Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Louisiana: A Population-Based Analysis.
items.abstract: Background Stage at diagnosis is a strong predictor of survival in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC). Gulf South population-level data on these disparities remain limited. Methods We analyzed 1344 patients with known stage at diagnosis from Louisiana Tumor Registry data (n = 1698 cases, 2018-2023). Geographic access was operationalized as straight-line distance from parish centroid to the nearest academic medical center (AMC), categorized as 50 miles. Multivariable logistic regression examined predictors of advanced-stage presentation (Stage III-IV) and nodal burden (N2-N3). Results Advanced-stage disease increased with distance from AMC (33.8%, 38.7%, 46.6%; Mantel-Haenszel χ 2 = 13.4, p = 0.0003). Distance > 50 miles independently predicted advanced-stage presentation (OR 1.56, p = 0.008) and high nodal burden (OR 1.44, p = 0.030). Black race (OR 2.25), Medicaid (OR 1.62), and smoking (OR 2.91) were independent predictors. HPV-positive histology was strongly protective (OR 0.33, p Conclusions Distance from specialty care independently predicts advanced-stage OPSCC and extensive nodal disease even after controlling for HPV status, race, insurance, and socioeconomic factors, supporting targeted teleoncology expansion and rural outreach initiatives.

items.title: The Influence of Nurses' Point-of-Care Documentation Practices on Nurse-Patient Interactions in Inpatient Care: A Qualitative Study.
items.abstract: Aim To generate practice-relevant insights into nurses' perceptions and practices regarding point-of-care documentation in inpatient settings and how these influence nurse-patient interactions and patient experiences. Design A qualitative Interpretive Description study. Methods Focused ethnography using participant observation and informal interviews. Data were generated between March and June 2025 in three inpatient wards at a Danish university hospital. Nurses and patients were purposively sampled from care situations involving point-of-care documentation. 30 nurses and 25 patients participated. 25 observations (135 h) were conducted. Data were analysed inductively using Interpretive Description. Data sources Field notes and interview transcripts from participant observations and informal interviews. Results An overarching theme: 'Professional judgement mediating point-of-care documentation and patient involvement' and two interrelated themes were identified: 'Point-of-care documentation as a conditional practice' and 'Unspoken understandings shaping patient involvement'. Nurses adapted when, where, and how they documented according to clinical routines, priorities and assessments of what was appropriate. Patients often remained silent because they trusted nurses, regarded documentation as the nurses' responsibility, or did not want to disturb busy nurses. Nurses also made assumptions about patients' knowledge and wishes without necessarily asking them. These patterns meant that point-of-care documentation did not automatically lead to patient involvement. When nurses explained the documentation or invited patients to contribute, patients described feeling more informed, heard, and secure. Conclusion Point-of-care documentation did not function as a person-centred practice but was incorporated into existing workflows and professional logics. A tension was evident between its intended role and its enactment in practice, with patient involvement remaining situational and contingent. Implications for the profession and/or patient care Introducing point-of-care is not sufficient to ensure patient involvement in documentation. Nurses and clinical leaders should consider how documentation is integrated into nurse-patient interactions and how nurses' professional judgement and established routines shape opportunities for patient participation. Impact Limited empirical knowledge exists on how point-of-care documentation is enacted and influences nurse-patient interaction and patient involvement. The findings highlight the need to consider the relational aspects of documentation when developing implementation and educational initiatives. Clinical leaders and educators can use these findings to inform discussions about how documentation practices can accommodate patient involvement. Reporting method SRQR reporting guidelines were followed.

items.title: The Role of Insurance Status and Race in Thyroid Nodule Evaluation.
items.abstract: Objective We examined the association between health insurance and race on thyroid nodule evaluation, including ultrasound referral, biopsy recommendation and completion, and time to diagnosis. Methods Retrospective, observational cohort study of 1404 adults (aged ≥ 18 years) referred for a new thyroid ultrasound between 2017 and 2019 at a tertiary academic center. Primary outcomes were (1) completion of recommended biopsy, (2) time from referral to ultrasound, and (3) time from ultrasound to biopsy. Secondary outcomes were ultrasound indication, visits in the year preceding ultrasound, and nodule presence and size. Results Among 1404 patients (77.1% women, 85.7% White, 64.3% privately insured), 59.8% had nodules on ultrasound. Biopsy was recommended in 360 patients (25.6%); among those, 82.8% were ultimately biopsied. Patients without insurance or on Medicaid were less likely to complete a recommended biopsy (OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.1-0.9). Black patients had a 23-day longer interval from ultrasound to biopsy (95% CI 13.5-35.1) than White patients. Black patients also required more prior visits before referral and presented with larger nodules. Ultrasounds for White patients were more frequently prompted by incidental findings; uninsured patients were less likely to have nodules detected incidentally on cross-sectional imaging. Conclusions Thyroid nodule evaluation is influenced by both insurance status and race. Underinsured patients-particularly those on Medicaid or without coverage-experience lower biopsy completion rates and longer diagnostic delays, independent of comorbidity or healthcare utilization. These findings underscore the critical role of insurance access in shaping timely and equitable endocrine evaluation. Level of evidence: 3

items.title: Humoral immunity to invasive meningococci following natural exposure and vaccination: insights into the MenW cc11 outbreak in the Netherlands.
items.abstract: Neisseria meningitidis colonization can result in invasive meningococcal disease. Following a meningococcus C outbreak in 2001-2002 and a subsequent MenC vaccination campaign, a MenW outbreak occurred in the Netherlands in 2017-2018, mostly caused by the same clonal complex 11 (cc11) as the earlier MenC outbreak. We investigated how meningococcal lineage and differences in humoral immunity to invasive MenC and MenW isolates may explain the MenW outbreak. Using rabbit serum bactericidal antibody assays (rSBAs), we assessed the serological protection against invasive meningococcal isolates ( n = 56) from the Netherlands (2001-2018), representing diverse serogroups and clonal complexes, using pooled serum from unvaccinated or vaccinated individuals. Prior to the MenW outbreak, a serum pool from unvaccinated individuals showed limited bactericidal activity against MenW strains, but higher activity against MenC strains. In serum from unvaccinated individuals, increased binding of immunoglobulin (Ig) A and IgM to unencapsulated, compared to encapsulated, strains was observed. After vaccination, capsule-specific antibodies increased, accompanied by enhanced antibody binding to encapsulated strains. Pooled serum from MenACWY-vaccinated individuals demonstrated bactericidal activity against all invasive isolates. However, sera from some individuals failed to kill MenC and especially MenW strains. In addition, sera from vaccinated adolescents showed higher SBA titers than those from vaccinated older adults. Our findings suggest that the 2017-2018 MenW cc11 outbreak in the Netherlands resulted from a combination of low naturally acquired population immunity to MenW and enhanced virulence of cc11 strains. Continuous surveillance of meningococcal epidemiology and population immunity remains essential to inform vaccine strategies and prevent future outbreaks. Importance The underlying cause of meningococcal outbreaks is only partly understood. Following a meningococcal C (MenC) outbreak of clonal type cc11, the same clonal complex was a major cause of a subsequent MenW outbreak in the Netherlands and other countries. We investigated natural and vaccine-induced immunity to invasive meningococcal isolates. Preceding the MenW outbreak, natural immunity in the population was lower to clinical MenW isolates compared with clinical MenC isolates of the previous outbreak. Natural immunity to these bacteria was mainly targeting membrane proteins with limited reactivity to the capsule in unvaccinated individuals. These data indicate that following meningococcal outbreaks, population immunity improves but is insufficient to prevent outbreaks by different meningococcal lineages. MenACWY vaccine-induced antibodies were bactericidal to all isolates tested, confirming the effectiveness of the vaccine to protect the population.

items.title: Correlates of Clinical Improvement of a Mobile Child Development-Community Policing (CD-CP) Program.
items.abstract: Purpose The Child Development-Community Policing (CD-CP) program aims to prevent the development of PTSD in children exposed to violence (CEV). The current study examines administrative data of a CD-CP program involving collaboration between law enforcement and clinicians who provide an immediate, mobilized response to CEV in the community. Materials and methods Case closure forms, containing case characteristics, interventions, and outcomes of 791 program participants, were examined from 2020-2023 through bivariate cross-tabulations and binary logistic regression analysis. The outcome included clinical improvement demonstrated by a documented reduction in acute traumatic stress symptoms. Results Mobile CD-CP program components that were associated with clinical improvement in the bivariate cross-tabulations included receipt of short-term acute trauma intervention, χ 2 (1)=182.00, Cramér's V = .48, providing psychoeducation to the guardian, χ 2 (1)=165.70, Cramér's V = .46, and making contact within 72 hours, χ 2 (1)=125.53, Cramér's V = .40 (all significant at p 2 (8)=231.53, p 2 of 53.1%; key correlates included receipt of the short-term acute trauma intervention, in-person service delivery, and intervention dosage. Discussion While several studies have been published on the original CD-CP model, the current study provides support for an adapted, mobilized CD-CP program. Core components of the mobile CD-CP program include delivering short-term acute traumatic stress interventions, responding to families within 72 hours of referral, and making in-person contact. Conclusion The study provides support that the adapted CD-CP program is associated with decreased acute stress disorder symptoms, and future research should explore if this leads to the prevention of PTSD.

items.title: Combined anterior cruciate ligament-medial collateral ligament injuries: Favourable outcomes with non-operative management of Grade I injuries and no clear benefit of acute over delayed treatment in Grade II and III Injuries-A multicentre retrospective study of the Francophone Arthroscopic Society.
items.abstract: Purpose To compare medial collateral ligament (MCL) management strategies in patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) for combined anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-MCL injuries. Primary outcomes were functional and return-to-sport measures; the secondary outcome was reoperation-free survivorship at one and three years. Methods A retrospective review of 731 ACLRs performed between January 2020 and June 2022 identified patients with combined ACL-MCL injuries treated with ACLR and either operative or non-operative MCL management. Multiligament injuries and concomitant cartilage or realignment procedures were excluded. Clinical examination included Lachman, pivot-shift and valgus stress testing; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessed MCL and meniscal pathology. Outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), Simple Knee Value (SKV) score, Tegner and ACL-Return to Sport after Injury (RSI) scores. Analyses considered MCL strategy, treatment type and timing (acute, within 12 weeks, vs. delayed). Reoperations, ACL re-rupture, contralateral ACL injury and survivorship were recorded. Results A total of 414 patients were included, with a mean age of 30.9 ± 10.2 years and a mean follow-up of 18.5 ± 5.2 months. Of these, 98 patients underwent operative MCL management and 316 were managed non-operatively. Operatively managed patients had more severe clinical instability and more MCL ruptures on MRI. Both groups improved in patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). Operative management was associated with lower IKDC and SKV scores in both unadjusted (p = 0.003 for both) and adjusted analyses (adjusted mean difference -5.51; 95% confidence interval [CI] -8.92 to -2.10; p = 0.002 for IKDC; -7.38; 95% CI -11.91 to -2.85; p = 0.001 for SKV), with no significant associations for ACL-RSI or Tegner. Given greater baseline injury severity in the operative group, this association may partly reflect confounding by indication rather than a true effect of surgery. No statistically significant differences in functional or return-to-sport outcomes were found between acute and delayed surgical treatment for either Grade II or Grade III MCL injuries, though subgroup sizes were small. Reoperation and re-rupture rates were similar between strategies. Conclusion In combined ACL-MCL injuries, non-operative management of Grade I MCL injuries was associated with favourable outcomes. For Grade II and III injuries, PROMs did not differ significantly between acute and delayed surgical management in this cohort. Subgroup sample sizes for these timing comparisons were small, and the findings should be considered exploratory rather than conclusive. The optimal timing of surgical intervention for higher-grade concomitant MCL injuries remains an open question requiring an adequately powered prospective study. items.title: Sleep in Non-Offending Parents of Children and Adolescents Exposed to Maltreatment: The Association with Parental Victimization History.
items.abstract: Objectives Sleep among non-offending parents of children exposed to maltreatment is insufficiently described, particularly in relation to parents' own victimization histories. We described sleep characteristics and examined differences according to parental childhood maltreatment and adulthood victimization. Methods The analytic cohort comprised 585 non-offending parents recruited through a national learning and coping center for children and adolescents with substantiated maltreatment. Childhood maltreatment was assessed with the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire and adulthood victimization with items on physical violence and sexual assault. Participants were classified into four groups: no victimization, adulthood only, childhood only, and both childhood and adulthood victimization. Sleep was self-reported for weekdays and weekends, and probable insomnia was defined using an approximation of DSM-5 criteria. Continuous outcomes were analyzed with robust linear regression and probable insomnia with modified Poisson regression, adjusted for age, sex, and education. Results Overall, 74.0% reported childhood and/or adulthood victimization, and 28.2% had probable insomnia. Compared with parents without reported victimization, all three victimization groups had lower sleep efficiency, greater sleep deficit, more wake after sleep onset, and shorter weekend sleep duration. Probable insomnia was more prevalent in the childhood-only group (PR 1.85, 95% CI 1.09-3.14) and the combined group (PR 1.86, 95% CI 1.16-2.99). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar estimates. Conclusions Non-offending parents of children exposed to maltreatment experience substantial sleep difficulties. Associations were most consistent for wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, and sleep deficit, and were also evident for sleep duration and probable insomnia, particularly among parents with childhood or repeated life-course victimization.

items.title: Dermatophytosis Among Schools Children in the Republic of Guinea.
items.abstract: Dermatophytosis, particularly tinea capitis (TC), is a common fungal infection among schoolchildren in Africa. However, its specific risk factors remain poorly understood, especially in Guinea. This descriptive, cross-sectional study aimed to assess the prevalence and associated factors of TC among primary school children in Guinea. From July 2021 to March 2023, the survey was conducted in ten schools across five different regions: Conakry, Boké, Labé, Kankan, and Nzérékoré. A total of 802 children aged 4 to 17 were randomly selected for a clinical examination of skin, nail, and scalp lesions. Sociodemographic data and clinical risk factors were collected using a questionnaire. Results showed a high prevalence of clinical dermatophytosis, affecting 61% (n = 487) of the children examined. Statistical analysis revealed that male sex, home haircutting, and family history were significantly associated with the infection (p < 0.0001). Multivariate analysis confirmed that male sex (OR = 2.26) and residence in Nzérékoré (OR = 2.60), a region characterized by high humidity and dense forest cover, were independent risk factors. Among the 200 dermatophyte isolates confirmed through sequencing, Trichophyton soudanense was the most prevalent species, accounting for 50% of the cases. It was followed by Microsporum audouinii (29%), Trichophyton rubrum (20%), and Trichophyton violaceum (1%). These findings highlight the significant public health burden of dermatophytosis among Guinean schoolchildren, particularly in areas with humid climates. Further research is needed to improve our understanding and develop effective prevention strategies.

items.title: Drone-Based Antenna Beam Calibration in the High Arctic
items.abstract: Precision calibration is a critical requirement for future ultra-low-frequency observations of the early universe. The Array of Long Baseline Antennas for Taking Radio Observations from the Seventy-Ninth Parallel (ALBATROS), a radio interferometer located in the Canadian high Arctic, is designed to map Galactic foreground emission as a pathfinder for these future experiments. Accurate antenna beam characterization at these frequencies is therefore essential, yet remains uniquely challenging. We present PteroSoar, a custom-built drone platform equipped with a calibrated radio-frequency transmitter that enables controlled, in-situ measurements of low-frequency antenna beams. As an initial demonstration, we produce a two-dimensional beam map of an LWA antenna at 50 MHz to a precision of approximately [Formula: see text] near zenith. We identify the dominant sources of systematic uncertainty, including timing imprecision, and outline hardware and software improvements that are expected to reduce beam measurement uncertainties to below [Formula: see text]. This target is sub-dominant to the [Formula: see text] amplitude variability introduced by ionospheric scintillation at these frequencies, providing a practical pathway toward precision beam calibration for ALBATROS and other ultra-low-frequency radio experiments.

items.title: Universal small-scale fluctuation spectrum of Vlasov-Poisson turbulence
items.abstract: The thermal' fluctuation spectrum of the electric field arising due to particle noise in a quiescent Vlasov--Poisson plasma was derived in the 1960s. Here, we derive the universal fluctuation spectrum of the electric field, at Debye and sub-Debye scales, for a turbulent Vlasov--Poisson plasma. This spectrum arises from what is likely to be the final cascade’—a universal regime to be encountered at the extreme small-scale end of any turbulent cascade in a nearly collisionless plasma. The cascaded invariant is the generalized (negative) entropy C 2 , which is the quadratic Casimir invariant of the particle distribution function. C 2 cascades to small scales in both position and velocity space via both linear and nonlinear phase mixing, in such a way that the timescales associated with the two processes are `critically balanced’ at every scale. We construct a phenomenological scaling theory of the fluctuation spectrum of C 2 in ( k , s ) space—and hence of the electric field in k space—in arbitrary dimensions, where k and s are the spatial and velocity wavenumbers, respectively. The electric-field spectrum is sufficiently steep for the nonlinear mixing to be controlled by the largest-scale electric fluctuations, and so the C 2 cascade resembles the Batchelor cascade of a passive scalar, albeit in the kinetic phase space. The conclusions of our theory are corroborated by direct numerical simulations of a forced 1D-1V plasma. We predict that the cascade is ultimately terminated at the (spatial) wavenumber where the turbulent electric-field spectrum gives way to the fluctuation spectrum associated with discrete particle noise; this transition scale is set by the amplitude of the turbulent electric fields and the plasma parameter. The characteristic timescale for this small-scale cutoff to be reached is the dynamical time of phase-space mixing times a logarithmic factor in the plasma parameter—this is the first concrete demonstration of this property of Vlasov–Poisson turbulence, analogous to how fluid turbulence dissipates energy at a rate independent (or nearly independent) of molecular diffusion. A key consequence is that the phase-space cascade enables the irreversibility of particle heating to be achieved on collisionless timescales. The mean distribution function arising from this process (in the case of forced 1D-1V turbulence) is shown to be obtainable from both quasilinear and statistical-mechanical considerations and is not a Maxwellian, but a flat top. A corollary of this work is the need for the development of a turbulent collision operator that would describe the effect of sub-Debye-scale turbulence on super-Debye-scale dynamics.

items.title: Quantgraph: A receding-horizon quantum graph solver
items.abstract: Dynamic programming is a cornerstone of graph-based optimization. While effective, it scales unfavorably with problem size. In this work, we present QuantGraph, a two-stage quantum-enhanced framework that casts local and global graph-optimization problems as quantum searches over discrete-trajectory spaces. The solver is designed to operate efficiently by first finding a sequence of locally optimal transitions in the graph (local stage), without considering full trajectories. The accumulated cost of the resulting candidate acts as a threshold that prunes the search space (up to 60% reduction for certain examples). The subsequent global stage, based on this threshold, refines the solution. To achieve scalability and robustness, we draw on principles from control theory and embed QuantGraph’s global stage within a receding-horizon model-predictive-control scheme. This classical layer stabilizes and guides the quantum search, improving precision and reducing computational burden. In practice, the resulting closed-loop system exhibits robust behavior and lower query complexity. Notably, for a fixed control horizon and query budget, QuantGraph supports approximately twice as many control discretization bits while still benefiting from Grover search’s inherent quadratic speedup compared with classical methods.

items.title: Nonlocal corrections to scalar field effective action in de Sitter spacetime
items.abstract: We investigate the one-loop effective action for a test scalar field in a general Friedmann-LemaîtreRobertson-Walker (FLRW) background, specifically focusing on quantum corrections up to the second order in the interaction strength. By employing the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, we derive the equation of motion for the field expectation value, which incorporates not only the standard local radiative corrections but also novel nonlocal features: a memory term and a stochastic noise term. We identify all ultraviolet divergent structures within these nonlocal terms and provide a consistent renormalization procedure. To analyze the physical impact of these terms, we apply a local approximation under the assumption of slowly-varying fields, by which the memory term acts as a negative contribution to the drift coefficient. As a concrete application, we consider a massive ϕ[4] theory and show that these one-loop corrections lead to a suppression of the field variance in the infrared regime compared to the tree-level results.

items.title: CFHT MegaCam Two Deep Fields Imaging Survey. I. Overview
items.abstract: We present the Two Deep Fields Imaging Survey (2DFIS), a wide-field imaging program conducted with the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) targeting two astrophysically distinct regions: one containing a repeating fast radio burst (FRB) source and another hosting a candidate of a rotating galaxy cluster. Achieving a depth of r ∼ 26 mag, the survey enables a search for faint optical counterparts and environmental signatures associated with the FRB, while the deep multiband imaging of the cluster field provides the input data for a future weak-lensing analysis of its mass distribution. This paper describes the observing strategy and data-processing methodology adopted for 2DFIS, including the use of the LSST Science Pipelines with survey-specific adaptations for CFHT/MegaCam data. We outline a complete workflow for transforming raw CFHT exposures into science-ready data products, including calibrated single-epoch images, multiband coadded mosaics, and extensive source catalogs. These data products provide the foundation for ongoing and future studies of FRB host environments, cluster mass reconstruction, and related cosmological applications.

items.title: Strain-tuned electronic structure of epitaxial films of the bilayer strontium ruthenate: Sr 3 Ru 2 O 7
items.abstract: We report a combined study of the low-energy electronic band structure of epitaxial Sr3Ru2O7 films using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and density functional theory (DFT). To investigate the effects of substrate dependence on the band structure, Sr3Ru2O7 thin films are epitaxially grown on SrTiO3 (100) (STO) and (LaAlO3)0.3(Sr2TaAlO6)0.7 (100) (LSAT) substrates using molecular beam epitaxy. The measured and calculated Fermi surfaces clearly show substantial changes in the Fermi surface topologies that originate from the underlying strain states. The compressively strained film grown on LSAT exhibits Fermi surface features consistent with an orthorhombic-like symmetry; and the tensile-strained film grown on STO features a tetragonal-like surface symmetry. In addition, the ARPES data for both films indicate weakly dispersive spectral features within ∼ 15 meV below the Fermi level. Our observations highlight the strong sensitivity of the low-energy electronic structure of Sr3Ru2O7 to epitaxial strain. These observations also establish substrate engineering as a promising approach for tailoring the electronic structure of Sr3Ru2O7 in thin films, with potential applications in strain-controlled oxide devices.

items.title: Structured generalized sliced Wasserstein distance for keV X-ray polarization analysis with gas pixel detector
items.abstract: Because of the special angular distribution of excited electrons by the photoelectric effect, the gas pixel detector (GPD) is effective in measuring keV X-ray polarization of astrophysical events (e.g. gamma-ray bursts), by capturing ionization tracks of excited electrons as polarized images. Traditionally, the emission angles of photoelectrons are extracted from polarized images first, and statistics are then performed on these angles to infer the polarization direction and intensity. However, observation with the wide field of view requires the incident angle of X-rays not directly attainable through the traditional analysis process. In this paper, we propose using the generalized sliced Wasserstein (GSW) distance, projected by neural networks with random weights, as a completely data-driven approach to analyze X-ray polarization based on two-dimensional polarized images. We find the structures of the randomized neural networks matter when focusing on different aspects of the polarized images, and take advantage of the discrimination abilities by different neural network structures. The proposed method, named the structured GSW distance, successfully distinguishes polarized images with different configurations of incident angles and polarization directions. Furthermore, we build a simplified statistical model based on the von Mises distribution and the circular Wasserstein distance and compare the model against the proposed method, showing their high consistency. The computational method reported in this paper may benefit GPD-based polarimetry in astroparticle experiments and also pattern analysis on raw data from pixel detectors.

items.title: Pseudogapped Fermi liquids from emergent quasiparticles
items.abstract: We propose an interacting model that is exactly solvable in any spatial dimension and gives rise to a Fermi liquid (FL) featuring a pseudogapped (PG) single-particle spectral function and a vanishing quasiparticle (QP) weight at half-filling, without invoking Mott physics. The PG originates from a purely fermionic mechanism through emergent QPs arising from a correlated hopping interaction. By employing an appropriate coherent-state basis, we derive a Gaussian path-integral representation of the partition function, which enables systematic treatments of deviations from the Gaussian limit using standard many-body techniques, such as diagrammatic perturbation theory or mean-field theory. We explicitly demonstrate and discuss several properties of the exactly solvable limit on the square lattice, including the mechanism for temperature-dependent PG opening, the singular behavior of the self-energy, the violation of the Luttinger sum rule, and the role of Luttinger and Fermi surfaces. Finally, we explore quantum phase transitions between PG-FLs and Landau FLs.

items.title: CFHT MegaCam Two Deep Fields Imaging Survey. II. Decoding the Lensing Profile of a “Rotating” Cluster with Deep CFHT Imaging
items.abstract: We present a multiwavelength analysis of the galaxy cluster RXCJ0110.0+1358 (z = 0.058), a rotating cluster candidate, combining deep Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) imaging, Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) photometry, spectroscopic redshifts, and XMM-Newton X-ray observations. We find a clear difference between the optical galaxy distribution and the X-ray morphology: the catalog selected galaxies form two pronounced concentrations in the southeast (SE) and northwest (NW), whereas the X-ray emission exhibits a single, smoothly extended component centered near the SE brightest cluster galaxy. The combined galaxy sample exhibits significant spatially correlated kinematic substructure and a rotation-like signal whose fitted projected axis approximately separates the two concentrations. Our weak lensing analysis identifies SE as the main detected mass concentration, spatially associated with the extended X-ray emission, and yields log (M 200 / M ⊙) = 14.0 4 − 0.40 + 0.24 for this component. No significant weak lensing peak is detected at the NW optical center. Our results favor an interpretation in which the SE and NW galaxy populations, separated on the sky and differing in mean redshift, produce a rotation-like signal when analyzed together.

items.title: The retraction epidemic in science across publishers, fields, and countries
items.abstract: Retractions are considered a proxy signal of problems in the scientific record. Prior studies have documented a rise in retractions, but the functional form of this growth, once the expansion of scientific output is accounted for, has not been quantified. We use one of the largest open bibliographic databases to develop incidence metrics normalized by population cohorts: retractions per publication and per active author by year of publication. Applying an epidemiological framework that models counts with exposure, we find evidence of exponential growth in retraction incidence, with approximately a 5-year doubling time at both the paper and author levels. These patterns vary significantly across scientific disciplines, publishing organizations, and national research systems. While scientific output is becoming more democratized globally, retractions are concentrated in fewer countries, creating a “concentration” paradox that calls for targeted monitoring. Despite exponential growth, the absolute incidence remains low (0.20% in 2023), allowing for corrective intervention. Incidence-based monitoring provides a framework for evaluating policies that safeguard research integrity at scale.

items.title: Power Studies For Two-Sample and Goodness-of-Fit Methods For Multivariate Data
items.abstract: We present the results of a large number of simulation studies regarding the power of various goodness-of-fit as well as nonparametric two-sample tests for multivariate data. In two dimensions this includes both continuous and discrete data, in higher dimensions continuous data only. In general no single method can be relied upon to provide good power: any one method may be quite good for some combination of null hypothesis and alternative and may fail badly for another. Based on the results of these studies we propose a fairly small number of methods chosen such that for any of the case studies included here at least one of the methods has good power, and we check these selections by leave-one-out cross-validation. In our case studies the aggregated MMD test as implemented in MD2sample is the best single method for the two-sample problem; it differs from the published MMDAgg test, and the result should not be assumed to carry over to it. For the goodness-of-fit problem in two dimensions, chi-square tests with a small number of bins are best, especially if the marginals are the same under the null hypothesis and the alternative. In five dimensions a hybrid test, a two-sample MMD test against a large Monte Carlo sample from the null hypothesis, has clearly higher power than the goodness-of-fit methods. The studies were carried out using the R packages MD2sample and MDgof, available from CRAN. All results, together with the true type I errors, are included in the packages, and the scripts that produce every table and figure are part of this paper.

items.title: Imaging the radio-wave emission from extensive air showers
items.abstract: We propose a new way to observe cosmic-ray-induced air showers by imaging the radio emission. With simulations we demonstrate key features for imaging the radio-wave emission from air showers, which show similarities to the well-established atmospheric imaging Cherenkov technique in gamma-ray astronomy. In addition, we find that imaging the emission with a camera, consisting of multiple antennas, resolves emission that is not accessible to a single antenna. Pursuing this technique, with a camera operating in the GHz frequency domain, might be beneficial ultra-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy (beyond 100 TeV) and other studies that include detailed observations of air showers.

items.title: Lateral shift as a control knob for localization transitions in a quasiperiodic ladder
items.abstract: This work reports rich localization-delocalization transitions in a quasiperiodic ladder, of which the two legs are subject to the same quasiperiodic onsite potential but can be shifted laterally relative to each other. It is found that the lateral shift between the two legs effectively generates a magnetic flux in the reciprocal momentum space. The lateral shift thus offers a control knob, allowing us to access and simulate rich phenomena including magnetic-flux-enhanced localization, magnetic-flux-suppressed localization, and magnetic-flux-induced reentrant localization transitions. The underlying physical mechanisms as well as the phase boundaries separating localized, mixed, and extended phases are both qualitatively and quantitatively understood, based on a band-structure analysis that employs a commensurate approximation to the quasiperiodic potential, requiring only unit cells of small to modest sizes. Our work establishes that a simple lateral shift between two quasiperiodic chains generates a synthetic magnetic flux in momentum space, providing a single experimental knob to access enhanced, suppressed, and reentrant localization.

items.title: MeerKAT thousand-pulsar polarization array: Searches for ultralight axionlike dark matter
items.abstract: We construct Pulsar Polarisation Arrays (PPA), using regular pulsars monitored in MeerKAT’s Thousand Pulsar Array (TPA) Programme, to search for Axion-like Dark Matter (ALDM) within Milky Way. Specifically, from a catalogue of 1237 regular pulsars, we select the 50 ones with the highest signal-to-noise ratio and set upper limits on the ALDM Chern-Simons coupling. We find no signals with statistical significance over the mass range of [ 10 − 23 , 10 − 20 ] e V in the six-year MeerKAT’s data. By combining the high-quality TPA pulsars and the accurate ionospheric subtraction of , we establish the most sensitive upper limits to the date on the ALDM Chern-Simons coupling, namely ≲ 10 − 14 − 3 × 10 − 13 GeV − 1 , for the mass range of [ 10 − 23 , 10 − 21 ] e V except at m a ≃ 1.3 × 10 − 22 eV. This study highlights the great promise of regular-pulsar PPAs, whose large population and flexible design open a powerful new window on fundamental physics with next-generation radio telescopes.

items.title: Multiparameter Maximum Information States for Coherent Diffraction Measurements
items.abstract: In metrology, Fisher information is an important metric that quantifies the precision that can be achieved in a measurement. For optical measurements using coherent light it has been shown that Fisher information can be expressed simply using the scattering matrix of the system. Fisher information can be maximized over the input modes to achieve maximum information states, which produce optimally precise estimates for a parameter when the system is limited by photon noise. Here, we extend this approach to multiparameter estimation, in which case Fisher information takes the form of a matrix. We consider several scalar functions of the Fisher matrix to optimize the precision in multiple parameters at the same time. We also consider strategies for dealing with nuisance parameters, which can degrade the achievable precision of other parameters but are not of interest to measure. We corroborate our findings numerically using a scattering system of 2D coupled dipoles.

items.title: Higher dimensional loop quantum black hole in de Sitter spacetime: quasinormal modes and shadow signatures
items.abstract: We investigate the dynamical and optical signatures of a higher-dimensional loop-quantum-corrected black hole in a de Sitter background. The physically admissible nonextremal solutions are restricted to a finite mass interval bounded by the extremal and Nariai configurations. We find that loop-quantum corrections produce moderate shifts in the scalar quasinormal spectrum, whereas increasing the spacetime dimension has a substantially stronger effect, enhancing both the oscillation frequency and the damping rate. All calculated modes have negative imaginary parts, supporting dynamical stability against massless scalar perturbations in the parameter range considered. Comparison with the corresponding classical backgrounds shows that the quantum-corrected spectrum remains continuously connected to the classical photon-sphere branch, with the quantum correction producing predominantly quantitative modifications. The black-hole shadow is also sensitive to the loop-quantum parameter, the cosmological constant, and the spacetime dimension, with extra dimensions generally reducing its size. Comparison with the Event Horizon Telescope measurement of M87 $$^*$$ ∗ constrains the allowed model parameters. Together, these results show that quasinormal modes and shadow observables provide complementary probes of loop-quantum corrections and higher-dimensional effects in the strong-field regime.

items.title: Clinical Impairment in Advanced Alzheimer's (High Alzheimer's Disease Neuropathological Change) Correlates with Quantitative Neurofibrillary Tangle Measures and Co-pathologies.
items.abstract: The current diagnostic criteria for Alzheimer's disease (AD) define discrete biological stages of the disease. Whereas discrete staging simplifies diagnosis, treatment, and participant stratification in clinical trials, discrete disease categories may mask a considerable range of variability in disease severity, even at what is pathologically considered "end stage" disease. We aimed to characterize the contributions of phosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) pathology and co-pathologies to variability in dementia severity in brain donors diagnosed with a high level of AD neuropathological change (ADNC). In a cohort of 197 donors with a primary diagnosis of high ADNC, we computed the association between quantitative measures of neocortical NFT load and an informant-based measure of clinical impairment. We examined the impact of co-pathologies on residuals from the canonical pathology-impairment relationship estimated in donors without known significant co-pathologies. We found a positive association (Spearman ρ195=0.321 ) between cortical NFT load and the clinical impairment measure. Clinical impairment was significantly greater than expected for NFT load in presence of co-pathologies, including limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (stage 2 or 3) and cerebrovascular disease. Categorizing high ADNC as a single homogeneous category masks a considerable range of pathological severity that contributes to clinical impairment. Complementing discrete staging with continuous measures of tau pathology and probabilistic measures of co-pathologies will improve clinicopathologic studies needed for a precision approach to diagnosis and treatment. items.title: The Critical Behavior of Brain Activity Across Mammalian Species.
items.abstract: This study investigates the functional implications of anatomical brain connectivity across 103 mammalian species, spanning 12 taxonomic orders and brain volumes over four orders of magnitude. It asks whether functional brain activity can be inferred from anatomy alone using whole-brain models. For each connectome, we construct a brain model composed of binary units interacting through structural connections, assuming brain activity operates near a critical point between order and disorder. We focus on two functional measures at criticality: the diversity of network states and susceptibility to external input, as functions of brain volume, known to shape mammalian connectome topology, spatial constraints, and network information. The results indicate that larger brains support richer dynamical repertoires and stronger responses to perturbations, persisting when controlling for shared evolutionary history. Furthermore, long-range connections are crucial for maintaining both the diversity of network states and the susceptibility to external input, and their contribution is stronger in larger brains. Finally, stochastic oscillation models show that the repertoire of synchronization patterns scales with brain size, supporting the view that larger connectomes enhance functional complexity. Our results suggest that evolutionary increases in brain size and associated connectome topology changes are accompanied by greater functional capacity driven by critical dynamics.

items.title: Plasma Metabolic Proteomics Links Phenoconversion and Disease-Specific Brain 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Pattern Expressions in Isolated REM Sleep Behavior Disorder.
items.abstract: Cellular metabolic dysfunction has emerged as a key contributor to neurodegeneration, but its role in Lewy body disease (LBD), particularly during prodromal stages, remains unclear. We investigated targeted blood-based proteomic profiles related to metabolic pathways across the REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)-LBD continuum, and explored their potential as biomarkers of disease severity and phenoconversion. In this prospective cohort study, we enrolled 116 patients across the RBD-LBD continuum, including 47 with polysomnography-confirmed isolated RBD (iRBD), 45 with Parkinson's disease (PD) with RBD, and 24 with dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) with RBD, along with 30 age-matched healthy controls. Plasma concentrations of 92 metabolism-related proteins were measured using a proximity extension assay. Motor function, neuropsychological assessments, and brain 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging were obtained. Patients with iRBD were prospectively followed for up to 4 years to monitor phenoconversion. Compared with controls, 16 differentially expressed metabolism-related proteins were identified across the RBD-LBD continuum, with predominant enrichment in neutrophil degranulation pathways. These protein alterations were mainly observed in patients with clinically manifest LBD, with DOPA decarboxylase demonstrating the most prominent differential expression and significant correlations with levodopa equivalent daily dose. In contrast, only N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was significantly upregulated in patients with iRBD. Elevated NT-proBNP levels were associated with orthostatic intolerance, increased PD- and DLB-related metabolic brain pattern expressions, and earlier phenoconversion. Plasma metabolic proteins showed stage-specific alterations across the RBD-LBD continuum. NT-proBNP may have potential as a marker of short-term phenoconversion risk in iRBD. ANN NEUROL 2026.

items.title: Decentering the Observer: A Neurocognitive Perspective on the Copernican Revolution.
items.abstract: The Copernican Revolution required humans to adopt a model of the universe that contradicted immediate perceptual experience. This article examines why heliocentrism is cognitively less intuitive than the experience of a stationary Earth and situates this problem within the broader history of the "Copernican turn" in philosophy and neuroscience. Integrating research on embodied spatial cognition, conceptual change, executive control, and science learning, we propose an observer-decentering framework in which egocentric representations and stable bodily experience constrain the acquisition of observer-independent scientific models. These mechanisms are not presented as causes of historical resistance to heliocentrism, but as enduring cognitive constraints that scientific reasoning must negotiate. We distinguish this account from Georg Northoff's proposed Copernican revolution in neuroscience, which concerns the brain-mind/world relationship, and consider empirical evidence showing how relational scaffolding can help learners coordinate Earth-based observations with space-based models. Heliocentrism is thus treated as a paradigmatic case of how scientific reasoning can transcend, without eliminating, observer-centered experience.

items.title: Highly selective visual circuits in mouse frontal cortex.
items.abstract: It is thought that elementary stimulus encoding happens primarily in the sensory cortex. We found that frontal cortex neurons in awake mice show highly selective visual spatial receptive fields, akin to the visual cortex. These neurons were most sensitive to binocular visual space, required retinotopically aligned V1 input and sent functional axonal feedback throughout the visual cortex, particularly binocular V1. This reveals a cortex-wide circuit suitable for selective feedback control of spatial vision.

items.title: A mitochondrial mechanism of nuclear histone acetylation dynamically regulates neuronal plasticity: a gateway to stress resilience, and a boosted efficacy of fluoxetine with exercise.
items.abstract: Histone acetylation is a key regulatory process of brain physiology and is dysregulated in main psychiatric illnesses. There is a gap in understanding intracellular sources of acetyl moieties for histone acetylation underlying brain functions. Here, we studied unknown source, fate, and consequences of mitochondrial carnitine acetyltransferase system for nuclear histone acetylation to regulate neuronal plasticity of a key sub-region of the hippocampus important for mood and cognition, the ventral dentate gyrus (vDG), in physiology and stress responses. We further studied the relevance of this novel mechanism for therapeutic efficacy. Using a cell-type specific loss-of-function genetic approach, we showed a physiological requirement of carnitine acetyltransferase (CrAT) expression in vDG glutamatergic neurons with the corresponding availability of the acetylcarnitine ester and acetyl-CoA for global and locus-specific acetylation of the active site lysine (K27) of histone H3 (H3K27ac) and key behaviors. Using four pharmacological approaches to perturb this pathway and fiber photometry, we found that induction of CrAT activity leads to an enhanced and specific acetylation of H3K27, but not of a different site (K9), to maintain neuronal activity and coordinated behavioral performances. This phenomenon is suppressed by blocking activity of nuclear histone acetyltransferase P300 and by blocking transferable acetyl moieties with acetyl-aminocarnitine, the isostere of acetylcarnitine. Next, we found that chronic but not shorter stressful exposure disrupts this mechanism leading to a loss of resilience to stress. Conversely, induction of CrAT expression in vDG glutamatergic neurons boosted stress resilience similarly to supplementation of acetylcarnitine, suggesting that, in the absence of endogenous CrAT, vDG neurons must rely on exogenous supply of acetylcarnitine to feed histone acetylation. Furthermore, stress- and genetic-induced ablation of CrAT expression led to compromised neuronal activity of vDG glutamatergic neurons during behavioral performances. Lastly, we found that this physiological mechanism is transcriptionally activated by a combined strategy with exercise and fluoxetine in a rodent model otherwise resistant to fluoxetine. The mitochondrial-nuclear model underlying brain functions introduced here represents an alternative model of intracellular roots subserving histone acetylation to regulate key brain functions and also provide molecular mechanisms for combined intervention strategies that may be useful in translation to human behavior and psychopathologies.
