items.title: Sex-specific reprogramming of immune and endocannabinoid networks in the placenta following prenatal cannabinoid exposure.
items.abstract: Cannabis use during pregnancy is increasing, yet its effects on placental biology and developmental programming remain poorly defined despite their critical role. Because the placenta expresses a functional endocannabinoid system and coordinates immune and metabolic pathways essential for fetal brain development, it represents a key target of exogenous cannabinoids. We performed parallel whole-transcriptomic analyses of placentae from pregnant rats exposed to cannabinoid vapor (THC:CBD 10:1; n = 40) and from a human pregnancy cohort (n = 93; 23 cannabis-exposed). Across species, prenatal cannabinoid exposure suppressed placental immune gene networks regulating neutrophil chemotaxis, cytokine signaling, and T cell-mediated responses, with pronounced male-specific vulnerability. In rats, exposure increased placental anandamide, oleoylethanolamide, and arachidonic acid levels and altered endocannabinoid-enriched transcriptional modules linked to nitric oxide-mediated neuroprotection and synaptic signaling. In the human cohort, immune network suppression was associated with increased anxiety-related behaviors, whereas phospholipid metabolism modules correlated with depressive symptom measures. These cross-species findings demonstrate sex-specific reprogramming of placental immune and lipid-endocannabinoid networks following prenatal cannabinoid exposure and implicate the placenta as a mechanistic interface linking maternal cannabis use to offspring neurobehavioral vulnerability.

items.title: Mycobacterial phenolic glycolipid triggers ATP-mediated neuronal signalling and cough.
items.abstract: Cough drives respiratory pathogen transmission, yet how microorganisms directly engage host nociceptive neurons to trigger cough is largely unknown. We previously demonstrated that Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) glycolipid sulfolipid-1 activates neurons and induces cough. Here we identify a phenolic glycolipid (PGL) produced by the hypertransmissible Mtb strain HN878 as an additional activator of mouse and human nociceptive neurons, and we show that purified PGL is sufficient to induce cough in guinea pigs. Together, PGL and sulfolipid-1 elicit greater neuronal activation than either glycolipid alone. By synthesizing various PGL analogues, we show that neuroactivity depends on saccharide chain length and structure. Mechanistically, neurons release ATP extracellularly following PGL stimulation, which engages neuronal P2X3 purinergic receptors. This effect is blocked by a P2X3 antagonist, gefapixant. These findings reveal a neuronal activation pathway co-opted by certain Mtb strains to induce cough and suggest inhibition of purinergic signalling as a potential strategy to block airborne spread of Mtb.

items.title: Rewiring cancer: peripheral nerves control tumours.
items.abstract: The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of cancer biology. Once considered passive bystanders, tumour-infiltrating neurites are now recognized as active components of the tumour microenvironment that influence tumour progression through direct and indirect interactions with malignant, immune, stromal, glial and vascular cells. Recent studies have demonstrated that peripheral tumours recruit and remodel infiltrating neurites, inducing transcriptional, structural and functional changes that resemble neural injury and regenerative programs. These reprogrammed neurites release neurotransmitters, neuropeptides and other factors that directly promote tumour cell proliferation, migration and survival while reshaping the surrounding microenvironment. Neural signalling influences antitumour immunity, reprogrammes fibroblasts and promotes angiogenesis, collectively generating conditions that support disease progression. In turn, tumour-associated neurites undergo profound alterations in their connectivity, activity and molecular state, highlighting the dynamic and reciprocal nature of tumour-nerve interactions. These discoveries have reshaped our understanding of how pro-tumorigenic microenvironments are established and maintained. Importantly, defining the molecular pathways that mediate neural regulation of cancer has revealed new therapeutic opportunities, including the potential repurposing of FDA-approved agents that target neural signalling pathways. As the field of cancer neuroscience continues to advance, the nervous system is increasingly recognized not only as a regulator of tumour behaviour but also as a promising target for therapeutic intervention.

items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy among health-care professionals: a systematic review of reported competency needs.
items.abstract: Widespread calls for artificial intelligence (AI) literacy among health-care professionals have outpaced evidence on the AI information that should be taught and prioritised. We conducted a systematic review of studies published until Feb 12, 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (protocol preregistered on Open Science Framework). 70 studies comprising 42 empirical and 28 perspective or commentary papers from 21 countries were included after screening 4095 records. Among empirical studies, conceptual understanding of the meaning of AI (AI fundamentals; 88·1%), application of ethical thinking to AI use in clinical practice (ethical reasoning; 71·4%), and knowledge of existing AI tools (tools and applications; 71·4%) were the most prevalent competency domains. Perspective papers showed a similar pattern, with comparatively less emphasis on tools and applications. In 20 studies that asked students and health-care professionals to rank competencies by importance, tools and applications and the ability to evaluate AI before adoption (pre-adoption evaluation) ranked the highest. These findings inform a candidate foundation for the development of clinical AI competency.

items.title: Functional Neuroimaging in Tinnitus: Review of Recent Advances.
items.abstract: Chronic subjective tinnitus, the perception of sound without an external source, is highly prevalent, clinically heterogeneous, and lacks a cure and objective diagnostic tests. This review examines how functional neuroimaging is closing that gap. Hemodynamic (functional MRI [fMRI], functional near-infrared spectroscopy, PET) and electrophysiological (electroencephalography, magnetoencephalography) modalities redefine tinnitus as a brain-network disorder involving auditory, limbic, and cognitive systems. Altered default mode network connectivity, auditory-limbic hyperconnectivity, and reduced thalamocortical inhibition are emerging as candidate biomarkers that track severity and may help stratify patients. These findings increasingly guide therapies such as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and real-time fMRI neurofeedback.

items.title: Large-Scale Neural Slowing Measured with Electroencephalography Indexes Secondary Thalamic Degeneration in Stroke.
items.abstract: A central priority in stroke recovery research is the development of useful biomarkers that reveal underlying disease states to aid diagnosis, prognosis, stratification, and treatment, ideally using tools that are readily available in clinical settings. Large-scale neural slowing has the potential to be such a biomarker, but its usefulness is currently limited by uncertainty about its nature and relation to underlying pathophysiology. In this work, we sought to address these gaps by parameterizing abnormal resting-state electroencephalography spectral features across the scalp and investigating their relationship to thalamic atrophy and dysfunction, using structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a computational model of corticothalamic circuit dynamics, respectively. As predicted, stroke patients (n = 25; 15 males, 10 females) exhibited widespread spectral abnormalities, including significantly increased aperiodic exponent and offset, lower alpha frequency, and reduced beta power, which together can account for the frequently observed shift in power toward low frequencies after stroke. Furthermore, corticothalamic models fit to power spectral densities across the scalp inferred broad thalamic disinhibition. Crucially, these abnormalities (except beta reductions) were strongly associated with ipsilesional thalamic atrophy measured with MRI, despite the lack of direct thalamus damage in this sample. Overall, this work provides a deeper characterization of large-scale electrophysiological abnormalities after stroke and reinforces their potential as clinically feasible biomarkers of poststroke pathophysiology.

items.title: Distinct yet complementary roles of temporal and spectral predictions in auditory detection.
items.abstract: Predictive processing enables the brain to anticipate both when and what sensory events will occur. Although temporal and spectral predictions are both known to facilitate perception, their functional contributions and interaction remain poorly understood, particularly in uncertain listening conditions where predictions must be inferred from implicit statistical regularities rather than explicit cues or rhythms. Here, we orthogonalized temporal and spectral predictability in a non-rhythmic auditory detection task and used a signal-detection framework to dissociate perceptual and decisional processes in humans of either sex. Temporal predictions primarily increased response readiness: predictable target timing led to faster responses and more hits but also more false alarms, reflecting a liberal shift in response bias. Spectral predictions, in contrast, selectively enhanced perceptual sensitivity without a comparable speeding of responses. Crucially, despite their distinct behavioral effects, temporal and spectral predictions interacted synergistically, such that perceptual sensitivity was greatest when both sound timing and frequency were predictable, consistent with a spectrotemporal filter mechanism. Furthermore, temporal and spectral variability were encoded differently: performance adapted strongly to the distribution of foreperiod durations but remained largely stable across the spectral distribution, suggesting that the brain exploits temporal and spectral statistics in distinct ways when forming predictions under uncertainty. Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal and spectral predictions make complementary contributions to auditory decision-making, interact synergistically to improve perceptual sensitivity, and rely on distinct encoding strategies for temporal and spectral variability.Significance statement In everyday listening, the brain must predict both when relevant sounds will occur and what they will sound like. Although temporal ("when") and spectral ("what") predictions are both known to support perception, their distinct functions and possible synergies are not well understood. Here, using a non-rhythmic auditory detection task and a signal-detection framework, we show that temporal predictions mainly increase response readiness, whereas spectral predictions selectively enhance perceptual sensitivity. When both are available, they interact synergistically to maximize sensitivity. These findings reveal that temporal and spectral predictions make complementary contributions to auditory decision-making and show how the brain combines multiple predictive dimensions to improve perception under uncertainty.

items.title: Brain Responses to Naturalistic Language During Movie-Watching as Markers of Current and Future Cognitive Function in Older Adults.
items.abstract: Monitoring global cognitive function in older adults is crucial for timely detection and intervention of cognitive impairment. While cognitive tests and traditional magnetic resonance imaging have been widely used, more sensitive methods are needed. Conventionally, language production rather than comprehension has been emphasized for monitoring cognitive decline, as comprehension appears preserved in controlled laboratory paradigms. However, naturalistic language comprehension engages multiple aging-sensitive cognitive systems, making language-related brain activations during naturalistic tasks potentially sensitive markers of global cognitive function. This study investigated whether language-related activations during naturalistic movie-watching functional magnetic resonance imaging (mw-fMRI) could effectively monitor older adults' global cognitive function as assessed by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). We recruited 97 (43 females and 54 males) non-demented participants aged 60 years or older to undergo MRI scans and complete the MoCA at baseline; 50 (28 females and 22 males) completed follow-up assessments after two years. Language comprehension during movie watching elicited activations in core frontotemporal and extended language networks that significantly correlated with MoCA scores. Using nested cross-validation, support vector classifiers demonstrated that mw-fMRI activation features effectively classified baseline cognitive status (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.811 ± 0.019) and forecasted two-year cognitive change (AUC = 0.763 ± 0.036), outperforming demographics and traditional MRI features. We localized predictive activations and discussed potential compensatory mechanisms underlying these patterns. Our findings highlight naturalistic language comprehension during mw-fMRI as a biologically interpretable, ecologically valid tool for monitoring global cognitive function in older adults.Significance Statement Detection of cognitive decline in older adults is critical for timely intervention, yet current methods have limitations. Conventional laboratory language tasks suggest comprehension remains intact with aging, leading researchers to focus on language production for monitoring decline. However, real-world language comprehension (e.g., understanding conversations in movies) requires coordinating multiple cognitive processes that are vulnerable to aging. We find that brain activations during naturalistic movie watching effectively detect current cognitive status and forecast future cognitive changes, outperforming traditional brain imaging approaches. This passive, engaging task requires no explicit responses, making it feasible for older adults and clinical populations. Our findings establish ecologically valid neural markers that could help identify individuals at risk for cognitive impairment before they meet diagnostic criteria for dementia.

items.title: Theta-mediated conceptual reinstatement in vmPFC precedes perceptual reinstatement in ventral visual cortex during memory recall.
items.abstract: During recall, different features of an experience, such as conceptual meaning and perceptual detail, are reconstructed and reinstated across distributed cortical regions. Evidence suggests that conceptual information becomes accessible before perceptual detail, but the cortical and oscillatory mechanisms coordinating this sequence remain unclear. Using MEG and time-resolved encoding-retrieval cross-phase classification analysis, we examined the cortical localization, frequency profiles, and directed interactions of conceptual and perceptual reinstatement during cued visual recall in 33 human participants (18 female). Conceptual reinstatement in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and perceptual reinstatement in the ventral visual cortex (VVC) were distinguished by their frequency profiles: theta for conceptual content and gamma for perceptual detail. Conceptual decoding in vmPFC preceded perceptual decoding in VVC. Cross-correlation and spectral Granger causality analyses showed that conceptual information in vmPFC predicted subsequent perceptual information in VVC, with a stronger vmPFC-to-VVC directed predictive dependency in the theta band. In addition, bottom-up connectivity from VVC to vmPFC was expressed in the alpha band. These findings are consistent with memory retrieval proceeding from abstract conceptual reconstruction to the reinstatement of perceptual details, mediated by theta oscillatory communication between prefrontal and sensory areas. We propose a hierarchical interactive model in which vmPFC initiates conceptual activation via top-down theta-band signals, while VVC provides alpha-band feedback from the reconstructed perceptual details.Significance Statement How the human brain retrieves vivid memories is a fundamental question in memory neuroscience. Using MEG combined with time-resolved decoding, we show that memory retrieval unfolds in a top-down hierarchy. Conceptual information is reinstated first in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, followed by the reconstruction of perceptual details in the visual cortex. These stages are supported by distinct neural rhythms: theta-band interactions are stronger in the prefrontal-to-sensory direction, whereas alpha-band signals provide feedback from the sensory cortex. Together, these findings reveal a hierarchical, interactive mechanism for episodic recall, demonstrating that remembering is not a simple replay of past experience but an active reconstruction guided by high-level knowledge.

items.title: Saccade direction and distractor location jointly drive spatial asymmetries in saccadic inhibition.
items.abstract: Saccadic inhibition (SI), the transient suppression of saccade generation following an abrupt visual transient (distractor), clearly demonstrates how sensory input interrupts ongoing oculomotor preparation. SI typically peaks 90-100 ms after transient onset, followed by a rebound in saccade probability. SI depends on distractor properties and its spatial relation to the planned saccade. However, it is unknown whether SI is spatially anisotropic across polar angles and whether such anisotropy is driven by the planned saccade endpoint, the distractor location, or their configuration. Sixteen human observers (8 female) completed two experiments, making speeded saccades to Gabor targets while a task-irrelevant Gabor distractor appeared shortly after target onset. In Experiment 1, saccade targets appeared at cardinal and distractors at intercardinal locations; Experiment 2 reversed this arrangement. Distractor-present trials were compared with target-location-matched no-distractor baselines to quantify SI strength and timing. Across experiments, distractors elicited a canonical SI profile. In Experiment 1, inhibition strength showed independent effects of both target and distractor locations: upward saccades were the most resistant to inhibition, while inhibition was stronger, earlier, and broader by upper-field than lower-field distractors. In Experiment 2, inhibition strength showed a reliable target-by-distractor interaction, with the strongest upper-distractor effect emerging for upper-field saccade targets. Across experiments, the timing of maximal inhibition was driven primarily by distractor location, while rebound dynamics mirrored inhibition strength. These findings reveal that SI is shaped by target-distractor configuration and exhibits an upper-field distractor advantage.Significance Statement Sudden visual events interrupt our planned eye movements. This interruption is often considered a global, uniform pause in the brain's oculomotor program. This study challenges that assumption by demonstrating that saccadic inhibition is highly sensitive to the exact spatial layout of both the intended eye movement and the distracting visual stimulus. Specifically, we show that upward eye movements are highly resistant to disruption, whereas distractors in the upper visual field exert the strongest inhibition, particularly when paired with upper-field targets. These findings reveal that sensorimotor gating in the brain is not a blanket suppression mechanism, but rather a tuned, asymmetric process. These findings provide critical insights into how the brain dynamically prioritizes competing visual inputs during active vision.

items.title: Persistent bilateral STAU1 elevation accompanies increases in p62, GFAP, and phosphorylated tau after traumatic brain injury.
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of long-term neurological disability and increases the risk of neurodegeneration and post-traumatic epileptogenesis. However, the molecular mechanisms responsible for sustained secondary injury and network dysfunction beyond the initial impact remain poorly understood. Staufen-1 (STAU1), an RNA-binding protein that controls mRNA decay, trafficking, and localization to subcellular compartments, is pathologically overabundant in multiple neurodegenerative disease models, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, dementia, and ataxias. Whether STAU1 abundance is altered following moderate controlled cortical impact (CCI), and whether these changes occur alongside increases in p62/SQSTM1, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and phosphorylated tau, remains unknown. Here, using Western blot analyses, we found that STAU1 is persistently elevated in both the ipsilateral hemisphere, including the injury and perilesional regions, and the contralateral cerebrum at 48-h, 1-week, and 1-month post-injury. These increases are accompanied by accumulation of the autophagy adaptor protein p62/SQSTM1, which may suggest changes in p62 synthesis, degradation, or autophagic cargo burden. In parallel, glial fibrillary acidic protein levels as well as phosphorylated tau levels are elevated bilaterally and remain increased 1-month after injury. Together, these findings show a persistent overaccumulation of STAU1 protein levels at several acute time points from 48-h through 1-month after TBI, the first evidence of a previously overlooked factor in the evolving molecular architecture after brain injury. The combination of elevated STAU1, p62, gliosis, and phosphorylated tau in our TBI model provides a basis for future studies on whether STAU1 contributes to injury-associated changes in protein homeostasis and neurological dysfunction, including post-traumatic epilepsy.

items.title: Percutaneous cannulation of the basal cisterns via a lumbar approach in pigs.
items.abstract: Cisternal access for sampling and intervention is relevant to many neurological disorders. Existing strategies risk injuring surrounding structures and contaminating the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with blood from the access site. Developing an approach that pairs the procedural safety of lumbar puncture with the favourable CSF circulatory properties of cisternal access is valuable. We describe percutaneous cannulation of the basal cisterns via a lumbar approach in anaesthetised pigs. The spinal subarachnoid space was accessed at L5-L6 using a Tuohy needle. An intravascular microcatheter was navigated over a steerable micro guidewire through the spinal canal and foramen magnum to the basal cisterns rostral to the brainstem, under fluoroscopic guidance. Catheter placement in a basal cistern was achieved in 16 pigs. Navigation time fell over the series but was longer during training of a second operator and after prolonged intervals. Iatrogenic subarachnoid haemorrhage occurred in three animals (19%) when the microcatheter was advanced against resistance; no further haemorrhage occurred once the technique was refined. This method avoids needle passage through cranio-cervical soft tissues, reduces access-site risk of injury to the brainstem and adjacent vessels, and avoids laminectomy and open dural incision. This minimally invasive, percutaneous technique provides access to CSF along the neuroaxis from a single lumbar entry point. It may support the development of therapies for central nervous system disorders.

items.title: Baseline appetite and weight symptoms and antidepressant response: an individual-level analysis of three cohorts.
items.abstract: Appetite and weight symptoms occur more often in severe major depressive disorder (MDD), so their prognostic value is uncertain. We tested their association with antidepressant response independently of other symptoms. We analyzed 3367 patients with MDD from GSRD, STAR*D and PANDORA. Appetite reduction was harmonized to a three-level score from MADRS and HAMD items; weight loss was available in the HAMD cohorts. Outcomes were response (primary), percentage improvement and endpoint severity. Pooled individual-level models adjusted for age, illness duration, body mass index and severity excluding the investigated items. Appetite reduction was associated with higher baseline severity and, in the pooled model, with response (OR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.09-1.34), with heterogeneity across cohorts (p = 0.026). The association was significant in GSRD (OR = 1.48) but not in STAR*D or PANDORA, and not without GSRD (OR = 1.10, 95% CI 0.97-1.24, p = 0.142). Removing appetite and weight items from the outcome attenuated the pooled estimate. Continuous outcomes showed the same pattern. Weight loss was not associated with response (OR = 1.07, 95% CI 0.92-1.25). Cohorts were selected by data availability and differed in scales, settings, treatments and outcome timing; GSRD baseline ratings were retrospective. Appetite reduction was associated with better response in a specialist-care cohort with retrospective MADRS ratings but not in two HAMD-rated cohorts, and is not a general prognostic marker. Weight loss was not associated with response.

items.title: Proteomic profiling of cytoskeletal interactomes using MT-ID and Act-ID.
items.abstract: The microtubule and actin cytoskeletons form dynamic, interconnected networks that are critical for eukaryotic cell function. These networks govern intracellular organization, cargo transport, cell migration, and tissue morphogenesis. Microtubules and actin filaments are regulated by diverse binding proteins that control many aspects of their function. However, identifying cytoskeletal-interacting proteins has been challenging due to the transient and weak nature of many interactions and the disruption of native architecture by conventional biochemical approaches. These limitations suggest that numerous physiologically relevant cytoskeletal regulators remain undiscovered. Identifying these factors requires novel and sensitive methodologies that can capture cytoskeletal interactions under native cellular conditions. Here, we present MT-ID and Act-ID, powerful proximity-labeling tools for identifying microtubule and actin-interacting proteins, respectively. MT-ID employs the microtubule-binding domain of MAP7 (EMTB) fused to TurboID, a highly active promiscuous biotin ligase. Act-ID utilizes the actin-binding domain of ITPKA (F-tractin) similarly fused to TurboID. We validate both approaches by successfully identifying numerous known cytoskeletal regulators and discovering potentially novel interacting proteins. Functional characterization reveals that LIMCH1 is a previously unrecognized microtubule-associated protein whose depletion increases microtubule density. Additionally, we identify FBXO30 as a novel actin-interacting protein, with its loss promoting increased focal adhesion formation. MT-ID and Act-ID will be useful not only to identify cytoskeletal interacting proteins but also to define changes to the cytoskeletal interactome when cells are exposed to changing physiological conditions.

items.title: Adult Hippocampal Neurogenesis at the Crossroads of Neuropathic Pain and Comorbid Depression: Molecular Mechanisms and Candidate Circuit Consequences.
items.abstract: Neuropathic pain frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, but the cellular processes linking sensory and affective dysfunction remain incompletely understood. Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN), particularly in the ventral dentate gyrus, is a candidate interface whose contribution depends on the number, maturation and integration, and activity of adult-born neurons. Pain-model studies report reduced differentiation-related measures, altered dendritic morphology and early changes in synaptic excitation-inhibition balance under different conditions. These findings challenge a uniform account based on newborn-neuron loss and suggest that functional consequences may differ across hippocampal subregions, injury models and disease stages. Afferent, neuroendocrine, neuroimmune and intrinsic stem-cell mechanisms provide candidate routes linking persistent pain to these cellular states. Molecular rescue can improve neurogenic and behavioral measures in parallel, whereas evidence from other paradigms shows context-dependent regulation of local hippocampal processing and downstream output. The direction and timing of the complete pain-related circuit sequence remain unresolved, and sparse sampling identifies times of detection rather than biological onset. Treatment-ablation studies support neurogenic contributions to selected behavioral benefits without establishing a general advantage of cellular restoration over circuit modulation. Distinguishing preservation of cell number, restoration of maturation and integration, and normalization of activity will clarify which functions support sustained recovery. Evidence remains dominated by male rodent studies, with limited independent replication and no direct validation of the proposed pathway in humans. This multidimensional framework links molecular and circuit findings while defining specific causal questions about pain-associated affective dysfunction.

items.title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neural Circuits of Neuropathic Pain: Potential Molecular Mechanisms and Targeted Therapies.
items.abstract: Neuropathic pain, defined as the pain originating from a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system, remains a challenging condition to treat effectively. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been repeatedly documented in neurons and glial cells in neuropathic pain models. Yet, most of this evidence describes cellular or tissue-level alterations, and how these alterations remodel pain circuit remains unclear. In this review, we propose "mitochondrial circuitopathy" as a working hypothesis: mitochondrial dysfunction in defined neuronal and glial populations alters how nociceptive circuits process information, and pathological circuit activity in turn sustains this dysfunction. To test this hypothesis, four criteria have been defined: cell-type or compartmental specificity, a circuit-level physiological consequence, behavioral specificity for a specific pain dimension, and bidirectional coupling with nociceptive activity. Then, the criteria are employed to evaluate the available evidence across the sensory, affective, and descending modulatory pathways. Causal evidence currently exists mainly for the DRG, superficial dorsal horn, and amygdala. The descending PAG-RVM pathway remains virtually unexamined. We further illustrate whether mitochondrial alterations act as causes, consequences, or compensatory responses, how glial mitochondrial dysfunction influences neuronal excitability, and which methods are available to assess mitochondrial function in pain research. Finally, we evaluate mitochondria-targeted pharmacological strategies, organized as the "TIMER" framework, together with emerging optogenetic and chemogenetic tools, and discuss the limitations in target specificity, delivery, and preservation of physiological nociception. This framework identifies the experiments needed to establish whether, and where, mitochondrial dysfunction drives neuropathic pain.

items.title: Translational Insights into Effort Regulation and Motivation in Affective Disorders.
items.abstract: Effort expenditure in goal pursuit is a fundamental aspect of motivation. Across neuropsychiatric and neurological conditions, impaired motivational regulation, cost/benefit analysis and reduced willingness to expend effort contribute to symptoms such as apathy, anergia and fatigue, which have proved difficult to treat. Conceptually, anticipatory and motivational components of these conditions can be distinguished from anhedonia, in which the primary dysfunction lies in the experience of pleasure. Animal models provide insight into the neurobiological mechanisms supporting normative effortful motivation and decision making and ways in which pathological conditions such as stress exposure alter these processes. Studies in depressed patients implicate many of the same systems but suggest that peripheral mechanisms likely also play an important role. Here we present evidence supporting a framework whereby interactions of neuromodulators and neurotransmitters within key brain regions and circuits enable organisms to engage in adaptive effortful behavior. We further highlight novel approaches to study effort regulation in naturalistic settings and with varying reinforcers as well as advancements in therapeutic development to treat motivational symptoms.

items.title: Causal inference in developmental psychopathology and human neuroscience.
items.abstract: Developmental psychopathologists and human neuroscientists seek to identify the causes and mechanisms underlying the emergence of psychopathology across development. In order to move closer to achieving this important goal, we argue that widespread adoption of methods emerging from the field of causal inference is needed. Causal inference is an interdisciplinary field that seeks to establish cause-and-effect relationships from data, whether experimental or observational. Evaluating causality in an observational setting requires invoking a set of identification assumptions: foundational conditions, often untestable from the data alone, under which a statistical estimator can be given a valid causal interpretation. Through detailing these assumptions-and their connection to core components of statistical models-in the context of the complexity inherent to doing developmental psychopathology and human neuroscience research, we give researchers the background to begin thinking through how to address causality using observational data. Finally, we detail steps for researchers to take to effectively integrate causal inference methods into their research program, from articulating their research questions, to designing studies, to effectively communicating the strengths and limitations of their results.

items.title: Connectivity, receptor architecture and gene expression are associated with brain-wide responses to intracranial electrical stimulation.
items.abstract: Understanding how neural activity propagates across brain networks is essential for explaining how focal interventions influence cognition and for guiding neuromodulation strategies. Intracranial electrical stimulation can evoke spatially distributed brain responses, yet the biological factors associated with these response patterns remain poorly understood. We studied 16 epilepsy patients who underwent medial temporal lobe stimulation during concurrent functional magnetic resonance imaging. Whole-brain blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses were quantified and related to intrinsic functional connectivity, neurotransmitter principal receptor gradient, and regional gene-expression profiles. Stimulation-evoked electrophysiological responses were examined using an independent cortico-cortical evoked potential (CCEP) dataset for comparison. Stimulation induced widespread BOLD activation extending beyond the stimulation site, including the insula and middle cingulate cortex. The spatial distribution of BOLD responses was jointly associated with functional connectivity, principal receptor gradient, and gene expression, and could be captured by these biological features in a multivariate model. In contrast, stimulation-evoked electrophysiological responses showed limited spatial correspondence with BOLD responses and were associated with partly different biological features. This suggests that hemodynamic and electrophysiological reactivity capture partly different aspects of stimulation effects. These findings link the spatial distribution of stimulation-induced brain responses to functional connectivity, receptor architecture, and transcriptional profiles. Identifying the biological features associated with this spatial variability may help characterize responses to targeted stimulation.

items.title: Evaluation of perivascular diffusivity alterations in Parkinson's disease patients with mood-related symptoms using the diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space index.
items.abstract: Previous studies have focused mainly on the relationship between perivascular diffusivity and motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease (PD). The relationship with non-motor symptoms, such as mood-related anxiety, depression and apathy, remains unclear. This study aimed to assess perivascular diffusivity in PD patients with mood symptoms using the diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index, and to identify which of its directional components account for any difference. Eighty-seven patients with PD and forty-three age- and sex-matched healthy controls were recruited. Anxiety, depression and apathy were quantified with the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and the Starkstein Apathy Scale, and patients were grouped according to the presence of each symptom. Within the PD cohort, Spearman correlation, partial correlation and multivariable linear regression were used to examine associations between the index and symptom scores. PD participants with anxiety, depression or apathy had lower ALPS indices than non-symptomatic PD patients and healthy controls, and the difference between the latter two groups was not significant. The index correlated negatively with all three symptom scores, but only apathy remained independently associated after adjustment for coexisting symptoms and clinical covariates. The reduction was accompanied by combined changes in the numerator and denominator diffusivities rather than by a change in a single directional component. Altered perivascular diffusion is therefore associated with mood-related symptoms in PD, and the index should be regarded as an exploratory, structure-dependent imaging marker rather than as a direct measure of glymphatic clearance.

items.title: A cross-modal hierarchical refinement network with uncertainty-guided multi-task learning for brain tumour segmentation, grading, and subtype classification.
items.abstract: Reliable brain-tumour assessment requires accurate volumetric delineation together with clinically meaningful grading. However, most existing pipelines treat segmentation, LGG/HGG classification, and low-grade glioma subtyping as separate tasks. We propose CMHRNet, a cross-modal hierarchical refinement network that jointly performs tumour segmentation from multimodal MRI, binary glioma grading, and astrocytoma versus oligodendroglioma classification using paired MRI and whole-slide histopathology images. The model combines a Hybrid Swin-Transformer segmentation encoder with deep supervision, Learnable Feature Pyramid Fusion and graph attention for LGG/HGG prediction, and a Cross-Modal Attention Transformer with supervised contrastive learning for subtype discrimination. The three stages are jointly optimized using an uncertainty-weighted multi-task objective, which facilitates cross-task feature reuse and reduces the need for manual loss-weight selection. Evaluation on BraTS-2020/2021, CPM-RadPath, and an institutional PGIMER cohort of 32 cases shows that CMHRNet achieves a whole-tumour Dice of 90.3%, LGG/HGG accuracy of 98.7%, and LGG-subtype F1 of 95.6 ± 0.4%. The segmentation performance is comparable to that of strong single-task baselines, while the integrated multi-task results, particularly for subtype classification, compare favourably with reported alternatives. Ablation studies, paired Wilcoxon tests, Grad-CAM visualizations, and failure-mode analysis support the contribution of feature fusion, graph attention, cross-modal attention, contrastive learning, and uncertainty weighting. CMHRNet therefore provides a unified radiology-pathology framework for hierarchical glioma assessment. Nevertheless, validation on larger multi-institutional cohorts is required before clinical deployment. Full multimodal operation depends on the availability of digitized histopathology; however, segmentation and grading remain available through the MRI-only fallback mode.

items.title: Neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease: from glial heterogeneity and gut-brain immune crosstalk to precision therapeutic strategies.
items.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, α-synuclein pathology, and a broad spectrum of motor and non-motor manifestations. Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as an important component of PD pathobiology; however, traditional frameworks have largely focused on canonical inflammatory pathways and simplified classifications of glial activation, which do not fully capture the spatial, temporal, and functional heterogeneity of immune responses in PD. Emerging evidence from single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, together with studies of peripheral immunity and the microbiota-gut-brain axis, indicates that PD-associated inflammation is dynamic, context dependent, and systemically integrated. In this review, we critically synthesize current evidence on microglial and astrocytic activation, bidirectional glial crosstalk, α-synuclein-inflammation feedback loops, and the selective vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons. We further discuss region- and disease-stage-dependent glial states, systemic immune and gut-brain interactions, and inflammation-associated microRNAs as potential links between peripheral and central inflammatory responses. Therapeutically, we evaluate conventional anti-inflammatory strategies alongside emerging RNA-based interventions and targeted delivery approaches. Particular attention is given to the persistent translational gap between robust preclinical efficacy and limited disease-modifying benefit in patients, including limitations related to disease models, therapeutic timing, biomarker availability, patient heterogeneity, and blood-brain barrier penetration. Collectively, current evidence supports a shift from broad suppression of inflammation toward biomarker-guided, disease-stage-specific, and cell- or pathway-selective immunomodulation in PD.

items.title: Orientation-invariant morphometry of dendritic spines: A landmark-based method applied to layer II pyramidal neurons of the petavoxel human connectome.
items.abstract: The classification of cortical dendritic spines into stubby, thin and mushroom subtypes has been shown to be unstable under rotation, so the structure of spine morphology cannot be read from measurements that depend on the viewing angle. We developed the Spine Morphometry Hub (SMH), a 12-point anatomical landmark framework that characterizes each spine in all three orthogonal planes, independently of the viewing angle, and extracts geometric, voxel-based, and mesh-based metrics. We applied it to 228 spines from five layer II pyramidal neurons in the H01 nanometer-resolution reconstruction of human temporal cortex. No morphometric distribution departed from unimodality, and all were right-skewed. Density-based clustering assigned most spines to noise, and a Monte Carlo test showed that this pattern is incompatible with a null model of two compact discrete types. Spines at the extremes of the distribution were clearly distinct in form, yet no boundary between classes emerged. Two explicit classification rules applied to the same three-dimensional measurements assigned the same name to only 33.3% of the spines, and because no viewing angle is involved, this disagreement arises from the classification rules themselves. Apical and basal spines did not differ in the six core morphometric variables. Although a continuum of spine forms has been reported in rodent and human cortex, this framework is original in applying an orientation-invariant, landmark-based measurement method to dendritic spines reconstructed at nanometer resolution in the H01 petavoxel dataset. We propose that it can serve as a common reference for studies of spine remodeling in neurological disorders.

items.title: Ventral striatal dopamine increases following hippocampal sharp-wave ripples.
items.abstract: The reactivation of task-related hippocampal activity during sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), often expressed as sequential "replay," is thought to contribute to behavior through both online and offline processes. During sleep and awake rest, replay supports memory consolidation, broadly defined as the updating and stabilization of knowledge structures for later use. During active task engagement, replay may also support decision-making through episodic memory retrieval and the generation of prospective scenarios1,2,3,4 (but see van der Meer and Bendor5). While disrupting SWR events impairs memory-guided behavior6,7,8,9 and augmenting them enhances such behavior,10,11 the neurophysiological mechanisms that enable replay to contribute to behavior remain unclear. Theories of replay-based learning posit the need for replay events to be followed by an evaluative signal. Dopamine (DA) is consistently associated with such teaching signals, particularly in the ventral striatum, where it reflects reward- and other prediction-error signals.12 Although hippocampal activity can influence mesolimbic DA signaling,13,14,15 whether SWRs are coupled to ventral striatal DA release is unknown. To address this, we simultaneously recorded dorsal CA1 local field potentials to detect SWRs and measured ventral striatal DA concentration using fiber photometry of the GRABDA2m sensor16 in freely moving mice. We found a significant increase in DA following SWRs. This coupling was more prominent during offline rest than during periods of immobility during behavior and was stronger following longer and higher-power SWRs. These results reveal coupling between hippocampal SWRs and striatal dopamine, providing a potential candidate mechanism through which internally generated hippocampal activity could engage evaluative signals during offline memory processing.

items.title: Repetitive levodopa treatment drives cell-type-specific striatal adaptations associated with progressive dyskinesia in parkinsonian mice.
items.abstract: The use of levodopa to manage Parkinson's disease (PD) symptoms leads to levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) and other motor fluctuations, which worsen with disease progression and repeated treatment. Aberrant activity of striatal D1- and D2-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-/D2-MSNs) underlies LID, but the mechanisms driving its progression remain unclear. Using the 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) mouse model of PD/LID, we combined in vivo and ex vivo recordings to isolate the effect of repeated treatment in LID worsening and other changes in the motor response to levodopa. We found that LID worsening is linked to potentiation of levodopa-evoked responses in both D1-/D2-MSNs, independent of changes in dopamine release or MSN intrinsic excitability. Instead, strengthening of glutamatergic synapses onto D1-MSNs emerged as a key signature. Moreover, we found that changes in D2-MSN activity are associated with LID duration, which parallels a reduction in D2 receptor (D2R) sensitivity. These findings reveal striatal adaptations contributing to the worsening of levodopa-related complications.

items.title: Subtype-specific radiographic outcomes following posterior decompression for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis based on the CARDS classification.
items.abstract: The management of degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis (DLS) remains controversial due to concerns regarding postoperative instability. This study aimed to evaluate whether the Clinical and Radiographic Degenerative Spondylolisthesis (CARDS) classification can predict changes in vertebral translation and intervertebral alignment following posterior decompression without fusion. We retrospectively analyzed 82 patients who underwent posterior decompression across 162 spinal segments, comprising 125 segments with DLS (classified into CARDS Types A-D) and 37 non-spondylolisthesis (Non-DS) segments. Radiographic parameters, including vertebral translation, intervertebral lordosis, and disc height, were evaluated preoperatively and at one-year follow-up. Primary analyses compared radiographic changes among the 125 DLS segments according to CARDS subtypes using linear mixed-effects models. Overall, decompression did not lead to a significant increase in vertebral translation. However, subtype analysis among DLS segments revealed distinct patterns: CARDS Types A and C segments showed a significant reduction in vertebral translation and an increase in intervertebral lordosis. In contrast, Type D segments demonstrated significant progression of vertebral translation postoperatively, despite achieving gains in lordosis similar to other types. Type A segments also showed a significant increase in postoperative disc height. The CARDS classification effectively identifies distinct radiographic responses to decompression surgery. While Types A and C tend to maintain or improve alignment, Type D is associated with a higher risk of progressive translation. These findings suggest that CARDS subtype-specific characteristics should be considered when assessing the risk of postoperative instability.

items.title: Brain and spinal cord chronic neuroinflammation in multiple sclerosis: a large-scale post-mortem study and longitudinal MRI cohort study.
items.abstract: Brain paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs) represent a subset of chronic active, or mixed active/inactive, lesions in multiple sclerosis (MS). Whether chronic neuroinflammation is synchronised across the craniospinal axis and can predict spinal cord degeneration remains unknown. We aimed to evaluate the correlation of pathology, including lesion types and microglial state, between the brain and spinal cord, and to determine if brain PRL count predicts longitudinal spinal cord atrophy. We combined a large-scale neuropathological study with an in vivo longitudinal clinical-MRI study. Brain and spinal cord tissues from 194 MS donors (5317 samples; 8874 lesions) were analysed to correlate lesion types and microglial state across central nervous system regions. For the clinical-MRI cohort, 173 adults with MS [118 women (68%); 48 progressive; median EDSS 1.5] underwent baseline 3T brain and spinal cord MRI, with longitudinal follow-up over a median of 2.5 years. Brain PRLs were identified via susceptibility-sensitive imaging. The spinal cord cross-sectional area (SCCSA) was measured longitudinally at C2-C3, C4-C5, and T4-T9 at two time points. Large-scale post-mortem analysis revealed that intra-donor proportions of mixed active/inactive lesions in the brain were correlated with those in the spinal cord (p = 2.22e-9, r = 0.41). Microglia/macrophage activity scores (p = 4.30e-6, r = 0.32) and microglial nodules (p = 3.55e-4) were similarly synchronised. In vivo, higher baseline brain PRL counts independently predicted accelerated spinal cord atrophy at C2-C3 (β = -0.049 mm2/year, p = 0.03), resulting in an ∼9% steeper SCCSA decline per PRL. The association remained significant after adjustment for T2 lesion burden and treatment. Neuroinflammation is concordant between the brain and spinal cord. In vivo, brain PRLs correlate with accelerated upper cervical spinal cord atrophy, supporting its potential as an imaging biomarker of progressive spinal cord neurodegeneration. items.title: Sex differences in parent-reported social-communicative and adaptive behaviors among toddlers at increased familial likelihood of autism.
items.abstract: Autism is diagnosed more frequently in males than females, although growing evidence suggests that autistic females may present a distinct behavioral phenotype and are often under-recognized, in part because diagnostic assessments were developed largely from male presentations. Early social engagement and social-communicative behaviors are important components of autism phenotyping, yet little is known about whether these behaviors differ between autistic girls and boys during toddlerhood. We examined sex differences in early social-communicative behaviors at 2 years of age in children with an increased familial likelihood of autism. Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II (VABS-II) data were obtained from 415 children enrolled in the Infant Brain Imaging Study (IBIS) Network who did and did not receive an autism classification. Multivariable logistic regression examined whether the combined pattern of 19 parent-reported social-communicative and adaptive items differed by sex within each group. In the autistic group, the pattern differed between girls and boys (χ2(20) = 33.21, p = .032); the non-autistic model was not significant. Within this profile, items reflecting early social engagement and communication of basic needs were associated with female sex, whereas items reflecting attention-seeking behaviors and responding to social and verbal cues were associated with male sex. A complementary interaction analysis found that sex differences in some early social communication behaviors varied by autism status. These associations suggest that autistic girls and boys may differ in their profile of early social-communicative behavior by age 2, providing a basis for future hypothesis-driven research on assessing autistic girls. LAY SUMMARY: Autistic girls may show different social-communicative behaviors than autistic boys during early development, which could contribute to differences in how autism presents across sexes. This study examined social-communicative behaviors in 2-year-old children with an older autistic sibling and found that the overall pattern of early social-communicative behaviors reported by parents differed between autistic girls and boys. These findings improve our understanding of early sex differences in autism and may help improve the early recognition of autism in girls, who are often diagnosed later than boys.

items.title: Stage-Dependent Associations of Amyloid Pathology and White Matter Hyperintensities With Cognitive Decline Across the Clinical Continuum.
items.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) and cerebral small vessel disease frequently coexist, and their hallmarks, amyloid pathology and white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), are each associated with cognitive decline. Whether these associations are independent or interactive remains unclear. This study investigated their joint associations with cognitive decline across the clinical continuum. This longitudinal study included 2 observational cohorts: the harmonization cohort, which recruited participants from Singaporean community and memory clinics, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), a multisite study in North America. Participants underwent MRI, amyloid biomarker assessments (plasma phosphorylated-tau 217 or amyloid PET), and neuropsychological assessments. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated independent and interactive associations of the amyloid biomarker and WMHs with cognitive decline, stratified by clinical stage. The study included 448 participants from harmonization (mean age 72.45 ± 8.13 years; 56% female) and 1,245 from ADNI (72.56 ± 7.35; 49% female). Among cognitively normal (CN) individuals, statistical interactions between the amyloid biomarker and WMHs were detected in both cohorts, with the joint association exceeding the sum of their individual associations: in harmonization, for global cognition (amyloid biomarker × WMHs × time β = -0.042, 95% CI -0.068 to -0.016, p = 0.002), memory and executive function; in ADNI, for global cognition (β = -0.081, -0.136 to -0.026, p = 0.004) and memory. At mild cognitive impairment (MCI), no interaction was detected; both markers were independently associated with decline in several domains (global cognition, memory, and executive function in harmonization; memory and language in ADNI), whereas an association was detected for the amyloid biomarker only in the remaining domains. At dementia, the amyloid biomarker was associated with decline in harmonization, while WMHs were not; neither reached significance in ADNI, likely reflecting the shorter follow-up. The joint association of amyloid pathology and WMHs with cognitive decline was stage dependent: at CN, it exceeded the sum of their individual associations; at MCI, both markers were independently associated with decline; and at dementia, an association was detected for the amyloid biomarker only. Clinical stage and WMH burden may therefore warrant consideration when interpreting disease-modifying therapy responses. However, the observational design limits causal inference, and the interaction reported is statistical rather than necessarily biological.

items.title: Clinical Reasoning: A 7-Year-Old Boy With Left-Sided Involuntary Movements.
items.abstract: Hemichorea is a rare movement disorder that can arise from a diversity of causes. In this case, a 7-year-old boy presented with subacute onset of involuntary movements involving the left upper extremity. This case highlights the importance of careful characterization of abnormal movements in children, as distinguishing chorea from myoclonus, tics, or epileptic automatisms directs subsequent diagnostic testing. It also underscores the broad differential diagnosis of hemichorea in pediatric patients and the need to consider systemic and vascular processes when imaging reveals focal findings. Through stepwise clinical reasoning, this case illustrates how integrating movement phenomenology with neuroimaging and systemic evaluation can uncover an underlying unifying diagnosis.

items.title: Can Testimonial Learning be Considered Rational?: Revisions, Extensions, and New Insights to a Theory of Selective Trust.
items.abstract: Numerous studies have shown that children selectively learn from others' testimony and are not indiscriminately trusting of all social interaction. Thirteen years ago, we published a paper (Sobel & Kushnir, 2013) that introduced a theory of selective trust in testimony grounded in rational learning mechanisms similar to those we developed with our mentor, Alison Gopnik, to explain children's causal reasoning and theory change. In honor of Alison receiving the Rumelhart Award, we take the opportunity to engage with our original claims, update them in light of new evidence, and propose ways to integrate the rational framework with new ideas in the field. We begin with a review of two recent meta-analyses that support the rational learning account. We then consider new data showing that testimony enhances processing of children's own observations and actions and discuss how this data might lead to extensions of our theory. We next revisit and modify our original claims about "emotional trust" and suggest that affiliative motives which conflict with truth-seeking motives may alter, or even undermine, the rational learning process. We end with new directions for selective trust research: examining developmental changes from infancy, integrating more cultural influences, and considering the role of selective trust in children's increasing interactions with AI and other technology.

items.title: Validity and Reliability of a 20-Item Caregiver-Based Speech-Language Screening Tool for Cantonese-Speaking Preschool Children.
items.abstract: Language and speech sound disorders impact more than 8% of young children, but confirming a diagnosis requires a comprehensive assessment. Caregiver screening tools are vital for identifying children who are at risk and in need of further evaluation. This study aims to examine the validity and reliability of a caregiver-reported screening measure, namely, the Cantonese Caregiver Speech-Language Screening for Preschoolers (CCSLS-P). A total of 114 Cantonese-speaking preschool children (aged 3-5 years) and 112 caregivers participated in this study. The children were divided into four study groups based on the assessment results: children with typical speech-language development (TD group), children with speech sound difficulties only (SSd group), children with language difficulties only (Ld group), and children with both speech and language difficulties (S&Ld group). The caregivers rated the 20 survey items (12 items in the language section and eight items in the speech section) on a 5-point Likert scale. Children with language difficulties demonstrated statistically significantly lower language section scores compared to those children without language difficulties, while children with speech sound difficulties exhibited comparable speech section scores with children with typical speech-language development. Structural validity, criterion validity, internal consistency, and test-retest reliability analyses provided preliminary evidence supporting the construct validity and reliability of the language section. The sensitivity and specificity of the language section scores for identifying possible language difficulties in the three age groups both exceeded 80%. The CCSLS-P language section provides preliminary evidence of validity and reliability for identifying possible language difficulties within the sample. Future investigations with larger and more balanced samples are recommended.

items.title: Phosphorylation-dependent ATPase activity regulates subunit shuffling dynamics in cyanobacterial circadian clock proteins.
items.abstract: Protein complexes are essential for cellular functions, with their dynamics increasingly recognized as key regulatory elements. In the cyanobacterial circadian clock, the KaiC hexamer is highly dynamic, undergoing phosphorylation-dependent monomer shuffling that synchronizes individual oscillators. However, the molecular mechanism of monomer shuffling is not fully understood. Here we combine a chromatography-based method with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to quantify subunit exchange in the hexamerization domain of KaiC (KaiC-CI) and in full-length KaiC. We show that ATPase activity is essential for monomer shuffling. Through quantitative modeling of experimental data, we found that adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis at two independent monomer-monomer interfaces disassembles a KaiC-CI hexamer into two oligomers. Two complementary oligomers from two different hexamers can rapidly reform a mixed hexamer. Mechanistically, ATP hydrolysis induces unstable, shuffling-competent states in hexamers, while nucleotide exchange stabilizes them, suppressing shuffling. The balance between these two processes quantitatively explains the relationship between shuffling rate and ATPase activity across KaiC mutants observed in our experiments. Applying this model to full-length KaiC revealed that phosphorylation of the KaiC-CII domain modulates shuffling primarily by affecting the nucleotide exchange rate in the CI domain. This establishes a feedback loop where CII phosphorylation alters CI ATPase activity, which in turn controls subunit exchange to synchronize CII phosphorylation across the KaiC hexamer population. Our findings provide a mechanistic framework linking ATPase-driven subunit exchange to the robustness of circadian clocks, with implications for activation-coupled dynamics in other molecular machines.

items.title: PRMT5 licenses AARS1-dependent histone lactylation to amplify microglial glycolytic reprogramming in neuropathic pain.
items.abstract: Neuropathic pain involves persistent metabolic and transcriptional remodeling in spinal microglia, but the mechanisms linking these processes remain unclear. Time-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing after chronic constriction injury identified increased PRMT5 expression in glycolysis-enriched activated microglia. Microglia-specific Prmt5 deletion or pharmacological inhibition reduced glycolytic remodeling and pain hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, PRMT5 associated with alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (AARS1), promoted AARS1-associated symmetric dimethylation and nuclear accumulation, and supported AARS1-dependent H3K18la and H4K12la. Disrupting AARS1 nuclear localization impaired histone lactylation and glycolytic responses. The pathway was validated in primary microglia, spinal microglia, and female mice. Chromatin profiling linked injury-associated histone lactylation to glycolytic gene programs. Finally, biomimetic siPRMT5 nanoparticles preferentially reduced PRMT5 in spinal microglia and alleviated pain hypersensitivity. These findings identify a PRMT5-AARS1-histone lactylation pathway that reinforces microglial glycolytic reprogramming and represents a potential therapeutic target for neuropathic pain.

items.title: Anterior cingulate cortex neurons parse speakers in a natural cocktail party.
items.abstract: The cocktail party problem-parsing relevant voices from competing speakers-has traditionally been studied as a sensory challenge for auditory cortex. Yet in natural communication, identifying speakers and coordinating interaction are inherently social processes. Here we recorded single neurons from anterior cingulate cortex (ACC, area 24) in freely moving marmosets engaged in spontaneous vocal exchanges within a noisy colony environment. ACC neurons selectively encoded vocalizations from a social partner versus other callers in the scene, effectively parsing speakers in the acoustic mixture. This selectivity was preserved even when vocalizations overlapped in time, indicating robustness to background interference. Apart from perception, ACC population activity represented vocal production, call type, and whether calls occurred within vocal turn-taking exchanges. Behaviorally, marmosets adjusted vocal timing based on the surrounding acoustic scene, and these interaction contexts were reliably reflected in ACC activity. Together, these findings suggest that neurons in ACC play a role in parsing conspecific speakers during communication in a natural "cocktail party," linking auditory scene analysis with social monitoring and coordinated interactions.

items.title: Differential vulnerability of stimulus-locked and persistent gamma oscillations: Implications in schizophrenia.
items.abstract: Working memory depends on gamma oscillations generated across sensory and prefrontal cortices. In primary visual cortex (V1), stimulus-locked gamma oscillations encode stimulus information, while in prefrontal cortex (PFC), persistent gamma oscillations maintain this information after the stimulus is removed. In schizophrenia (SZ), gamma power is reduced in both V1 and PFC, consistent with deficits in sensory encoding and working memory maintenance. Both oscillation regimes arise from a canonical microcircuit involving pyramidal neurons (PNs) and parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVIs). Yet, whether the two regimes are similarly or differentially vulnerable to synaptic alterations within this circuit in SZ remains unknown. To investigate this question, we used a mean-field model of the PN-PVI circuit, in which the two regimes were distinguished by NMDA conductance values reflecting the difference in GluN2B expression between human PFC and V1. We then assessed three synaptic alterations quantified using molecular and structural proxies in postmortem SZ brains: lower excitatory inputs to PVIs (E→I), lower inhibitory inputs to PNs (I→E), and greater variability in E→I strength. Each alteration produced larger gamma power deficits in the persistent regime than in the stimulus-locked regime. Applied together, these alterations interacted synergistically to reduce gamma power, with the persistent regime exhibiting a more pronounced deficit. Bifurcation analyses revealed that this differential vulnerability arises from a wider margin of oscillatory stability in the stimulus-locked regime, and that reduced I→E strength additionally abolished the bistability required for the persistent regime. These findings predict that a larger magnitude of synaptic alteration is required to disrupt gamma oscillations in V1 than in PFC, consistent with postmortem reports of more severe alterations in V1 in SZ. Together, they establish a differential vulnerability model of cortical gamma oscillations in SZ, in which regional differences in oscillatory stability determine how much synaptic alteration is required to disrupt oscillations with distinct dynamics.

items.title: Occupational balance and associated factors among newly graduated healthcare and social work professionals in Sweden: A repeated cross-sectional multicentre study.
items.abstract: Background Research highlights the complex interplay between structural and individual factors affecting healthcare and social work professionals' ability to maintain work-life and occupational balance. This study aimed to explore how occupational balance is associated with health, health-promoting resources, a healthy lifestyle and social factors among newly graduated healthcare and social work professionals one and three years after graduation and to compare these associations between age groups. Methods We used a repeated cross-sectional multicentre study design. Data were collected using a self-reported, web-based questionnaire based on validated instruments: the Occupational Balance Questionnaire (OBQ11), the Sense of Coherence (SOC) Scale, the Salutogenic Health Indicator Scale (SHIS) and five questions derived from the General Nordic Questionnaire (QPS Nordic), together with questions about general health and lifestyle factors. Results At Y1, 115 of 1,751 invited professionals participated (6.6%), and at Y3, 165 of 1,751 participated (9.4%). Higher SHIS scores were independently associated with higher OBQ scores at both Y1 (B = 0.218, 95% CI 0.091-0.340) and Y3 (B = 0.193, 95% CI 0.100-0.287). At Y3, younger age (B = -0.136, 95% CI -0.237 to -0.036) and living alone (B = 2.291, 95% CI 0.194-4.387) were also independently associated with higher OBQ scores. Conclusions The findings indicate that occupational balance is associated with health and well-being during early working life and may be relevant when considering workforce sustainability. Younger professionals tended to report higher occupational balance, suggesting that age may be relevant to how health-related resources contribute to well-being in early working life.

items.title: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit.
items.abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) is a key regulator of animal physiology. Here, we uncover a function for NO in the integration of UV exposure and the gating of a UV-avoidance circuit. We studied UV/violet avoidance mediated by brain ciliary photoreceptors (cPRCs) in larvae of the annelid Platynereis dumerilii. In the larva, NOS is expressed in interneurons (INNOS) postsynaptic to cPRCs. UV stimulation of cPRCs triggers INNOS activation and NO production. NO signals retrogradely to cPRCs to induce their sustained post-stimulus activation through an unconventional guanylate cyclase. This late activation drives ciliary beating through serotonergic ciliomotor neurons during UV avoidance. In NOS mutants, retrograde signalling, ciliary activation, and UV avoidance are defective. By mathematical modelling, we recapitulate phototransduction and circuit dynamics in wild-type and mutant larvae. Our results reveal how NO-mediated retrograde signalling gates a synaptic circuit and induces short-term memory of UV exposure to orchestrate light-avoidance behaviour.

items.title: VMH astrocytes support cold-induced synaptic potentiation on SF1 neurons and sustained brown adipose thermogenesis.
items.abstract: Whether transient cold induces prolonged changes in hypothalamic function and thermogenesis remains unclear. Here, we show in mice that a brief cold challenge elicits sustained potentiation of excitatory synaptic transmission onto steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1) neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), accompanied by a prolonged increase in interscapular brown adipose tissue (iBAT) temperature. Both responses persist for up to two days. Cold rapidly increases VMH norepinephrine dynamics and astrocytic Ca2+ activity. Ablation of VMH astrocytes prevents cold-induced synaptic potentiation in SF1 neurons and attenuates the thermogenic and oxidative responses in iBAT. Pharmacological manipulations further implicate VMH α1-adrenergic receptor signaling, NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activation, and NMDAR co-agonist-site availability in cold-induced synaptic potentiation. SF1 neuronal activity contributes to the iBAT responses, with its oxidative effects requiring intact iBAT innervation. These findings indicate a prolonged neural and thermogenic response to transient cold exposure and suggest VMH astrocytes as important cellular contributors to its regulation.

items.title: Cortical astrocytes flexibly encode reward contingencies and shape motivated response adaptation.
items.abstract: Learned associations between cues and reward drive motivated behavior, yet how specific cell types support this process remains unclear. Using two-photon calcium imaging, we tracked dorsal medial prefrontal cortical astrocytes throughout the acquisition and reversal of Pavlovian sucrose conditioning. As learning progressed, astrocytes exhibited time-locked, spatially coordinated activity that differentiated correct behavior from mistakes, evolving from broad outcome encoding to selective representation of responses associated with reward-conditioned stimuli. Omission testing revealed that prefrontal astrocytes preferentially encoded the cue-reward association, rather than cue or reward alone. When reward contingencies were reversed, astrocytic activity rapidly adapted to track the new cue-reward association and encoded updated and outdated motivated behavioral actions. Finally, disrupting astrocytic coupling through hemichannel inhibition enhanced behavioral responding to the reward-paired cue across acquisition but impaired behavioral flexibility when reward contingencies were updated or unpredictable. Results reveal prefrontal astrocytes are functionally plastic elements that regulate reward seeking across associative learning.

items.title: Structural Conditions in Health Care Systems and Cardiovascular Health After Release From Prison: Protocol for the SCHARP Prospective Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Compared with the general population, people released from prison experience a disproportionate prevalence of poor cardiovascular (CV) health, CV events, and CV mortality following release. Access to community health care services is key to preventing poor CV outcomes, yet people released from prison report barriers to accessing health care. In the Structural Conditions and Health After Release from Prison (SCHARP) study, we aim to examine how structural conditions, or the policies, procedures, and practices, within health care systems are associated with health care utilization and CV outcomes experienced by people recently released from prison. We recruited people recently released from prisons in Colorado into an observational cohort to follow their utilization outcomes over 12 months after study enrollment. Participants' CV health based on Life's Essential 8 (blood pressure, lipids, glucose, BMI, physical activity, diet, tobacco use, and sleep) was measured at enrollment. At enrollment, self-reported exposure to health care system conditions (eg, access experiences related to insurance status, use of peer navigators, experiences of health care discrimination, receipt of support for health-related social risk factors, and access to specialized services such as substance use treatment) since release were assessed. Using the Colorado All Payer Claims Database, we will next examine the association between exposure to structural conditions and primary outcomes of health care utilization (clinic visits, emergency visits, and hospitalization) and secondary outcome of CV hospitalization. This study was funded in September 2022. Between August 2023 and September 2025, we enrolled 508 participants. Data collection is expected to be completed in 2027 and data analysis in 2028. In a large prospective cohort of people released from prison, the SCHARP study will systematically measure CV health, identify exposure to structural conditions, and link these exposures to health care utilization and CV hospitalization. These findings will be used to develop and disseminate resources for health care systems interested in improving health care utilization and CV outcomes for people released from prison. items.title: Exploring the Requirements of Clinicians for Transparent and Trustworthy Decision Support Systems in Intensive Care: Focus Group Study.
items.abstract: Understanding how digital systems can support clinical decision-making is crucial, especially with the growing deployment of increasingly complex AI models. This complexity raises concerns about trustworthiness, affecting the safe and effective adoption of such technologies. In intensive care units (ICUs), where clinicians make high-stakes, time-sensitive decisions, decision support tools must be designed to align with clinical needs and cognitive workflows. A better understanding of decision-making processes and requirements for decision support tools is vital for providing effective solutions. This study investigates ICU clinicians' decision-making processes, their use of decision support systems (DSSs), and the design requirements for DSSs to ensure transparent and trustworthy recommendations. We conducted 2 virtual focus groups with 7 ICU clinicians from 1 hospital in September 2024. Participants included nurses, charge nurses, and medical doctors, each with at least three years of professional experience. The focus groups explored participants' perspectives on DSSs in relation to our study objectives. Reflexive thematic analysis was applied to the focus group transcripts, and analytic decisions were made inductively using open coding. Both semantic and latent coding were used. Following independent coding, a combined codebook was developed collaboratively, from which key themes and subsequent design recommendations were identified. Three core themes emerged from the analysis: ICU Decision-Making Relies on a Wide Range of Factors (theme 1); Complexity of Patient State Is Challenging for Shared Decision-Making (theme 2); and Acceptability and Usability of DSSs (theme 3). Five design recommendations derived from clinical input provide insights to inform future DSSs for intensive care: provide variable levels of detail (recommendation 1); support integration into existing clinical systems (recommendation 2); present explanations with additional contextual information (recommendation 3); prompt independent thought (recommendation 4); and facilitate communication of patient state (recommendation 5). DSSs have the potential to enhance ICU decision-making, but their adoption depends on alignment with clinicians' needs and workflows. To improve trust and usability, future systems must provide transparent recommendations, adapt to varying levels of patient complexity, and facilitate rather than replace human expertise. Our findings inform the development of transparent and trustworthy DSSs, which may improve their acceptance in ICU settings.
