items.title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
items.abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $τ= 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($β_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

items.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
items.abstract: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

items.title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.

items.title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech
items.abstract: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. Measured planner latency constrains this path; a deterministic retail schema attains 31.7% RFES, compared with 32.0% for the complete policy. In a separate 30-task $τ$-Voice simulation, schema-derived candidates with cached text-to-speech (TTS) audio attain 21/30 task-level RFES. Eligible audio begins 1.51 seconds before the user-audio endpoint among the 22 tasks with early speech, or 1.11 seconds over all 30 tasks with zero for tasks without eligible early speech. Semantic veto and endpoint waiting each pass 16/30 tasks. Together, the studies demonstrate a controlled coverage-compatibility trade-off and schema-based pre-endpoint operation, making the supported public commitment an explicit unit of voice-agent control.

items.title: Leakage-Safe Auditing of Attribution-Driven Data Curation in Medical Imaging
items.abstract: When can an attribution-derived anomaly justify changing a medical-imaging training set? We formulate attribution-driven curation as three separately testable claims: anomaly detection, harmfulness estimation, and intervention utility. We test the first and third using a patient-disjoint, identifier-preserving audit of a 3D convolutional classifier for computed tomography angiography aneurysm candidates. We identify 232 exactly zero-valued arrays among 1,201 positive patches, including 170 training positives, and invalidate a historical 321-patch attention-failure subgroup whose identifier-free records were joined to files by position. On the held-out test set, GradCAM++ spatial concentration is central for every candidate class, reversing the historical pattern. GradCAM++ and Integrated Gradients show negative rank-order agreement for positives, limiting method-independent anatomical interpretation. Across five paired training seeds, removing the 170 corrupted training positives yields AUC 0.9617 +/- 0.0044 versus 0.9652 +/- 0.0039 for full-data training (difference -0.0035; 95% CI -0.0082 to 0.0007). Excluding 34 raw-zero test positives widens rather than closes the gap, countering a blank-memorization explanation. Budget-matched random-removal controls suggest the result is not simply an effect of reducing training size. Input corruption does not necessarily imply that deletion improves generalization. Our framework makes leakage control, sample identity, and intervention testing explicit in attribution-driven medical-imaging data curation.

items.title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
items.abstract: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).

items.title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
items.abstract: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

items.title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
items.abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

items.title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
items.abstract: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

items.title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
items.abstract: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

items.title: AlphaDefect: Expert-Level AI for Slay the Spire 2
items.abstract: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character, one network trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) makes every decision of a run, in combat and outside it. At the highest difficulty, Ascension 10, on two versions of the game current in November 2026 and on test seeds not played in training, AlphaDefect wins 62-77% of runs across six characters with greedy play and 68-80% with test-time search, after 1.3 to 6.7 billion decisions of training per character; runs uploaded by human players of all levels are won 11-20% of the time at the same difficulty. The networks read the game as entity records that identify each card, relic and enemy through a learned embedding and attributes from the game data, together with consequences of public information computed by the engine. Ablations show how much the agent depends on this encoding: without these identities, the network did not win a single run, and without the computed consequences it won 8.3 points fewer. To our knowledge, AlphaDefect is the strongest publicly reported STS2 agent as of November 2026.

items.title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning
items.abstract: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.

items.title: A Comparison of Uncertainty in AI and Dynamical Climate Ensembles
items.abstract: Climate model ensembles and their uncertainty estimates are essential for evaluating risk and designing climate policy. Yet, in the assessment of newly developed AI climate models, evaluating uncertainty is often secondary to diagnosing mean-state climate biases and trends. In this work, we conduct the first systematic comparison of uncertainty representation in ensembles of state-of-the-art AI and dynamical atmospheric climate models. Examining 2-meter temperature, 500 hPa geopotential height, and precipitable water, we find that the AI ensemble exhibits reduced internal variability and model uncertainty across variables relative to the dynamical ensemble. We show that this dampened variability causes the AI ensemble to produce more limited climate extremes and yields underdispersion relative to ERA5. Under a uniform warming scenario, the AI ensemble shows increased model uncertainty. Dynamical models grapple with their own challenges, exhibiting stronger miscalibration (overdispersion) relative to ERA5 and larger climate biases than the AI models. As AI and dynamical climate models are mutually integrated into operational climate prediction, careful consideration of their differences in uncertainty representations is crucial for grounded assessment of climate risk.

items.title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

items.title: DKnown-Jev-2: Article-Level Answer-Evidence Classification and Efficient Inference with a Pre-trained Language Model
items.abstract: Evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering requires determining whether a candidate article contains content that directly supports an answer under the applicable conditions of the question. We present DKnown-Jev-2, an article-level answer evidence classifier designed for evidence integration across multiple paragraphs. The model jointly encodes question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, and uses a pointer-style classification head to predict Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE) in a single forward pass. Ona manually annotated test set of 972 evaluation instances, DKnown-Jev-2 achieves 91.77% accuracy and 91.28% macro-F1, outperforming Jev by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, while reducing both evidence misses and non-evidence false positives. The test set contains 317 multi-paragraph instances, with a maximum body length of 9,322 characters. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification support low-latency inference. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for article-level evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering.

items.title: CAST: A Deployed Speech-to-Text Cascade for Closed Captioning of Entertainment Television
items.abstract: Despite rapid progress in automatic speech recognition (ASR), caption generation for long-form entertainment video remains challenging for content dense in music and effects, rich in accents, crosstalk, and noise. The transcript quality depends on segmentation and surrounding modules as much as the acoustic model. A single pass voice activity detection (VAD) can miss faint, low-energy voice while forwarding near-silent segments that induce hallucination and repetition in an autoregressive decoder. These competing errors motivate a hierarchical VAD that revisits rejected segments under semantic and acoustic retention checks. We present Captioning ASR Stack for Television (CAST), an integrated speech-to-text pipeline for closed captioning (CC) combining frozen Whisper large-v3 with segmentation, language identification, lyrics routing, and targeted hallucination detection and repair on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. On 100 in-house assets spanning 60.46 hours, CAST reduces normalized WER from 6.99% to 5.36% and subtitle edit rate from 254.2 to 221.9 min/hour against the WhisperX pipeline, and improves deletion rate by 11% on public datasets. We also present the behavior of each stage in the pipeline. CAST entered the production speech-to-text (STT) stage of our CC pipeline in late August 2026; we report the evaluation evidence and path to full-scale operation.

items.title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization
items.abstract: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.

items.title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

items.title: Grower-in-the-loop AI for Deployable Precision Fertilisation in Sustainable Agriculture
items.abstract: In agriculture, typically over half of the applied nitrogen fertiliser is lost to water and to air. Precision fertilisation aims to reduce these losses while maintaining yield and quality, yet existing tools struggle to capture farm-specific challenges in determining optimal nitrogen rates. Static recommendations are common and overlook on-farm constraints, such as delays due to weather or machinery availability, or change in budgets. Each constraint governs when and how growers apply fertiliser in practice. Here we present a grower-in-the-loop framework for winter wheat in England, combining baseline fertilisation planning from a machine learning-derived nitrogen-response curve with in-season adaptation via a large language model. We evaluated the framework using data from long-term experiments (LTEs), replicated field trials, and farm deployments. Retrospective model validation using LTEs confirmed low economic decision-loss across multiple seasons. Using field and farm trials, baseline schedules were shown to match standard-practice yields with less nitrogen, whereas in-season adjusted schedules additionally retained grain quality standards. Given this enhanced performance, in-season adaptation absorbed weather, machinery and budget constraints to keep recommendations executable. The framework therefore shows promise for translating static recommendations into adaptable, grower-informed decisions for sustainable fertiliser management.

items.title: Boltz-Flow: Generating High-Quality Robot Action from Boltzmann Machine
items.abstract: Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves $π_{0.5}$ across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.

items.title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
items.abstract: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

items.title: ComputeWise: Measuring and Fixing GPU Waste by AI Research Agents
items.abstract: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.

items.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Soft-Constrained AC-OPF in Multiphase Distribution Systems
items.abstract: This paper presents a self-supervised learning framework for fast, soft-constrained AC optimal power flow (OPF) in unbalanced multiphase distribution systems. The soft AC-OPF objective balances operating cost, renewable energy curtailment, and penalties for violating operating limits. A neural network predicts distributed energy resource (DER) setpoints conditioned on operating conditions, switch configurations, and objective weights. The predicted setpoints are then processed through a DER projection and differentiable AC power flow to enforce device limits and network equalities. The framework is trained by directly minimizing the AC-OPF objective, without optimal-solution labels. Experiments on 123-, 240-, and 906-bus systems yield mean objective gaps of 0.32%, 0.92%, and 0.56%, respectively, relative to IPOPT, across wide operating ranges. Across these systems and the evaluated high-load/low-generation and low-load/high-generation scenarios, the largest mean gap is 1.04%, with mean speedups of 58-5272 times relative to IPOPT.

items.title: Parsing Visual Latents for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
items.abstract: Spatial reasoning across multiple views requires inferring the 3D relations between objects and the camera from 2D observations, which depends on cross-view correspondence and scene geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) do not reliably extract. Pretrained vision encoders already capture this information in their latent features, with CLIP linking objects to image regions, DINOv3 matching semantics across views, and VGGT encoding multi-view geometry. However, VLMs do not benefit from these features when we present them directly in context as grayscale feature images. We therefore propose LatentParse, a training-free framework that parses latent features into explicit spatial evidence for VLMs. In LatentParse, an analyst VLM probes the features of all three encoders with predefined tools that locate objects, track them across views, and measure motion between views. It then distills the results into a concise text report, which is provided together with the images to the VLM to answer the question. We evaluate LatentParse on MMSI-Bench, MV-RoboBench and SPAR-Bench, where it improves all five VLMs over the photo-only baseline by 0.7-2.4 percentage points on average. On MMSI-Bench, it raises Qwen3.8-27B from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest improvements of 19.2 percentage points on the camera-related questions. These results suggest that latent features become useful for spatial reasoning once they are parsed into relation evidence, without training. Code is available at https://github.com/Harvard-AI-and-Robotics-Lab/LatentParse.

items.title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
items.abstract: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.

items.title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
items.abstract: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. At a 5% error margin, it could decide for or against emergencies for about half of users. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

items.title: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation
items.abstract: As incentives to digitize more and more aspects of medical healthcare are gaining traction, additional medical data is becoming available. A major goal is to use this data to gain further insights, support medical staff, and ultimately improve patient care. This demands sophisticated solutions that can handle current and future vast amounts of data, all without disrupting well-established workflows of care takers. Additionally, the solution must fulfill the documentation and risk-management obligations of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), which governs whether a device may be used in patient care in Europe. In this context, we introduce the AMPEL platform, an open-source solution for creating clinical decision support systems (CDSS) that fulfil the requirements of the MDR. Centered around a message broker (Kafka), it adopts an event-driven, distributed architecture, allowing for scaling and efficient processing of medical data as it gets generated. Relying on platform-specific events to implicitly describe the platform's interfaces makes it both extensible and agnostic to the hospital information system in use. With these events being defined in the Protocol Buffers format, medically evaluated algorithms can be independently implemented in a variety of programming languages and easily linked to the platform, extending its analytic capabilities as desired. The platform features a basic UI and alert functionality that can be used to gain medical staff's attention and present analysis results in a traceable and explainable fashion. We further show in a use case how the platform was used to build LAMPE, a CDSS developed and operated at University of Leipzig Medical Center. It demonstrates how the platform solution can be used in a complex and already established environment, while acknowledging current limitations and outlining planned developments to overcome these.

items.title: From joint attention to shared symbols: A free-energy principle account
items.abstract: Joint attention precedes vocabulary acquisition. How can attending to the same object help two people with different sensory experiences come to use a shared word? In a free-energy principle account, marginalizing the common object induces a statistical dependence between private perceptual states. In a categorical world, the joint prior inherits a mixture structure whose component index provides a candidate for shared reference. The collective predictive coding model approximates this prior by representing the dependence through that shared index. An established Metropolis-Hastings naming game lets agents infer and exchange words using private evidence. Toy and multiview image experiments illustrate how word exchange can coordinate private categories and improve the fit of collective models. The account connects joint attention to shared symbols through the coupling of private inference.

items.title: Second-Order Dynamics in Noisy RNNs Produce Exploration and Temporal Compression in Replay
items.abstract: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained to path-integrate. Replay in these networks is described as Langevin sampling, but this theory alone fails to capture the environmental exploration and temporal compression observed in real biological replay. To close this gap, we re-examine spontaneous noisy RNN activity ("replay") as Langevin sampling, one timestep at a time, from a time-series distribution resembling lived experiences (unlike previous works which defined sampling as Monte Carlo inference over a static distribution). We provide a normative second-order Langevin sampling framework wherein spike-frequency adaptation drives spatial exploration at the cost of speed, and momentum via dendritic input differentiation drives temporal compression. We numerically verify our framework via simulations of noisy RNNs trained on 2D triangular and T-maze navigation activity, and others trained on place cell activity of synthetic rats. Crucially, we observe that simultaneous adaptation and momentum increases both replay exploration and speed, and provide one of the first accounts for biologically plausible temporal compression in rate-based RNN replay. Our findings encourage experiments into whether dendritic input differentiation, or other mechanisms, may support temporal compression in memory circuits like the hippocampus.

items.title: Active sensing as control over sensory acquisition
items.abstract: The term "active sensing" is used across neuroscience and engineering to describe a wide range of sensing behaviors, but there is no consensus on what makes sensing "active." We propose that the behaviors grouped under this label are better understood as forms of control over sensory acquisition and develop a framework that distinguishes three interacting forms of control. Mechanistic control physically structures sensory input, strategic control modulates sensing in closed loop through adaptive and attentional processes, and agentic control concerns the sensing policies available to an agent and its authority to choose among them. These forms of control can occur separately or in combination, and have distinct consequences for sensory input, perception, behavior, and performance. The framework clarifies active-passive comparisons and provides a common basis for analyzing biological, engineered, and hybrid sensing systems by asking what is controlled, how, and by whom.

items.title: VLT, Keck, and Gemini characterization of the temporarily captured flyby 2026 QQ$_8$
items.abstract: Very Large Telescope, Keck I, and Gemini North photometry of 2026 QQ$_8$ on November 7-21 gives Sloan Digital Sky Survey-equivalent colors $g-r=0.594^{+0.056}_{-0.053}$, $g-i=0.840^{+0.066}_{-0.065}$, and $i-z=-0.104^{+0.067}_{-0.057}$ mag. Apollo 17 basalt slabs 75075,197 and 71055,239 fit the colors (reduced $χ^2$ of 0.57 and 0.89). The Bus-DeMeo Sq- and K-type templates give reduced $χ^2=0.87$ and 0.90, respectively. The colors permit both an Sq-like asteroid and exposed lunar basalt. With revised Keck timing uncertainties, 71 positions (August 19-November 21) give an outward acceleration of $(1.363\pm0.090)\times10^{-10}$ au day$^{-2}$ at 1 au, implying an area-to-mass ratio of $(6.02\pm0.40)\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$ kg$^{-1}$ for a unit radiation-pressure coefficient. For pre-encounter analogues, NEOMOD3 assigns source probabilities of 78.8% to the $ν_6$ resonance and 20.6% to Jupiter's 3:1 resonance. For a sphere with $H=31.37\pm0.34$, the diameter, density, and mass are ($1.44^{+0.28}_{-0.23}$ m, $1.73^{+0.36}_{-0.30}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $2.73^{+1.19}_{-0.82}\times10^3$ kg) for the Sq albedo ($p_V=0.243\pm0.039$), ($1.62^{+0.28}_{-0.24}$ m, $1.54^{+0.29}_{-0.24}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $3.43^{+1.30}_{-0.94}\times10^3$ kg) for NEOMOD3 ($p_V=0.191$), and ($2.49^{+0.42}_{-0.36}$ m, $1.00^{+0.19}_{-0.16}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $8.09^{+3.06}_{-2.22}\times10^3$ kg) for lunar slabs ($p_V=0.081$). With radiation pressure, nominal capture lasts 224.96 days (April 26-December 7). Sun-Earth corotating geocentric longitude advances 0.76 turns, classifying 2026 QQ$_8$ as a temporarily captured flyby. Its three-dimensional corotating path tangent turns 1.33 revolutions. After 10,000 yr, about 800 of 1,000 clones survive in each model, with about 200 colliding with Earth. The paired survival difference (radiation pressure plus gravity minus gravity only) is ~2 percentage points.

items.title: Probabilistic, facility-specific prioritisation of temperate exoplanets for atmospheric characterisation with JWST and the ELT
items.abstract: Deciding which temperate exoplanets to observe first matters for JWST transit spectroscopy and for planned ELT reflected-light instruments, yet signal-to-noise metrics ignore habitability and similarity indices ignore observability. We present an open Monte Carlo framework (UHI v6.1) that builds probabilistic priority lists separately for each facility and composition class, never as a single ranking. For each of 6,112 planets in the NASA Exoplanet Archive, 10,000 draws carry catalogue uncertainties through climate, cumulative stellar-XUV atmospheric retention, per-draw rocky, Hycean or gas-rich classes, and a JWST (transiting) or ELT/PCS (non-transiting) detection model, giving each planet a survival probability, a conditional score and a top-N probability. At $5σ$, 255 rocky and 71 Hycean candidates remain viable. A Saltelli--Sobol analysis of 32 assumptions ($N = 512$) shows that the location and width of the XUV shoreline dominate the rocky lists, with total-order indices of 0.22 and 0.12 at $5σ$ (0.25 and 0.14 at $3σ$), and all ten leading indices have 95% bootstrap half-widths below 0.05. For Hycean planets most outputs are degenerate and the analysis does not converge, so that branch is reported as indicative. Membership of these lists is limited mainly by whether a planet survives the habitability vetoes: at $5σ$, 3 of the nominal JWST and 4 of the nominal ELT rocky top-10 targets enter the top 10 in at least half of all draws, yet every one of them stays in the top 10 in more than half of the draws in which it survives. Code, per-planet posterior summaries, sensitivity tables and maps are public, so observers can rerun the lists under their own instrument assumptions and see which inputs would most change a target's priority.

items.title: Self-similar Inequality Dynamics in Biased Competition for a Conserved Resource
items.abstract: In many complex systems the redistribution of a conserved resource can generate strong inequality. Important examples are cities exchanging inhabitants, farms competing for farmland, or agents for wealth in saturated markets. Here we model such systems as agents competing for a fixed total resource, and show that coupling agent extinction to a bias favoring richer agents dynamically amplifies this inequality over time. Drawing on an analogy with emulsions, where droplets compete for a conserved quantity, we introduce a dynamical critical resource size that determines an agent's fate. Crucially, this threshold grows in time, continuously raising the bar for survival and further reinforcing inequality. Increasing the bias strength, we find a transition from a continuous resource concentration towards a winner-takes-all outcome. Furthermore, the case of continuous resource concentration is characterized by a self-similar dynamics accompanied by a power-law or exponential increase in inequality, quantified by the Gini coefficient. We derive these results analytically in a mean-field model and compare them to agent-based simulations, showing excellent agreement.

items.title: Dawn of the Gaia Era: Revisiting Cold Jupiters Orbiting M Dwarfs with Astrometry+Doppler Data Joint Analysis
items.abstract: We perform a joint analysis of ground-based radial velocities (RVs), Hipparcos Intermediate Astrometric Data, and two-epoch Gaia astrometry for known M dwarfs hosting cold Jupiters discovered through long-term spectroscopic monitoring. Among a sample of 25 planets in 19 systems, we derive robust absolute masses and orbital solutions for 13 planets in 11 systems with companion inclination uncertainties lower than 30 degrees. These include first mass measurements for five planets: GJ 328b, GJ 649b, GJ 849b and c, and GJ 9066c. We also reclassify one object, HIP 79431B, as a brown dwarf. We further compare the mass ratios of these 13 cold Jupiter systems with those of giant planets orbiting M stars characterized via transit, microlensing, and direct imaging. Without correcting for detection bias, we find that (1) there is likely a deficiency of high-mass-ratio hot Jupiters around M dwarfs compared with cold Jupiters, and (2) the local cold Jupiters orbiting M stars found by RV observations exhibit a similar mass ratio distribution as the counterparts in the Galactic bulge found by microlensing. Cold Jupiters orbiting stars with masses above $0.65~M_\odot$ tend to be more massive than those around M dwarfs. Our study establishes a sample of local cold Jupiters with precise mass determinations around M dwarfs, and reveal a tip of the iceberg in the upcoming Gaia DR4 and DR5.

items.title: Origins of City Reputation: Measuring Trust and Bias in Online Reviews Using Agentic AI and NLP
items.abstract: Online reviews aggregate millions of individual judgments into signals that shape where people eat, stay and travel to, and increasingly read them as evidence of the reputation of places. Nevertheless, whether such reputations really reflect the places or more the instruments used to measure them is unclear. Here we compare two instruments for measuring trust and bias in 100,000 Yelp reviews from ten US cities: a large language model based agentic system including an evaluator critic loop, and a corpus-based tool built on pretrained classifiers, lexicons and rule-based features. Our results show that the two instruments agree on credibility, but not at all on plausibility. They also respond to different use of words and phrases. The corpus-based better flagged complaints and generalizations, whereas the agent better quoted references to social groups. We also found that with five examples, the agent treats ordinary superlatives as bias far more often than with none or one. Aggregated to cities, both instruments find little variation as less than half a percent of the variance of review level reputation lies between cities. This small differences between cities mostly arise from different levels of trust (in case of the agentic tool) and from bias (in case of the corpus-based tool), and the two instruments rank the cities differently. Reputation derived from platform reviews therefore depends on how the reviews are processed and analyzed. As platforms delegate this to language models, the definitions and examples built into these models become part of how places are valued.

items.title: Early Realignment of Eccentric Planetary Orbits without Orbital Decay
items.abstract: Warm Jupiters are, on average, more closely aligned with their host stars than hot Jupiters, even at high eccentricities. The low projected obliquities of eccentric warm Jupiters on the tidal migration track are difficult to reconcile with high-eccentricity migration (HEM) pathways that excite large misalignments. We examine whether tides acting on the star can realign initially misaligned systems before their orbits circularize. We extend a frequency-dependent tidal model to arbitrary eccentricities and focus on the $(1,0)$ obliquity tide. This component is stationary in the inertial frame, dissipates stellar rotational energy, and can change spin obliquity while leaving the semimajor axis and eccentricity unchanged. Its forcing frequency in the stellar rotating frame coincides with that of the rigid spin-over mode, which is non-dissipative. The strength of dissipation by non-rigid motions at this same frequency remains uncertain. In our models, enhancing the dissipative response by a factor of $10^7$ produces appreciable obliquity damping for Jupiter-mass planets. The stronger damping for more massive planets suggests that an enhancement of $10^6$ may suffice for super-Jupiters. Realignment can outpace circularization if the planet is already on an eccentric warm orbit while the star is still inflated and rapidly rotating during the pre-main sequence (PMS). If alignment occurs then, present-day stellar effective temperature may be a weak predictor of obliquity. In binary-driven HEM runs initialized at the zero-age main sequence, orbital circularization outpaces realignment in systems with sustained eccentricity forcing. The stellar quadrupole scaling suggests substantially stronger suppression of eccentricity excitation for PMS starts. These results cast doubt on binary-driven HEM as the origin of such aligned eccentric warm Jupiters, even when they lie along the tidal migration track.

items.title: Cross-calibration of Hera/HyperScout-H with MRO/CRISM and MEx/OMEGA based on Mars observations
items.abstract: On March 12, 2025, Hera, the European Space Agency's planetary defense mission, performed a Mars flyby en route to the asteroid system (65803) Didymos-Dimorphos. During this event, HyperScout-H (HS-H), the spacecraft's hyperspectral imager, acquired five high spatial resolution images over the southern hemisphere of Mars. These observations provide an opportunity for systematic cross-calibration of HS-H with two established Mars orbital instruments, Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) on board the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Murchie et al., 2007), and Observatoire pour la Minéralogie, l'Eau, les Glaces et l'Activité (OMEGA) on board Mars Express (Bibring et al., 2004). This study evaluates the performance, reliability, and readiness of HS-H for the forthcoming asteroid observation phase by comparing it with CRISM and OMEGA data. We selected 21 surface regions spanning diverse terrain types from three HS-H images in which the Martian surface fills the entire field of view. These images were corrected, calibrated, and co-registered to associate each pixel with latitude and longitude. The relative inter-channel correction factors are close to unity for bands 3-25 (0.688-0.952 μm), with standard deviations of 0.52% for OMEGA and 0.62% for CRISM, indicating good agreement in spectral shape. Bands 1 and 2 show a systematic mismatch of 4.7% and 3.6%. The absolute flux correction factors reveal offsets of 8% relative to OMEGA and approximately 0.7% relative to CRISM, with mean inter-image standard deviations below 2%. These results confirm the radiometric stability of HS-H and establish a calibration framework for future Didymos-Dimorphos observations.

items.title: Estimating M Dwarf Ages using their Transiting Brown Dwarf Companions
items.abstract: Determining M dwarf ages remains challenging because of their slow main-sequence evolution. We investigate using transiting brown dwarfs to constrain system ages through their measured masses and thermal emission. We report Palomar/WIRC secondary-eclipse observations of two close-in brown dwarfs, LP 261-75C and AD 3116B, measuring eclipse depths of $6.1 \pm 0.3$ parts per thousand (ppt) in $K_s$ and $9.1 \pm 0.6$ ppt in $J$, respectively. Combining these observations with space-based transit photometry, radial velocities, and host star spectra, we infer brown dwarf internal luminosities and, assuming coevality, host star ages using five sets of atmospheric and evolutionary models. For LP 261-75C, model-dependent median ages span 1.3-2.9 Gyr, substantially older than the previously proposed age of 0.1-0.2 Gyr based on presumed membership in the AB Doradus moving group. This result, the host star's high metallicity, and the companion's measured radius disfavor AB Dor membership. The revised age implies a mass of $\approx 62$-$68$ $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ for the wide-orbit companion LP 261-75B, compared with an earlier estimate of $\approx 21$ $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$. AD 3116B, a member of the 0.6-0.8 Gyr Praesepe cluster, provides a test of brown dwarf evolutionary models through independent constraints on its mass, age, and luminosity. Its inferred age depends strongly on cloud treatment, spanning 0.4-0.6 Gyr for cloudy models and 1.0-1.3 Gyr for cloudless models. Among the models considered, Sonora Diamondback, which includes cloud condensation and cloud clearing across the L/T boundary, provides a plausible simultaneous match to the observed eclipse depth and radius. These results demonstrate a new method to constrain M dwarf ages using emission observations of their brown dwarf companions, while highlighting the sensitivity of the inferred temperatures and ages to evolutionary model differences.

items.title: Centimetre-sized meteoroids from the active asteroid (3200) Phaethon: lunar impact flashes during the 2018 and 2025 Geminids
items.abstract: Centimetre-sized meteoroids released by the active asteroid (3200) Phaethon, parent of the Geminid meteor shower, probe the ejection of refractory material from a comet-asteroid transition object and the age of the stream; lunar impact flashes (LIFs) are the only ground-based technique that samples this size range. We determine the impact flux, mass and size distributions, and expected crater sizes of Geminid meteoroids on the Moon from campaigns at the 2018 and 2025 maxima, and test the stability of the centimetre-sized population over seven years. Both campaigns used the Nihon University 0.40 m "GUNDAM" telescope with CMOS video cameras at 60 fps, with candidates validated at independent stations; a common aperture-photometry pipeline calibrated in the Cousins R band gave peak magnitudes to 0.1-0.25 mag. Eleven LIFs were detected in 3.3 h in 2018 and nine in 2.2 h in 2025, all with Geminid probabilities of 0.87-0.96. With monitored areas measured on the video frames, the campaigns give consistent fluxes of $4.2\times10^{-7}$ and $5.2\times10^{-7}$ km$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$ (merged: $4.6\times10^{-7}$ km$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$). For a luminous efficiency of $1.4\times10^{-3}$ the impactors have masses of 10-320 g, diameters of 1.8-5.9 cm, and predicted crater rim diameters of 2-5 m. The combined sample gives a maximum-likelihood mass index $s=1.76\pm0.17$ and a population index $r=2.0\pm0.3$, markedly shallower than the NELIOTA all-flash values; a single power law with this slope connects the Global Meteor Network millimetre flux to the LIF centimetre flux. The Geminid stream delivers an excess of large particles relative to the sporadic background, consistent with an asteroidal origin, and its stable centimetre-sized flux over seven years constrains stream-formation models with ages of $2\times10^3$-$2\times10^4$ yr.

items.title: Shifting the snow line in protoplanetary disks by planet-induced multiple spiral shocks
items.abstract: The snow line location provides important constraints on rocky planet formation. Recent magnetohydrodynamical simulations suggest that Joule heating associated with gas accretion is so inefficient that the snow line can be located inside 1 au around a solar-type star. This challenges in-situ formation of the terrestrial planets in the solar system unless other internal heating processes are present. Previous studies have proposed that spiral shocks induced by an embedded planet potentially shift the snow line outward. In this study, we investigate the impact of shock heating induced by a giant planet on the location of the snow line in two steps. First, we perform two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of a disk with a giant planet to model shock heating rates. We construct an empirical formula for total entropy jumps due to multiple spiral shocks interior to the planetary orbit. Second, we calculate the radial temperature profile based on the thermal balance with the modeled shock heating rates. We find that shock heating can substantially increase the disk temperature in inner regions far from the planet when the planetary mass and disk optical depth are sufficiently high. For example, assuming a fixed surface density profile and an opacity of $κ= 1~\rm cm^2\,g^{-1}$, a planet with one-third of Jupiter's current mass at 5 au can shift the snow line outward beyond 1 au. Our results suggest that the early formation of proto-Jupiter in the solar nebula may have enabled rocky planetesimals and protoplanets to form in the present-day terrestrial planet region without invoking additional water removal processes.

items.title: No Evidence of Cold Trapping in the Dayside Atmosphere of WASP-33 b
items.abstract: Ultra-hot Jupiters allow simultaneous measurements of volatile molecules and refractory metals, providing constraints on atmospheric chemistry and refractory-element sequestration. We reanalyze the previously published Gemini-N/IGRINS-2 dayside emission spectra of WASP-33~b, extending the analysis to neutral refractory species. Using cross-correlation (CC) and likelihood-based (LL) detection methods, we recover the strongest species detection signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) from CO ($\rm CC~S/N=5.29,\ LL~S/N=5.62$). \ion{Mg}{1} ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=4.73$) and OH ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=3.89$) are recovered at lower significance in both metrics. H$_2$O remains marginal, appearing only in the cross-correlation analysis ($\rm CC~S/N=3.24$), while \ion{Ti}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=3.70$) and \ion{Ca}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=2.98$) show tentative signals. We do not detect \ion{Fe}{1}, \ion{Si}{1}, and \ion{V}{1} in this dataset. A chemical-equilibrium retrieval with a flexible Bezier-spline pressure--temperature profile yields ${\rm C/O}=0.65^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$ and $[{\rm M/H}]=-0.48^{+0.24}_{-0.18}$, and a refractory-to-volatile ratio of $[R/V]_{\rm p}=-0.15^{+0.24}_{-0.23}$. The corresponding stellar-normalized value is $[R/V]_{\rm p/ \star}=0.37^{+0.38}_{-0.36}$, but this value is sensitive to the stellar oxygen abundance. We find that the atmospheric Ti/Mg and Ca/Mg ratios of WASP-33~b are consistent with their respective stellar values within 68\% confidence. This is in contrast to other ultra-hot Jupiters with lower equilibrium temperatures that often show depleted Ti abundances compared to other metals, indicative of cold-trapping. This would suggest that even the nightside of WASP-33~b is too hot for significant condensation and sequestration to occur. Comparison with disk-chemistry models remains exploratory because the carbon-to-refractory posterior overlaps several formation scenarios.

items.title: Friendship paradoxes in networks
items.abstract: Since Scott L. Feld's seminal paper entitled ``Why your friends have more friends than you do'' [Am.~J.~Sociol.~\textbf{96}, 1464 (1991)], the friendship paradox (FP) has been extensively studied in network science and related fields over the last decades. In this paper we survey the literature on the FP and its generalizations. We first introduce definitions and general results of the FPs defined in networks, and then overview their results on model networks. Empirical results using various social network data as well as applications to real-world problems, such as early detection of outbreaks and network sampling, are also summarized. Finally, we conclude by discussing several directions of possible future works.

items.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
items.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

items.title: Investigating Motor Skill Acquisition in Mice and Humans: Towards A Cross-Species Paradigm
items.abstract: Relating non-invasive observations of human brain plasticity to cellular processes identified in animal models remains a major challenge in neuroscience. We address this challenge by introducing a paradigm for studying motor skill acquisition across species. We designed a human chopstick grasping task modeled after the rodent single-pellet reaching task, resulting in a comparable sequence of reach-to-grasp movements across species. We studied 48 young adult male C57BL/6N mice and 71 young men, comparing trained groups with untrained controls. In both mice and humans, structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed before, during, and after motor training. The functional form of behavioral performance gains on the trained task was highly similar across species. In trained compared to control mice, analysis of the early learning interval revealed decreases in regional volume in contralateral primary motor and forelimb somatosensory cortices, with greater volume reductions in primary motor cortex associated with better reaching performance. In humans, performance gains transferred to other chopstick tasks but not to general dexterity, and no reliable changes in gray matter volume were observed. Quantitative MRI, however, revealed early training-related changes in tissue-sensitive measures, including increases in magnetization transfer saturation (MT sat ) and longitudinal relaxation rate (R 1 ) in contralateral motor and frontal regions, potentially reflecting an increase in intracortical myelin. Thus, early structural changes in the contralateral motor cortex were detected in both species, but the degree to which these changes reflect a common biological mechanism is unclear. We conclude that the present cross-species paradigm provides a viable starting point for studying brain plasticity across species. Future work needs to relate macroscopic structural changes more directly to cellular processes by applying longitudinal microscopic imaging and MRI in the same animals.

items.title: Feature processing for single-trial semantic decoding from EEG: a factorial comparison with pre-registered replication
items.abstract: Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain–computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices—signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set—into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time–frequency decomposition including the delta band (2–4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.

items.title: Attentional Bias as an Intermediate Mechanism Linking Executive Dysfunction to Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD
items.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is increasingly recognised as involving persistent difficulties in emotion regulation alongside well-established executive dysfunction. However, the cognitive mechanisms linking executive control impairments to emotional dysregulation remain insufficiently integrated within existing theoretical models. The present conceptual review proposes that attentional bias toward emotionally salient stimuli represents an intermediate cognitive-affective mechanism linking executive dysfunction to emotional dysregulation in ADHD. Drawing on evidence from attentional processing, executive control, affective neuroscience, and neurobiological models of ADHD, the review argues that impaired top-down prefrontal regulatory systems reduce the ability to suppress stimulus-driven attentional capture by emotionally salient information. Consequently, biased attentional allocation may amplify emotional reactivity, prolong engagement with negative affective stimuli, and interfere with adaptive emotion regulation processes. Neurobiologically, disrupted functional connectivity between prefrontal regulatory networks and salience-processing systems, including the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and ventral striatum, may contribute to both attentional and emotional dysregulation in ADHD. The review further discusses theoretical and clinical implications of this framework, including the potential value of interventions targeting attentional control and emotional attentional processing. Limitations of the current evidence base and directions for future longitudinal and neurobiological research are also considered. Conceptualising attentional bias within a broader neurocognitive framework may provide a more integrated and mechanistically coherent account of emotional dysregulation in ADHD.

items.title: Theoretical Challenges in Psychology in the 2000s: Top-5
items.abstract: Psychology entered the twenty-first century with an exceptionally large empirical base and a conspicuously thin theoretical infrastructure. The expansion of cognitive neuroscience, the institutionalization of evidence-based practice, and mounting evidence of a replication crisis exposed foundational assumptions to scrutiny of a kind the discipline had not faced since the paradigm debates of the mid-twentieth century. This article offers a structured critical overview of the five most consequential theoretical problems that shaped psychological science between 2000 and 2010 and traces their trajectory through 2026. The problems are ranked according to three explicit criteria—logical priority, breadth of disciplinary impact, and urgency for scientific and applied practice—and the ranking itself is defended as an argument, with alternative orderings considered and rejected. The resulting order is: (1) fragmentation of psychological theory and the absence of a unifying metatheory; (2) the crisis of construct validity and operationalism; (3) the mind–brain identity problem and the reductionism debate; (4) the cultural challenge to universalist assumptions; and (5) the methodological–epistemological tension between positivist and interpretivist traditions. Each problem is analyzed with respect to its antecedents, its specific manifestations during the 2000s, and the partial responses advanced in the subsequent decade and a half. The central claim is that the five problems form an interlocking system whose keystone is metatheoretical fragmentation; because the terms in which the remaining four problems are stated presuppose unsettled metatheoretical commitments, piecemeal reform cannot produce durable resolution. The concluding section outlines a research agenda centered on integrative theoretical reconstruction and epistemologically grounded methodological pluralism.

items.title: Moral Preferences Theory of Redistribution
items.abstract: In recent years, the steady rise of economic inequality across the globe has accompanied an ever-increasing focus on the question of redistribution. Though the majority of people believe that economic inequality is a problem, policy decisions to redistribute resources are typically highly contentious. Previous psychological, sociological, and political science theories which attempt to explain the paradox between stated beliefs and actual behavior in redistributive choice have largely relied upon an unverified assumption that redistributive preferences are derived from perceptions about pre-existing inequality. Here, we propose a Moral Preferences Theory of Redistribution, which integrates intuitions and prior research derived from various modeling frameworks across psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and economics. This theory posits that that redistributive behavior is guided by multiple moral principles, and that the preferences that guide the selection of these principles are both context-dependent and reflect dispositional individual values. This theory was tested using a multi-methodological approach: across two experiments – a large behavioral experiment (N = 231) and a direct fMRI follow-up study (N = 50) – the data show converging evidence to support the Moral Preferences Theory across multiple levels of analysis: political, psychometric, computational, and neural.

items.title: The role of neuroscience for psychological causal explanation
items.abstract: Psychology provides causal explanations of behavior but it remains contested whether such explanations are scientifically legitimate without grounding in neuroscience. Two prominent arguments have been put forward to argue for the dependence of psychology on neuroscience: first, the classical causal exclusion argument argues that higher-level causes are excluded by lower-level causes. Second, according to a more recent argument, psychological models only provide how-possibly explanations but not how-actually explanations unless the variables and relations they postulate correspond to underlying neural mechanisms. In this article, we defend the independence of psychological causal explanation. Based on an interventionist account of causation, we argue that a psychological model is causally explanatory when it identifies variables that serve as points of intervention. Still, we show that neuroscience sometimes has a crucial role for validating psychological models: when a psychological model identifies points of interventions that cannot be intervened on at the psychological level.

items.title: Covert control over the real-time dynamics of human interactions with Ducksoup
items.abstract: Uncovering how facial and vocal signals shape social interactions is difficult because researcherscannot control how humans behave during free conversations. Here we demonstrate that recentadvances in AI-based transformation filters enable researchers to have covert experimental controlover the real-time dynamics of social interactions. We introduce Ducksoup, a scientificvideoconference platform that allows researchers to collect social interaction experiments online,realistically transform participants' faces and voices in real time mid-conversation, record thesynchronized interactions and extract multimodal time series from recordings for analysis. In apreregistered experiment (N = 64 participants), we replicate recent laboratory findings in a fullyonline setup: artificially aligning participants’ smiles increased mutual enjoyment while remainingundetected. The paradigm also revealed feedback effects on participants’ spontaneous facial, vocaland verbal behavior. By combining the ecological validity of free interactions with experimentalcontrol and scalable data collection, Ducksoup turns natural conversations into a causalexperimental paradigm for psychology and neuroscience.
