items.title: Viscophoretic Nanoparticle Transport
items.abstract: Viscosity is a fundamental property of liquids and sets the diffusivity of suspended particles. When viscosity varies in space, diffusivity does too; under isothermal conditions, stochastic thermodynamics predicts a particle drift term v = ∂xD(x) arising from position-dependent viscosity. Here, we impose steep, stable viscosity gradients in a microfluidic channel and directly image nanoparticle motion at the single-particle level using high-resolution microscopy. We find viscous-gradient-driven drift velocities that exceed Stokes–Einstein-based estimates, and we quantify this discrepancy through simultaneous measurements of local diffusivity and drift extracted from the same trajectories. We then illustrate how such controlled gradients enable passive focusing in a phoretic trap that combines viscophoresis with diffusiophoresis. Our measurements provide a quantitative single-particle characterization of viscous-gradient-driven transport that is of importance in any system and any application exhibiting viscosity gradients, from membrane separation processes to inter- and intracellular biomolecular transport.

items.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Transit Timing Variation Characterization: A Case Study of the Kepler-88 System
items.abstract: Transit timing variation (TTV) provides rich information about the mass and orbital properties of exoplanets, which are often obtained by solving an inverse problem via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). In this paper, we design a new data-driven approach that potentially can be applied to problems that are hard for traditional MCMC methods, such as the case with only one planet transiting. Specifically, we use a deep learning approach to predict the parameters of a nontransit companion for the single transit system with transit information (i.e., TTV and transit duration variation (TDV)) as input. This approach is constructed using the Transformer -based architecture that can extract long-range interactions from TTV sequential data. We focus on two-planet systems based on Kepler-88 as a starting point, with the inner planet fixed to the properties of Kepler-88 and the mass and orbital elements of the outer planet varied. Applying to Kepler-88, we obtained an overall fractional error of ≲10% on semimajor axis and eccentricity, and ∼10%−30% on planet mass (assuming that the stellar and transiting planet parameters are known), based on a training set of a million simulations. When applied to the test set, our model achieves low fractional errors of less than a few percent for systems with TTV semiamplitudes ranging from ∼0.3 s to ∼5 minutes. Extending our approach to a broader range of planetary architectures, including systems with substantially weaker or stronger TTV signals and those containing additional planets or stellar companions, remains an important direction for future work.

items.title: Ozone decrease observed in the upper atmosphere following the 11 May 2024 Mother's Day and the 8 June solar storms
items.abstract: On 11 May 2024, a succession of coronal mass ejections merged and struck the Earth, inducing large-scale perturbations in the magnetosphere. During this event, satellite observations revealed that an extreme geomagnetic storm occurred alongside a moderate solar proton event (SPE). Simultaneously, atmospheric ozone and temperature were measured by the AURA/MLS instrument. In this work, we present the first observations of the effect of the extreme storm of May and the subsequent SPE of 8 June on ozone concentration and temperature throughout the atmosphere. The observations of the MLS instrument show that the event of May led to stronger depletion of O 3 in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere (MLT) than in June and that noticeable depletion mainly occurred in the Southern Hemisphere. This difference is explained by the type and intensity of energetic particle precipitation (EPP) that occurred during the two events, with both protons and electrons in May and only protons in June. In May, mesospheric ozone depletion peaked at 60 % at 80 km and reached 30 % at 75 km, lasting for 5 d. The SPE of June also caused a decrease of mesospheric ozone that lasted for 2 d down to 70 km. Below 60 km, no significant changes in ozone volume mixing ratio (vmr) were observed after either event.

items.title: Diagnosing the Effects of Spectroscopic Training Set Imperfection on Photometric Redshift Performance
items.abstract: Most LSST extragalactic science will rely on photometric redshifts (photo-z) to extract distance information for the galaxies. However, an incomplete or non-representative training set can introduce bias into photo-z estimation. It is necessary to understand how various forms of training set imperfection, such as incompleteness and non-trivial spectroscopic target selection, affect photo-z estimation algorithms, and to identify metrics best-suited to quantify the impact. This work aims to systematically study metrics for diagnosing how various photo-z methods react to certain types of training set incompleteness and non-representativeness. We use methods available through the open-source Python library Redshift Assessment Infrastructure Layers (RAIL) to systematically test the algorithms CMNN, GPz, FlexZBoost, and PZFlow on mock training data degraded in accordance with several existing spectroscopic sky surveys, as well as under conditions of inverse redshift incompleteness, which approximately mimics observed patterns of incompleteness at high redshift. We employ the algorithm TrainZ as a control. Finally, we quantify photo-z algorithm performance using a variety of statistical metrics implemented externally to RAIL. We determine that the Kullback-Liebler Divergence, Wasserstein Distance, and Probability Integral Transform are particularly informative metrics with which to assess the impact of training set imperfection on algorithmic performance. We also find that inverse redshift incompleteness effects alone lack the complexity to realistically represent anticipated training data.

items.title: Simulating AGN wind feedback with variable feedback efficiencies in idealised disc galaxies
items.abstract: Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) feedback plays a critical role in galaxy formation and evolution. AGN-driven winds can significantly influence their host galaxies, although the details of their impact remain unclear. In this study, we investigate the feedback effects of AGN winds on idealized disc galaxies using the SWIFT hydrodynamical code with COLIBRE subgrid physics. We implement a new thermal AGN feedback model in which the energy injection coupling efficiency has a power-law dependence on the Eddington ratio of the black hole (BH) accretion rate, motivated by scaling relations for AGN winds from numerical models and observations. We simulate idealised Milky Way-mass galaxies, incorporating a BH, cold gas disc, stellar disc, and hot circumgalactic medium, within a static dark matter halo. We vary the BH mass and the slope and normalisation of the new coupling efficiency model. For a fixed BH mass, we find that while systematic trends with coupling efficiency exist, most galaxy and BH properties show only modest variations. This likely reflects BH self-regulation in the COLIBRE model, which modulates the effects of changes in the feedback efficiency, provided the BH mass is sufficiently high. Key exceptions are the BH accretion rate and mass growth history, and outflow behaviour, where lower coupling efficiencies lead to faster BH growth and weaker outflows, potentially helping to explain the presence of overmassive BHs at high redshifts. Varying the BH mass, however, has a much larger impact, confirming that BH mass remains the primary factor shaping galaxy and BH evolution in our simulations.

items.title: Field-level Inference from Galaxies: Baryon Acoustic Oscillation Reconstruction
items.abstract: Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) underpin the key cosmological results from modern spectroscopic galaxy surveys, but nonlinear gravitational evolution limits the precision achievable with traditional analysis methods. To overcome this, we develop field-level inference for BAO, first reconstructing the initial linear density field and then fitting the BAO signal therein. We benchmark three reconstruction methods: (i) traditional reconstruction based on linear theory, (ii) explicit field-level inference using differentiable forward modeling with hybrid effective field theory, and (iii) implicit field-level inference using a convolutional neural network to augment traditional reconstruction. Using DESI-like luminous red galaxy (LRG) and Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) catalogs, we find that field-level approaches significantly sharpen the BAO feature relative to traditional reconstruction. For LRGs, explicit field-level inference improves constraints on the BAO scale parameters ( α iso , α ap ) by 23%–26%, while implicit inference improves constraints by 33%–34%, corresponding to a 2.2× improvement in figure of merit (FoM). For the higher-density, lower-redshift BGS sample, field-level inference enables information extraction from smaller scales, yielding an improvement in constraints of up to 46%, corresponding to a 3.2× improvement in FoM. Crucially, we address longstanding concerns regarding the robustness of field-level reconstruction by leveraging 1000 mock realizations to perform extensive coverage tests. Our results are both unbiased and statistically well calibrated, maintaining nominal coverage even when using tight simulation-informed priors and under model misspecification.

items.title: Revisiting constraints on primordial curvature power spectrum from PBH abundances
items.abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) can form in the early Universe, for instance during radiation domination, from the collapse of large-amplitude density perturbations shortly after horizon re-entry. This mechanism establishes an approximate one-to-one correspondence between the PBH mass and the scale of the peak in the primordial curvature perturbations. Consequently, the constraints on PBH abundances can be translated into upper limits on the amplitude of the primordial curvature power spectrum, thereby providing an indirect probe of the last e-folds of inflation corresponding to these smaller scales. Assuming Gaussian primordial curvature perturbations, we derive constraints on the amplitude of primordial curvature power spectra with both narrow and broad peaks using the most up-to-date bounds on PBH abundances. Given the theoretical uncertainties in PBH formation, we systematically compare the constraints obtained using the Press–Schechter (PS) formalism and peak theory, accounting for the nonlinear relation between curvature perturbations and density contrast, and assess the impact of different window functions and the transfer function. We quantify the impact of spherical versus non-spherical collapse criteria and show that including non-sphericity significantly increases the inferred amplitude of the primordial power spectrum, reflecting the larger threshold density contrast required for PBH formation. We also find that whereas the constraints obtained using the PS formalism and peak theory remain largely similar for the monochromatic case, they differ in the case of a broad primordial power spectrum. This discrepancy underscores that current constraints remain sensitive to the choice of statistical formalism. Our consistent treatment of monochromatic and extended mass functions provides a systematic mapping based on existing methodologies, while highlighting that reducing these theoretical uncertainties is a crucial step toward probing the early Universe through PBHs.

items.title: Blueshifted lines from the inner accretion disc’s rotation can explain quasar absorption “forests”
items.abstract: Recent XRISM observations of active galactic nuclei (AGN) such as PDS 456 have revealed “forests” of absorption lines best modeled by five distinct absorption zones with varying large blueshifts. We propose a model in which these relativistic blueshifts originate from the motion of the accretion disc itself, rather than from a clumpy super-Eddington outflow at hundreds of gravitational radii rg ≡ GM/c2. We demonstrate that thin fragments of absorbing material lying just above the accretion disc at varying radii can produce the observed energy shifts and separations of the absorption zones. In this model, the PDS 456 X-ray transmission spectrum is well reproduced by fragments of azimuthal rings with radial widths Δr ≲ 1rg at locations between the black hole’s innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) and ≈15rg. This model suggests that the absorption forests seen in XRISM observations can probe the surface structure of the innermost (≲ 15rg) regions of quasar accretion discs and predicts the presence of redshifted absorbers.

items.title: Alternate states and intermingledness in complex high-dimensional systems
items.abstract: Many natural systems posses, and can transition between, multiple alternative states. For example, a climate “tipping element” is a climate component that can transition to an alternative steady state due to an external perturbation such as global warming. Despite the potential impact, existence of alternate states in realistic, complex simulations (e.g., climate models) remain poorly understood. Arguably a reason for this is the lack of applicable methodology that explicitly targets finite yet high-dimensional datasets. In this work we utilize recent progress in computational nonlinear dynamics to formulate a workflow that analyses potentially multi-state simulation data and decides algorithmically what are the alternate states contained within, if any are clearly distinguishable. The framework undergoes an optimization routine that showcases which observables in the data best differentiate the alternate states, and which ones do not differentiate at all, which could be used to guide monitoring and early-warning for multistable components in climate or ecosystems. Finally, once the alternate states have been found, we define an indicator called “intermingledness”. It quantifies differences and similarities between alternate states, as well as for their basins of attraction (if applicable), across various diagnostic variables. We analyse and present results using three diverse climate datasets: Atlantic ocean circulation, atmospheric midlatitude flow, and habitability of exoplanets. The method is not exclusive to climatic data, but applicable to a variety of cases characterised by high dimensional data and presence of alternate states, including complex networks such as power grids or biological networks. We also provide easy-to-use open source code for applying the workflow to new data.

items.title: Nonintegral flux trapping in frustrated Josephson networks of triplet superconductors
items.abstract: In a Josephson junction network, anisotropic coupling between spin triplet pairing correlations can lead to frustrated d vector textures that support spontaneous Josephson currents and nonintegral flux trapping. Such networks can appear in superconducting polycrystals, as well as single-crystal superconductors. In analogy to classical spin systems, in which the presence of geometric frustration and anisotropic superexchange can lead to nontrivial spin textures, Josephson networks with anisotropic Josephson couplings cannot simultaneously optimize their U ( 1 ) superconducting phase differences and relative d vector orientations. The internal pairing structure of Cooper pairs twists as they tunnel across the Josephson junction, and the d vector texture enters as an emergent geometric phase which can spontaneously trap fractional flux. For real-valued Josephson couplings between unitary d vectors, the emergent geometric phase reduces to a ℤ 2 structure, allowing for spontaneous π -flux trapping above a critical antisymmetric coupling, distinct from usual half-quantum vortices. Further, we demonstrate a continuously tunable nonintegral flux for complex Josephson couplings. The results of this work reveal new routes to engineer frustrated Josephson networks from the interplay of magnetic textures and spin triplet superconducting pairing order.

items.title: Measurement of the Weyl Potential Evolution and $E_G$ Statistic from KiDS-1000, BOSS and 2dFLenS
items.abstract: A recently developed model-independent approach to measuring the Weyl potential has shown some tensions with $\Lambda$CDM (Lambda Cold Dark Matter) in DES (Dark Energy Survey) Y3 data. We apply this framework to Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS-1000) weak lensing and BOSS/2dFLenS galaxy clustering using the KiDS Cosmology Analysis Pipeline (KCAP) in two redshift bins. To apply this method to the BOSS spectroscopic wedges, we take the early-time power spectrum from a redshift where General Relativity (GR) is recovered and jointly fit the late-time observables $\hat{b}$, $\hat{f}$, and $\hat{J}$. With Planck18 priors, the CMASS measurement of $\hat{J}$ is $1.50\sigma$ below the GR prediction, while the LOWZ measurement remains consistent with it. The decrease in the central value of $\hat{J}$ from LOWZ to CMASS provides a mild indication of the previously reported ``Lensing is low'' behavior. Without Planck18 priors, we obtain $E_G(0.38)=0.503\pm0.054$ and $E_G(0.61)=0.444\pm0.054$, both consistent with GR. Furthermore, phenomenological gravity tests also show no significant preference for modified gravity.

items.title: Millimeter-wave Detections of Symbiotic Stars in SPT and ACT Data
items.abstract: We present the results of a joint targeted search of candidate symbiotic stars at millimeter wavelengths using the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT). Candidates are selected from the New Online Database of Symbiotic Variables, restricting to objects that are within either the SPT-3G or ACT~DR6 footprint, covering most of the southern hemisphere and up to a declination of + 20 ∘ . Forced photometry on the 828 candidate symbiotic star locations in SPT and ACT data results in 31 unique objects detected with more than a 3 σ significance using two frequency bands: 18 confirmed and 13 suspected symbiotic stars. We provide the SPT and ACT 95/98, 150, and 220~GHz light curves, along with optical and infrared light curves from 2016–2026, as well as spectral energy distributions, physical parameters from the literature, and brief summaries regarding the nature of each individual object. Using Herschel SPIRE data from 2013, we place upper limits on millimeter flux for CN Cha near the beginning of the optical rise in its 2012/2013 nova, which suggests a strong variability and lag at millimeter wavelengths and results in a rare observance of a potential Galactic millimeter slow transient. In addition, we provide coadded thumbnails and light curves for the remaining 797 candidate symbiotic stars that did not pass our detection thresholds. Millimeter-wave emission from symbiotic stars is primarily a combination of free-free emission of the ionization region and optically thick blackbody emission of the cooler dust components of the system. When combined with contemporaneous multi-wavelength observations, millimeter-wave observations can be used to test binary models of symbiotic stars and provide insight on the geometry and physical properties of these systems.

items.title: Citizenship Education in Addressing the Dynamics of Digital Society in Papua
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital society has fundamentally reshaped how citizens access information, communicate, learn, and engage in public life. In Papua, this digital transformation presents substantial opportunities alongside persistent structural challenges, including uneven technological infrastructure, limited digital literacy, the proliferation of disinformation, and ethical vulnerabilities in online spaces. This study examines the strategic role of Citizenship Education in addressing these dynamics and formulates a context-responsive conceptual framework tailored to Papua’s regional realities. Employing a qualitative approach through an integrative literature review, the research synthesizes scholarly publications and policy documents on digital society, digital literacy, digital ethics, digital citizenship, and local Papuan contexts via thematic categorization and conceptual synthesis. The findings demonstrate that meaningful digital inclusion extends beyond physical connectivity and device availability, requiring citizens to critically evaluate information, uphold ethical standards, and participate constructively in civic life. The novelty of this article lies in synthesizing digital literacy, Pancasila-grounded digital ethics, and civic competence into an integrated pedagogical framework explicitly contextualized within Papua’s geographical barriers, sociocultural plurality, and unequal educational access. Theoretically, this framework offers curriculum developers and educators a structured foundation for designing inclusive, hybrid Civic Education strategies that bridge digital divides without assuming uniform connectivity. Practically, it establishes an analytical baseline for policymakers and future empirical research to formulate measurable learning outcomes and validate context-appropriate instructional interventions across Papuan educational institutions.

items.title: The cyborg fly: reflexes survive engineered actuators, coordination needs stand-ins
items.abstract: Two wiring diagrams now cover the whole central nervous system of an adult fruit fly: one female, one male. Can such a diagram, run as a network of spiking neurons, drive a body? And if we swap the body's muscles for engineered actuators, what survives? We ran both connectomes, BANC and MaleCNS, as leaky integrate-and-fire networks of about 160,000 neurons each, and closed the loop through simulated sensors, actuators and bodies for walking and flight. The actuators are port-Hamiltonian, so energy is audited at every step, and swapping one for another changes only a configuration file. Null networks shuffled at five levels, from the whole nervous system to synapse counts, test whether a result depends on the wiring. The wiring produced specific functions: sugar on the labellum drove the proboscis motor neuron, leg joints resisted imposed movement, leg circuits oscillated, a looming disc drove a take-off signal on its side (in MaleCNS), and descending neurons throttled and steered flight. The resistance reflex survived 20 of 20 actuator settings in MaleCNS and 19 of 20 in BANC, including a Hill-type muscle pair and a geared DC motor; the actuator set walking speed and energy cost instead. Coordinated six-leg walking, flight stability and the correction of perturbations did not emerge. Each needed a labelled engineered stand-in, which the connectome could command. Such stand-ins can also manufacture an apparent dependence on wiring: in a rebuild of a published closed loop, odour navigation came from a hand-written rule, and the network entered only through one valence number. The two animals differed on some functions, and the differences traced to wiring, such as a haltere drive of the flight power muscles found only in MaleCNS. A whole-CNS connectome, embodied, gives reflexes, rhythms and command signals, but not the coordination that turns them into behaviour.

items.title: The Self-Assembling Brain: Emergent Routing and Its Open Challenges
items.abstract: Biologically inspired alternatives to backpropagation, such as feedback alignment, relax the requirement for exact synaptic weight symmetry but still presuppose a fixed, pre-wired correspondence between forward and feedback pathways, an impasse Liao et al. (PNAS, 2026) term "architectural circularity." This commentary examines their Self-Assembling Motif (SAM), which reframes credit assignment as a self-organizing process driven by local synaptic rules. By linking ascending inference and descending feedback streams through initially random cross-stream connections, SAM supports local bridge alignment and emergent pathway alignment during stable training without fixed neuron-to-neuron pairing. Its resulting learning dynamics also exhibit adaptive preconditioning. The commentary highlights the algorithmic, biophysical, and temporal challenges that define the next research frontier: loss of neuron-specific nonlinear gating under straight-through approximation, compounding routing errors in deeper hierarchies, low-dimensional routing bottlenecks, the cortical implementation of non-driving modulatory connections, and the shift from alternating inference-update phases to continuous sensory processing.

items.title: The rotation period of the near-Earth comet (875163) 1998 SH2 and the limits of a single-apparition phase curve
items.abstract: The near-Earth object (875163) 1998 SH2 was recently shown to be a weakly active comet: its 1998-2025 astrometry reveals a non-gravitational acceleration too large to be radiative in origin, and large-aperture imaging during its 2025 apparition revealed a faint tail (Farnocchia et al. 2026). No rotation period had been reported. We derive one from dense TTT2 photometry obtained on five nights of the same apparition: from 2392 calibrated measurements we find a synodic rotation period P = 6.970 +/- 0.020 h. The folded light curve is markedly bimodal (A2/A1 ~ 6.4) with a peak-to-peak amplitude of ~0.18 mag, implying a/b >~ 1.18. Combined with the published radar Doppler bandwidth, the period is consistent with an elongated body whose rotation the radar alone could not constrain. Over the narrow observed phase-angle range (3.7-9.3 deg) the IAU H,G and H,G1,G2 slope parameters are not physically constrained. The inter-night magnitude gradient, beta_app = 0.074 +/- 0.005 mag/deg, is steeper than the default G=0.15 and lies in the upper part of the Jupiter-family comet (JFC) distribution (median 0.046; Kokotanekova et al. 2017); because the object was weakly and increasingly active during the run, we treat this value as an upper limit to the intrinsic surface phase slope. Under the population prior of little or no opposition surge, as found in available JFC nucleus phase curves, the phase behaviour is best described by a linear law, giving a provisional H_Lum(1,1,0) ~ 20.9-21.0 over 3.7-9.3 deg in the Luminance band.

items.title: Eccentricities and inclinations are decoupled in super-Earth systems
items.abstract: Recent work on the longterm evolution of the inner Solar System has shown that the inclination contribution to the Angular Momentum Deficit (AMD) is almost constant even though inclinations and eccentricities are highly coupled in expansions of the perturbing function. We wish to characterize the conservation of the eccentricity AMD and inclination AMD, respectively describing the average eccentricity and mutual inclination of planetary orbits, beyond the case of the Solar System. We aim at showing that this conservation is a general feature of the stable planetary systems dynamics, in particular, in the context of low mass multiplanetary systems. We perform a series of numerical simulations using both N-body and secular codes to study the dynamics over billions of orbits. Taking as a template four equal mass Super-Earth with non uniform orbital spacing, we consider sets of systems with different AMD and use the orbital elements evolution to assess the conservation of inclination and eccentricity AMD components. For stable systems, the inclination AMD and eccentricity AMD relative variation is typically below 1%, making them quasi-integrals of motion. At low AMD, despite short Lyapunov timescales, the secular diffusion is confined and the dynamics almost quasi-periodic. As the AMD increases, the emergence of large scale secular chaos only weakly affects the conservation of the quasi-integrals, which breaks when systems become fully unstable. The eccentricity and inclination evolution (as measured by the variation of their AMD contributions) are largely decoupled for low mass multiplanetary systems. Combined with the weak diffusion of the Laplace-Lagrange modes at low AMD, these findings paint a picture where the secular dynamics are not necessarily ergodic. The uncovering of these quasi-integrals opens a new path to relate the observed planetary architecture to its formation.

items.title: Airport-level runway-incursion rates normalized by movements: hierarchical shrinkage estimates, ranking uncertainty and severity for FAA-towered airports, FY2008-FY2024
items.abstract: Runway incursions are one of ICAO's five high-risk occurrence categories, yet airport-level comparisons of incursion risk in the United States still rest on raw counts or on fixed-count thresholds that select on sampling noise. We assemble an airport-fiscal-year panel of 565 FAA-towered airports holding 27,079 runway-incursion records from the FAA Runway Safety database as held in the FlightFinder corpus (himaxym.com), normalized by tower operations from the FAA Terminal Area Forecast (ATADS/OPSNET actuals). A hierarchical negative-binomial model with log operations as an exposure offset, airport random effects, fiscal-year effects and traffic-mix covariates yields, for every airport, a shrinkage-adjusted rate per million operations, an exceedance probability relative to the national median, and a posterior rank with a 90% interval in the manner of Goldstein and Spiegelhalter. Severity (Category A-D) is modeled separately as an ordinal outcome, and empirical-Bayes and fully Bayesian shrinkage are compared. The crude national rate is 29.4 incursions per million operations (95% interval 29.1-29.8), with an index of dispersion of 8.61. Between-airport dispersion after exposure adjustment is sigma_u = 1.05: an airport one standard deviation above the mean carries 2.84 times the national rate. 199 of 565 airports exceed the national median with probability above 0.9, and the 90% rank interval at the median airport spans 134 positions, so much of the league table is statistically indistinguishable from its middle. Severity and frequency respond to different determinants: the airport-level rank correlation between them is -0.08 (90% interval -0.14 to -0.02), so a frequency ranking carries little information about where a severe outcome is likely. The results offer a reproducible, uncertainty-aware alternative to count thresholds for prioritizing runway-safety interventions.

items.title: The Jupiter ICy moons Explorer (JUICE) Mission: Post-Launch Status and Mission Overview
items.abstract: The JUpiter ICy Moons Explorer (JUICE) is the first large-class mission in ESA's Cosmic Vision programme. Proposed in 2007 and selected in 2012, it was launched on 14 April 2023 from Kourou and is now en route towards Jupiter. After arrival in July 2031, JUICE will spend approximately four years studying the Jupiter system, performing multiple flybys of three of its Galilean moons, the icy moons Ganymede, Europa, and Callisto, before entering orbit around Ganymede for its final year. The mission will investigate conditions that may support habitable environments within the satellites, all of which are thought to contain subsurface liquid water oceans. Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System, is a prime target due to its internal structure and possible subsurface ocean, its unique intrinsic magnetic field, and its complex interactions with Jupiter's magnetosphere, offering a natural laboratory for studying the emergence, evolution and potential habitability of icy worlds around giant planets. JUICE will also conduct a global investigation of the Jupiter system as the archetype for gaseous giant planet systems: it will study Jupiter's atmospheric circulation, composition, and flow of energy from the cloud tops to the thermosphere and characterise the 3D structure of the magnetosphere and its coupling with the ionosphere and thermosphere. Interactions between the moons and the magnetosphere, as well as tidal and gravitational evolution within the Galilean system, will also be assessed. Additional science objectives include the innermost Galilean moon, Io and its neutral cloud and plasma torus, some small inner and irregular moons, and the ring systems. The payload includes 10 instruments and one experiment using the spacecraft's telecommunications system to connect with ground-based radio telescopes, plus an onboard radiation monitor.

items.title: An exact and fast solution for the common overlap of three disks in mutual transits and eclipses
items.abstract: The area common to three disks determines how much light is blocked during mutual events of transiting planets, moons, and eclipsing multiple stars. We present a new solution that removes every case distinction from the evaluation and corrects several errors in earlier work. We prove that a non-degenerate overlap has at most four corners, which reduces the geometry to five topologies that a single directed walk along the boundary arcs resolves. Green's theorem then yields the area as a sum of circular segments and a vertex polygon. The evaluation needs one arctangent per arc, suffers no subtractive cancellation, and handles arcs longer than $π$ without a special case. We verify the solution for all cases and show that the algorithm is componentwise backward stable. Five public packages that compute the same area fail on some of our test configurations, either through undefined values, missing topologies, or lost precision. Our complete computation takes 45 ns per configuration on one CPU core, which is four to several thousand times faster than the public packages. The same decomposition also delivers the centroid of the overlap in closed form.

items.title: A New Population of Jovian Exoplanets Suitable For Direct Imaging with the Habitable Worlds Observatory, the Roman Coronagraph, and ELTs Identified from HARPS Radial-Velocity Data and Hipparcos-Gaia Astrometry
items.abstract: We jointly analyze archival radial-velocity data from the HARPS spectrograph and astrometry from Hipparcos and Gaia to identify and constrain the dynamical properties of new and known long-period jovian exoplanets. Our search yields 14 new confirmed planets with masses of 0.04--6.1 $M_{\rm Jup}$ and semimajor axes of 0.1--12.6 au. Planets include a super-Jupiter in a near-Saturn-like orbit producing a strong astrometric acceleration (HIP 669 b), an eccentric Jupiter around a K star with a modest acceleration (HIP 39039 b), a 74-day-orbit warm Neptune (HIP 64550 b), and a giant planet around a Tier A Habitable Worlds Observatory target that may endanger any habitable zone Earth (HIP 17378 b). Three systems show evidence for candidate planets requiring additional data for confirmation. Our modeling also constrains the dynamical masses and orbits for 32 previously known radial-velocity-discovered planets. Orbits, masses, and ages for our sample show that five targets are potentially detectable in reflected light with the Roman Coronagraph, 28 should be imageable in reflected light with the Habitable Worlds Observatory, and six may be detectable in thermal emission with E-ELT/METIS. These results demonstrate the power of combining archival radial-velocity data with astrometry to discover and characterize long-period giant planets, a capability that will only grow with Gaia DR4. It provides a new sample of targets for future direct-imaging observations, and shows a path forward for timely vetting of targets for exo-Earth imaging with the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

items.title: From residuals to warps: Probing disk geometry with gas kinematics
items.abstract: Evidence of shadowing among protoplanetary disks suggests that warped protoplanetary disks are widespread, making it crucial to constrain their three-dimensional shape in order to understand their dynamical evolution and origin. Yet, inferring this warp shape from observations is challenging, as the typical signatures of a warp, especially shadows, are often degenerate with the warp shape. Kinematics of disks may provide a method to recover the shape by interpreting the residuals from a Keplerian disk model as local changes in inclination and position angle. In this work, we test its applicability and limitations. We perform radiative transfer simulations of disks with a parametrized warp shape to create synthetic maps of $^{12}\mathrm{CO}$ rotational line emission at ALMA wavelengths and compare the fitted warp with the true warp shape. We find that the warp shape can be recovered for nearly face-on disks with small warp misalignments of a few degrees, even without knowledge about disk properties such as emission height. The overall warp shape remains traceable even at moderate spectral resolutions up to $0.8\,\mathrm{km/s}$. However, we identify regimes where the method breaks down, including disks with an inclination higher than $40^\circ$, a high emission height of the tracer, and sharp warp transitions. In addition, radial and vertical motions can introduce apparent warps and twists, motivating extensions of the method to account for these effects.

items.title: Revisiting TOI-2120 b: Updated mass and radius constraints on a sub-Neptune orbiting an M4 dwarf
items.abstract: We present updated mass and radius measurements of TOI-2120 b, a short-period (5.80 days) planet orbiting a mid-M dwarf identified by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). TOI-2120 b was previously validated through transit photometry and high-resolution imaging, with a radius near the upper boundary of the radius valley around low-mass stars. We refined the planetary properties by combining archival TESS and ground-based photometry with new transit observations from the ARC 3.5m and Red Buttes Observatory (RBO) telescopes and new precision RV measurements obtained with the Habitable-zone Planet Finder (HPF) spectrograph. Our joint analysis yields a radius of $2.31\pm0.7$ Rearth, larger than previously reported. We also measure a planetary mass of $5.81^{+2.94}_{-2.69}$ Mearth at 2$σ$, corresponding to a bulk density of $2.62^{+1.37}_{-1.22}$ g cm$^{-3}$, positioning TOI-2120 b toward the water-rich region predicted by isocomposition models. Additional RV observations will be needed to further constrain its mass and composition.

items.title: Refining the Architecture of the Quadruple Pre-main-sequence System HD 98800: Improved Orbits, Dynamical Masses, and a Transiting Circumbinary Disk
items.abstract: We present new spectroscopic and interferometric observations of the pre-main-sequence hierarchical quadruple system HD 98800, a member of the nearby TW Hya association. Our radial velocity monitoring extends the total coverage to over 36 years, sampling the periastron passage in the $\sim$240-yr outer orbit. By combining these velocities with new and archival interferometric observations of both inner binaries (A and B), we significantly refine the system orbits and constrain the dynamical masses of all four stars to $\leq$ 2.6 percent. The resulting stellar properties (masses, effective temperatures, and absolute magnitudes) are found to agree well with current stellar evolution models. Notably, binary B hosts a known circumbinary disk in a polar orientation. Our interferometric imaging, as well as ground-based photometry by others, capture binary A currently passing directly behind the disk, a striking alignment given the outer orbit's long period. We use the photometry to infer the optical extinction produced by the disk material. The eclipse is expected to last about a decade, and offers an unprecedented opportunity to probe the structure and composition of the potentially planet-forming disk. Our refined orbits and component masses provide a robust dynamical framework to support ongoing and future studies of this unique event.

items.title: orbitize! v4: Joint Orbit Fitting with Gaia DR4 Astrometry and Flexible Analytic Linear Marginalization
items.abstract: orbitize! is a Python package for Bayesian orbit fitting of planetary and stellar companions (Blunt et al., 2020). It provides a unified framework for fitting relative astrometry, radial velocities, and absolute astrometry, supporting analyses of both resolved and unresolved systems. Available posterior sampling methods include parallel-tempered Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) through ptemcee (Foreman-Mackey et al., 2013; Vousden et al., 2016) and nested sampling through dynesty (Speagle, 2020), nautilus (Lange, 2023), and pymultinest (Buchner et al., 2014; Feroz et al., 2019). This paper accompanies the release of orbitize! version 4.0 and describes the functionality added since version 3.0 (Blunt et al., 2024), with a particular focus on joint orbit fitting with Gaia DR4 epoch astrometry and the implementation of the Orbits for the Extremely Impatient (OFTeI) algorithm (Blunt et al. 2026b, in preparation).

items.title: Turbulent Epidemics: Scale-dependent Fluctuations as a Probe of Population Heterogeneity
items.abstract: Heterogeneous dynamics, including phenomena such as superspreading and clustering, is a hallmark of many infectious diseases. A key challenge lies in identifying observables that constrain heterogeneous dynamics. We here adapt the technique of turbulence decomposition from fluid dynamics to extract scale-dependent fluctuation spectra and correlation functions from disaggregated epidemiological data as a probe of population heterogeneity. To investigate possible explanations for the observed heterogeneities during the COVID-19 winter wave in Germany in 2020/21, we calculate synthetic observables using the new network-based simulation code \textsc{Epimetheus} for an idealized structured population. The code can flexibly incorporate clustering, heterogeneous connectivity and susceptibility, superspreading as well as temporal modulations of transmission risk and factors like waning of immunity and vaccination. A qualitative comparison of simulated and observed fluctuation spectra and correlation functions as well as the secondary attack rate and the overdispersion indicates that both clustering and variations of susceptibility across population substructures of all scales are required to produce the observed dynamics. Combined with heterogeneous connectivity, it is likely that self-limiting effects would have limited the winter outbreak to $0.2\texttt{-}0.35$ of the population without further behavioral changes after the autumn of 2020. A uniform population-wide reduction of transmission risk alone does not adequately explain the observed heterogeneities. Further analysis of the relative contributions and interplay of interventions and self-limiting effects on COVID-19 disease dynamics is required. We outline avenues towards a better integration of heterogeneity in models for predicting infectious disease dynamics and diagnosing effects of interventions.

items.title: Self-gravitating dust clumps: linear theory sets the threshold, the onset time and the spacing of their formation, then slow coarsening erases this pattern
items.abstract: Planets form in disks of gas and dust. One step of their formation is the gathering of dust grains into dense clumps, under their own gravity. This work tries to predict when these clumps appear and how far apart they are. The grains attract each other through a gravity of finite range. The gas slows them down, and its turbulence spreads them out. The grains also cannot go beyond maximum packing: this is volume filling. The dimensionless model depends on two numbers. The first one is the gravitational number $χ$, which compares attraction with turbulent spreading. The second one is the mean volume fraction $ρ_b$, which measures the amount of grains. We solve the model with second-order finite volumes on an adaptive Cartesian mesh. We then treat each field as an image. An Otsu threshold and a watershed transform isolate the clumps. The code conserves mass to within $10^{-15}$ and converges at second order. Two designs of experiments give 192 simulations in total, with $2\leχ\le40$ and $0.05\leρ_b\le0.7$. Linear stability theory predicts the start of clump formation. The instability starts at time $t_{on}\simeq3.0/σ^*$, where $σ^*$ is the growth rate of the most amplified mode. The dominant wavelength equals the most amplified wavelength to within $10\%$. The area fraction of the clumps equals $ρ_b$. The clumps then go through slow coarsening. A sensitivity analysis attributes most of the variance to $χ$. The adaptive mesh reduces the computational cost only a little, because the clumps fill the whole domain.

items.title: Prediction of Acetaminophen-Induced Hepatotoxicity in Acetylcysteine-Treated Patients Using Routine Admission Biomarkers.
items.abstract: Study objective Some acetaminophen-overdose patients develop hepatotoxicity despite acetylcysteine treatment. Established tools struggle to prospectively identify subsequent toxicity. We developed a model using only routine admission biomarkers to identify acetylcysteine-treated patients at highest risk and compared it with the current benchmark, the acetaminophen-aminotransferase multiplication product (AT product). Methods Retrospective cohort study of acetaminophen overdose admissions aged 12 years and older (International Classification of Diseases 10th revision code of T39.1) with alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ≤1,000 U/L at admission from 3 UK hospitals (2008-2024). We fitted elastic-net logistic models stratified by presentation ALT. The outcome was peak ALT >1,000 U/L. Performance was assessed on a 25% held-out test set and benchmarked against the AT product >1,500. Results Of 4,705 admissions, 119 (2.5%) developed hepatotoxicity. The model used 7 routine blood tests, 4 per stratum. At presentation, those with ALT ≤50 U/L, acetaminophen, sodium, potassium, and lymphocyte count remained in the model. In those with ALT 51 to 1,000 U/L at presentation, ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lymphocyte count were used. In the test set (n=1,175), it achieved an area under the curve of 0.93 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.89 to 0.97) versus 0.82 (0.72 to 0.91) for the AT product (paired difference 0.11; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.22; P=.03), with higher specificity and a higher positive likelihood ratio at every matched sensitivity. The model had a specificity of 82.5%, whereas an AT product > 1,500 had a specificity of 62.6%. The model positive likelihood ratio was 5.1 versus 2.4 for the AT product, with half the number of false-positive escalations (171 versus 365 per 1,000 patients). Conclusion A stratified model using only routine admission biomarkers (the Edinburgh Risk Score) identifies acetylcysteine-treated patients at the highest residual hepatotoxicity risk, outperforming the AT product >1,500 across decision thresholds, supporting selection for intensified therapy.

items.title: Nightmare Engineering: Current State and Future Directions in Nightmare Treatment.
items.abstract: Approximately, 85% of nightmare sufferers do not seek treatment and 70% of healthcare professionals have a substantial lack of knowledge how to treat nightmares. To improve patients' care, we propose several strategies, which can increase the incidence of patients seeking help, treatment efficiency and accessibility. First, we encourage stronger communicating strategies for accessible and feasible nightmare therapies. Second, within our concept of nightmare engineering, we present novel and tech-driven treatment methods against nightmares that may improve both accessibility and efficiency of treatment. Digital and app-based therapies offer location-independent, flexible and low-threshold self-guided therapy, incorporating structured elements of classical imagery rehearsal therapy (IRT) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). With the current rise of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) open up the potential of human-like, individual-personalised and empathic-like conversations for nightmare treatment. Virtual reality (VR) technologies offer immersive realities for rescripting nightmares. Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) can reinforce and stabilise emotional rescripting elements by means of targeted sensory reactivation. Targeted lucidity reactivation (TLR) can be used to induce the state of lucid dreaming for promoting active control over nightmares by means of external stimuli via modern wearable technologies. Recent studies have shown preliminary efficacy of these potentially promising and future-oriented treatment methods, opening up new frontiers in nightmare engineering and nightmare treatment research. We critically discuss each treatment method in light of potential benefits, challenges and clinical relevance.

items.title: Microglial SIRT3 restrains maladaptive inflammatory-phagocytic activation and neuronal vulnerability in acute tau models.
items.abstract: Background Tau pathology is a defining feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related tauopathies. Microglia play important roles in tau uptake, clearance, and propagation, yet the mechanisms that govern their functional responses to tau-associated stress remain incompletely understood. Sirtuin-3 (SIRT3), an NAD + -dependent deacetylase predominantly localized to mitochondria, is a key regulator of mitochondrial integrity and metabolic homeostasis; however, its role in microglial responses to tau pathology remains unclear. Methods We employed complementary in vitro and in vivo models to investigate the role of microglial SIRT3 under tau-associated conditions. SIRT3-deficient HMC3 cells and human monocyte-derived microglia-like cells (MDMi) were assessed for mitochondrial integrity, inflammatory activation, tau uptake, and metabolic alterations using transcriptomic and functional metabolic analyses. In vivo, microglia-specific inducible SIRT3 knockout mice were examined in acute tau challenge models using fluorescently labeled and disease-associated tau preparations to assess neuroinflammatory responses, tau accumulation, mitochondrial damage, and neuronal vulnerability. In addition, AD-derived MDMi and postmortem cortical tissues were analyzed to examine microglial SIRT3 expression in relation to tau pathology. Results SIRT3 deficiency caused marked mitochondrial structural abnormalities and functional impairment in microglia, accompanied by increased ROS production, enhanced migration, inflammatory activation, and increased uptake of tau. Transcriptomic profiling and functional metabolic analyses further demonstrated a shift toward glycolysis-biased metabolism together with activation of stress- and microenvironment-responsive transcriptional programs. In vivo, microglia-specific SIRT3 deletion exacerbated neuroinflammatory responses, tau accumulation, mitochondrial damage, and neuronal vulnerability in acute tau challenge models using fluorescently labeled and disease-associated tau preparations. Notably, SIRT3 expression was increased in AD patient-derived MDMi and in microglia within postmortem cortical regions with high tau burden in AD patients. Consistent with a context-dependent response, tau exposure induced dynamic changes in microglial SIRT3 expression over time. Conclusions Microglial SIRT3 functions as a stress-responsive metabolic checkpoint linking mitochondrial homeostasis to inflammatory-phagocytic activation under acute tau-associated stress. SIRT3 deficiency promotes mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory activation, glycolysis-biased metabolic remodeling, and altered tau handling, which are associated with increased neuronal vulnerability. These findings identify SIRT3-dependent mitochondrial regulation as an important component of microglial response to tau-associated stress and provide a framework for further investigating how metabolic dysfunction contributes to microglial maladaptation in tau-related neurodegenerative diseases.

items.title: Discordance Between Guidelines and Practice in ICP Monitoring in Traumatic Brain Injury: Insights from the CENTER-TBI Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Background/objective Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring is important in selected patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI). This study aims to quantify variability in ICP monitoring practices across European trauma centres, to analyse associations with patient and imaging characteristics and to explore concordance between the practice of ICP monitoring and guideline recommendations. Methods In the Collaborative European Neurotrauma Effectiveness Research in Traumatic Brain Injury (CENTER-TBI) database, we assessed concordance between ICP monitoring and guideline recommendations, defined by a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ≤ 8 and a positive computed tomography (CT) scan (Marshall score > 1) on presentation. To determine between-centre differences, the case-mix-adjusted percentage of ICP placements and duration of monitoring per centre were determined in the mixed-effects logistic regression model. To determine patient and imaging characteristics associated with the insertion of an ICP monitor, a mixed-effects logistic regression model was performed. Results Among 2138 patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), 921 patients (43%) received an ICP device. Among 900 patients meeting guideline recommendations for ICP monitoring, 571 (64%) received an ICP monitor. There were large between-centre variations in ICP-monitor placements and the duration of ICP monitoring [median odds ratio (MOR) 2.5, 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.1-2.8 and MOR 3.2, 95% CI 2.4-3.8, respectively]. Factors associated with ICP monitoring were a lower GCS score on admission [odds ratio (OR) 0.9, 95% CI 0.8-0.9], at least one pupil that was unreactive to light (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.1-2.5) and the presence of CT abnormalities (i.e. contusion: OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.9-3.2). Conclusions This study provides a detailed patient-level description of ICP monitoring decision-making. ICP monitoring decisions frequently extended beyond guideline criteria and were influenced by neurological, radiological and treatment-related considerations. The observed variation may reflect both differences in practice and limitations of existing guideline frameworks. These findings provide a foundation for future efforts aimed at developing ICP monitoring recommendations that are more closely aligned with real-world expert decision-making.

items.title: Coma Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Therapy in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Revisiting the Curing Coma<sup>®</sup> Campaign COME TOGETHER Survey.
items.abstract: Background The Curing Coma Campaign (CCC) initiated a survey to assess global practices in coma management but lacked of sufficient data from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). A follow-up survey in India provided regional insights, which cannot be generalized to all LMICs. The aim of this study was to conduct a dedicated survey across various LMICs to understand local practices and challenges in the care of comatose patients. Methods This was a cross-sectional online survey of 163 healthcare professionals from 32 LMICs, categorized into six geographical regions following the World Bank classification. The survey, an adaptation of the original COME TOGETHER questionnaire, covered coma definition, etiology, diagnostic tools, management, and prognostication. Results The majority of respondents were from South Asia (41.1%). Most worked in urban areas (96%), in government teaching hospitals (64%). There was substantial agreement on three cardinal features of coma: a Glascow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤ 8, absence of wakefulness, and failure to respond purposefully to stimuli. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) was the most common etiology (45%). GCS was the most frequently used assessment tool (96%). Most respondents reported no formal policy for the withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies (63%), and ethicists were rarely involved in such discussions (70%). The majority (76%) of respondents reported no patient follow-up after intensive care unit (ICU) discharge. Conclusions This survey highlights significant variability and critical gaps in coma management across LMICs. The findings underscore the need for standardized protocols, targeted training for healthcare professionals, and international collaboration to improve patient outcomes in resource-limited settings.

items.title: Presynaptic functional organization by phase separation.
items.abstract: Neurons and their synaptic connections harbor numerous and diverse activities through functional organization, thereby enabling nervous system complexity. Within densely packed presynaptic terminals, there exists a mix of molecules, organelles and synaptic vesicles arranged as a set of distinct domains, each with a specific composition that enables discrete functional programs. For example, a subset of synaptic vesicles is made available at the active zone for immediate use, while the vast majority of vesicles are located away from this region and reserved. Likewise, synaptic vesicle recycling and proteolytic processes take place in domains away from the synaptic vesicle cluster. An emerging body of work has established that these functional domains are maintained and regulated by phase separation of molecules, that is, the formation of non-membrane-bound macromolecular condensates. Thus, characterizing the phase separation of molecules and organelles within the presynapse and its role in facilitating robust functional output, diversity and coordination within the presynaptic terminal is crucial for elucidating the vesicle trafficking mechanisms that underlie synaptic transmission.

items.title: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain.
items.abstract: Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience. Multilingual neural network models offer a way to answer this question by representing linguistic content across languages in a shared space. Leveraging these advances, we evaluated the similarity of linguistic representations in speakers of 21 languages. Here we combined existing (12 languages across 4 language families) and newly collected functional magnetic resonance imaging data (9 languages across 4 families) to test encoding models predicting brain activity in the language network using representations from multilingual models. Model representations predicted brain responses reliably within each language. Critically, encoding models trained on one set of languages generalized zero-shot to previously unseen languages, accurately predicting neural responses without exposure to the target language. This cross-lingual generalization extended across variation in language family, stimulus type and presentation modality. These findings point to a shared cross-lingual component for meaning across human languages.

items.title: Linguistic contextualization in the human hippocampus.
items.abstract: Word meanings in language are contextualized by surrounding words. Inspired by the self-attention mechanism in transformer-based large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that structural composition in the brain arises from combining canonical (non-contextual) word representations with those of nearby words. We analysed single unit activity in the human hippocampus, a region involved in semantic and contextual processing, while n = 10 participants listened to podcasts. We found that hippocampal neurons encoded word position within a clause, using both ordinal and frequency-domain positional encoding. Moreover, neural responses to specific words reflected both the lexical semantics of the word and a weighted sum of the embeddings of preceding words. The relative weighting of these contextualizing words correlated with LLM self-attention weights. These findings suggest that contextualization in the brain makes use of vectorial shifts that have a resemblance to attentional reweighting in LLMs, and highlight the role of the mesial temporal lobe within the broader language network.

items.title: Meningococcal ACWY quadrivalent conjugate vaccination responses in myasthenia gravis before complement inhibition.
items.abstract: Background Patients receiving complement inhibitor therapy are at increased risk of life-threatening meningococcal disease. Although quadrivalent meningococcal ACWY (MenACWY) vaccination is required before therapy initiation, the degree of seroprotection achieved in immunosuppressed patients and the importance of a second dose are uncertain. We evaluated serological protection after MenACWY vaccination in patients with myasthenia gravis (MG) undergoing complement inhibition. Methods In this prospective cohort study, consecutive adults with MG candidates for complement inhibitors received one MenACWY conjugate vaccine dose at least two weeks before treatment initiation; a second dose was recommended because of prior or ongoing immunosuppression. Serological protection against meningococcal serogroups A, C, W, and Y was assessed using serum bactericidal antibody assay with baby rabbit complement. Titers of 1:8 or greater were considered protective. Results Among 43 patients, median age at vaccination was 55 years (IQR, 45-66 years) and 27 (63%) were female. Complete protection was achieved in 15/38 patients (39.5%) after the first dose and 21/38 (55.3%) after the second dose. In 33 patients with paired data after two doses, complete protection increased from 12 (36.4%) to 19 patients (57.6%; p = 0.02). Prior rituximab exposure was associated with lower complete protection after the first dose (1/11 vs 14/27; p = 0.03) and second dose (2/11 vs 19/27; p = 0.005). Conclusions In patients with MG undergoing complement inhibition, one MenACWY vaccine dose provided complete protection in only 39.5% of patients. A second dose improved protection, supporting a two-dose vaccination schedule. Responses remained poor after rituximab exposure, favoring vaccination before B-cell-depleting therapy whenever possible.

items.title: Molecular PET imaging of cellular senescence: from current tracers to emerging biomarker-driven strategies.
items.abstract: Cellular senescence is a dynamic and multifaceted biological process that contributes to aging and a wide spectrum of age-related diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders. Despite increasing recognition of its pathological significance, the ability to quantify senescence noninvasively in vivo remains a major limitation, particularly for longitudinal studies and therapeutic evaluation. Positron emission tomography (PET) offers a powerful platform to address this gap by enabling quantitative imaging of molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances have led to the development of PET radiotracers targeting senescence-associated features, including lysosomal β-galactosidase activity, cell-surface markers (uPAR), and intracellular accumulation products (lipofuscin). These first-generation approaches have established proof-of-concept for imaging senescence biology; however, they primarily reflect downstream hallmarks and have been largely evaluated in non-central nervous system (CNS) models, while their ability to quantify senescent-cell burden in naturally aged tissues and the CNS remains insufficiently established. Emerging evidence motivates the study of biomarker-driven and pathway-oriented imaging strategies that may provide complementary information about senescence-associated molecular mechanisms without necessarily offering greater biological specificity. Advances in senescence biology, including curated gene sets and insights from senotherapeutic interventions, provide a framework for identifying imaging targets based on mechanistic relevance, disease association, and ligandability. Target classes spanning nuclear architecture, epigenetic regulation, metabolic reprogramming, and DNA damage signaling represent promising avenues for next-generation tracer development. This review provides a comprehensive overview of current PET tracers for cellular senescence, discusses challenges associated with CNS translation, and proposes a biomarker-driven framework for next-generation tracer development. We further introduce a comparative target-assessment framework and a stepwise validation roadmap addressing biological specificity, quantitative clinical qualification, and multimodal biomarker integration. Together, these considerations establish a framework for developing and interpreting PET biomarkers for mechanistic studies and evaluation of senescence-targeted interventions.

items.title: Pediatric research for the future of children: introduction to the conference proceedings.
items.abstract: The inaugural Pediatric Research Forum for the Future of Children (PRFC), held in Geneva, Switzerland, brought together leading investigators and emerging scientists from across the globe to discuss the future trajectory of pediatric research. Organized collaboratively by the Society for Pediatric Research (SPR) and the European Society for Paediatric Research (ESPR), the meeting was designed to foster international collaboration, highlight transformative research directions, and cultivate the next generation of pediatric clinician-scientists. A distinctive feature of the conference was its paired presentation format, in which established senior investigators presented alongside early-career researchers across five thematic domains: precision medicine and novel therapies, big data in pediatric research, early life determinants of health and disease, child mental health and development, and global pediatric research and workforce development. The meeting emphasized the importance of interdisciplinary science, equitable global partnerships, and translational pathways that accelerate the integration of discoveries into clinical practice. Key insights included the rapid expansion of genomic medicine in pediatrics, the potential and limitations of artificial intelligence and big data, the profound influence of early life exposures on lifelong health trajectories, the urgent need to address pediatric mental health, and the critical role of global collaboration and clinician-scientist training in advancing child health. The PRFC demonstrated that innovative meeting structures and cross-generational dialog can catalyze new research directions and strengthen the pediatric research ecosystem. IMPACT: This article highlights the presentations given at the Inaugural Pediatric Research for the Future of Children, held in Geneva in February, 2026.

items.title: A Differentially Methylated Region in the TNXB Gene is Associated with Relapse Activity in Multiple Sclerosis.
items.abstract: The mechanisms driving heterogeneity in disease activity in relapsing-remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) are incompletely understood. Changes in DNA methylation, at the intersection between genetic background and environment, are crucial for MS pathogenesis, but their role in disease activity is incompletely understood. We herein investigated DNA methylation signatures of relapse in peripheral immune cells of RRMS patients. We profiled the peripheral immune methylome of 236 untreated RRMS patients from two centres using Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChips. Differential methylation analysis compared patients who relapsed (as per McDonald criteria) in the year preceding sampling (n = 160), versus patients who did not (n = 76). Regression models and causal inference testing (CIT) were used to elucidate causality between DNA methylation, genetic variation, and disease activity. One differentially methylated region (DMR), comprising 5 CpG sites, was hypomethylated in relapsed patients, and mapped within an enhancer of TNXB in the HLA class III region. We found methylation levels in this region to be extensively modulated by proximal genetic variation, particularly by variants known to influence MS risk in a large-scale GWAS. Through CIT, we observed that for 2 Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) methylation levels in the TNXB DMR acted as mediator of the genetic impact on disease activity. Furthermore, we found a correlation between methylation levels within the DMR, SNPs and TNXB gene expression in the immune cells from MS patients. DNA methylation within TNXB influences gene expression and may mediate relapse activity in RRMS. These findings highlight HLA class III regulatory mechanisms as key contributors to relapse biology.

items.title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype-expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.
items.abstract: Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological-environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure-function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic-exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

items.title: Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception.
items.abstract: We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership? Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership. Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm. Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116-156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184-232 ms. These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

items.title: ALK<sup>R1275Q</sup> expands Schwann cell precursor-like cells during sympathoadrenal commitment, creating a permissive state for neuroblastoma initiation.
items.abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) arises from neural crest-derived cells of the sympathoadrenal lineage, yet how predisposing genetic lesions influence early human development remains poorly understood. Here, we use patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models carrying the familial ALK R1275Q mutation to investigate its role during sympathoadrenal differentiation. We show that ALK R1275Q delays lineage maturation and sustains a proliferative progenitor state characterized by elevated ALK signaling and expansion of a Schwann cell precursor (SCP)-like population. This SCP-like state persists during differentiation and is reduced by ALK inhibition or CRISPR-based mutation correction. Although ALK R1275Q alone is insufficient to drive tumor formation in vivo, it enhances susceptibility to oncogenic transformation in cooperation with MYCN. Together, these findings support a model in which ALK R1275Q reshapes developmental trajectories by maintaining a proliferative SCP-like progenitor state, thereby creating a permissive cellular context for NB initiation.

items.title: Familial VAMP2-Related Disorder With Generalized Epilepsy Caused by an Intronic Regulatory Variant With Evidence of Haploinsufficiency.
items.abstract: Pathogenic variants in VAMP2, encoding the synaptic vesicle SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2, cause a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy, and movement disorders. Reported variants are predominantly de novo missense changes affecting the SNARE motif; loss-of-function variants are associated with haploinsufficiency, causing milder phenotypes. We describe a proband and his mother carrying a heterozygous intronic VAMP2 variant (NM_014232.3:c.2+4A>G) identified by exome sequencing. We performed clinical and functional RNA analyses to investigate pathogenicity. The proband's phenotype included moderate intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and valproate-responsive childhood absence epilepsy. The affected mother had juvenile absence epilepsy, intellectual disability, and bipolar disorder. Quantitative RNA analysis demonstrated reduced VAMP2 expression in both affected individuals, supporting a loss-of-function mechanism consistent with haploinsufficiency. Our findings expand the genetic and inheritance spectrum of VAMP2-related disorders by demonstrating a familial syndrome caused by a regulatory intronic variant associated with reduced gene expression.

items.title: Disproportionate orphan drug costs limit equitable access to therapy.
items.abstract: Advances in drug development have transformed orphan disease care, yet high prices limit access, particularly in developing countries. Complement therapeutics illustrate this challenge. Regulatory reforms are needed and should include dynamic pricing that recognizes public research contributions, tailored incentives reflecting clinical benefits, and periodic reassessment as drug usage evolves, while prioritizing equitable patient access.

items.title: Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing during Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.
items.abstract: Language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation. Here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations. We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels. In contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components. These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties. Significance statement Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages. Using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level. These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.
