items.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
items.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

items.title: Introducing ReTiNA-Cinema: Real-Time Neuro-Augmented Cinema via Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is currently revolutionizing content creation across various media. Between those who fear it will replace human creativity and those who regard it solely as a tool, many in the creative industries are beginning to view generative AI as a collaborator. Yet interaction with these systems often relies on discrete, turn-based prompting that can interrupt flow and constrain expression to symbolic text. We explore physiological signals as a source of continuous adaptation without explicit commands, as a path toward embodied co-creation. This paper presents ReTiNA-Cinema, a methodological proof-of-concept that integrates electroencephalography (EEG) with generative AI to enable physiologically guided visual modulation of cinematic material. By linking physiological activity to the evolving appearance of a film, the system provides a basis for exploring embodied sense-making, in which viewers' bodily responses contribute to shaping the sensory experience through which they interpret the unfolding scenes. The system combines real-time EEG signal processing with a generative AI pipeline based on Stable Diffusion Turbo for frame-level image transformation. Single-user and two-user configurations map EEG-derived features to prompt selection and transformation strength. ReTiNA-Cinema offers a framework for exploring how the physiology of viewers might influence a film's visual presentation, extending the possibilities for participation in cinematic experiences and storytelling. This system raises questions about the effects on engagement, perceived agency, and emotional response, which remain open to future empirical study. items.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
items.abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

items.title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
items.abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $π_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

items.title: Rethinking Utility in Differentially Private Visualization: A Channel-Centric Perspective
items.abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.

items.title: Temporal Contrastive Alignment of EEG and Naturalistic Video Only Beats Linear Decoding On In-Sample Stimuli
items.abstract: Neural tracking, the temporal alignment between a continuous stimulus and the elicited brain response, enables decoding of attention from electroencephalography (EEG), yet its application to naturalistic video remains largely unexplored and mainly relies on linear canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We investigate whether a temporal contrastive model, pairing pretrained VideoMAE features with a lightweight EEG encoder trained on a correlation-based InfoNCE objective, can strengthen EEG-video alignment. Benchmarked against CCA under three generalization regimes, the model outperforms CCA across subjects (leave-one-subject-out), matches it within the stimulus manifold (leave-video-segment-out), and falls behind CCA when extrapolating to entirely novel videos (leave-one-video-out). Because this advantage appears only for seen stimuli, we probe its basis: a sham control shows that a high accuracy does not certify genuine alignment, as a synthesized correspondence fit to the seen stimuli can reproduce it without genuine temporal alignment in the training pairs. This does not preclude practical use: on a downstream attention-decoding task with seen stimuli, the model remains better than CCA since the decoding only requires a strong statistical coupling, regardless of whether that coupling is physiologically meaningful. Using a group-averaged EEG reference, we further show that genuine, generalizable coupling is nonetheless learned, only buried in the noise of single-subject EEG. These results indicate that progress hinges on data scale, diversity, and single-subject denoising.

items.title: Regime-dependent reconstruction of structural connectivity: an in silico study of spatially constrained modular neuronal networks
items.abstract: Inferring structural connectivity from neuronal activity is a major challenge in neuroscience, yet the conditions under which inferred interactions faithfully reflect anatomical connections remain unclear. Here, we investigate in silico how spatial constraints in a neuronal network and its dynamical regime jointly shape structural recoverability. We construct modular networks with varying average axonal lengths and simulate spontaneous activity using the Izhikevich model with synaptic depression across a broad range of excitatory strengths and background noise levels. Using Generalized Transfer Entropy, we infer effective connectivity and compare it with the underlying structural ground-truth at the levels of individual connections and global topology. We observe that the richness in the repertoire of activity patterns is highest in an intermediate regime between globally synchronized and noise-dominated activity, reflecting a balance between global excitation and stochasticity. Optimal structural reconstruction generally occurs under these same conditions, although this correspondence depends on network architecture and is weaker in highly modular networks. Together, these results show that structural recoverability depends jointly on network organization and dynamical regime. More broadly, our findings highlight the risks of treating inferred effective connectivity as a direct surrogate for structural connectivity.

items.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
items.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.

items.title: Demographic inference in exoplanet chemistry is shaped by retrieval assumptions
items.abstract: Understanding the chemical diversity of exoplanet atmospheres is crucial for linking atmospheric composition to planetary formation history. Atmospheric C/O can provide clues about where and how planets form, particularly through the accretion of gas and solids across disk snowlines. Since planetary migration can change orbital distances and hence equilibrium temperatures ($T_{eq}$), investigating C/O across different planetary populations may provide insights into their formation and evolution. As observational precision improves with the JWST, the limits of standard atmospheric retrieval methods that assume altitude-independent molecular abundances have become apparent. We present atmospheric retrievals for 20 transiting planets with published JWST transmission spectra, including complementary HST spectra for targets where such data are available, spanning gas giants, warm Neptunes, and temperate/warm sub-Neptunes, to test how population-level chemical inferences depend on retrieval assumptions. Free-chemistry retrievals show a visually non-monotonic C/O-$T_{eq}$ distribution, but this apparent pattern is not statistically robust and is sensitive to sample composition. When molecular abundances are constrained by a grid of disequilibrium models, the inferred C/O distribution becomes more restricted, showing that demographic chemical trends can depend strongly on the adopted retrieval parameterization. Several hot Jupiters converge to low C/O ($\leq$ 0.05), whereas colder, cloudy planets retain broad posteriors that reflect limited information content of their spectra. Our results suggest that population-level chemical trends inferred from free-chemistry retrievals should be interpreted with caution unless sample selection, residual structure, prior sensitivity, and chemical assumptions are explicitly tested.

items.title: Lower-Mass Giants Can Spare Inner Planets during High-Eccentricity Migration
items.abstract: The survival of an inner planet next to a close-in giant is commonly used to argue against high-eccentricity migration (HEM), because the eccentric giant is expected to destabilize the inner system. Existing survival calculations have concentrated on Jupiter-mass migrants, although several Jupiter-sized close-in giants with nearby companions have sub-Jovian masses. We use dissipative three-body integrations to measure the collision-survival boundary at seven giant masses from $0.25$ to $1.0,M_{\rm Jup}$ and combine it with uncompressed equilibrium-tide circularization times. At fixed physical periapse, lower giant mass weakens the forcing of the inner orbit and shifts the survival boundary inward. It also shortens the circularization time for a common radius and tidal prescription. These dynamical and tidal limits enclose a viable HEM region in which a sub-Jovian giant can circularize within a system age while retaining an ultra-short-period companion. We screen known companion-hosting close-in giants and perform system-specific integrations of WASP-132; every current candidate lies outside the region. A future system inside it would show directly that HEM can produce a close-in giant while preserving an inner planet, converting companion survival into positive evidence for this formation channel.

items.title: How Should Candidates Be Weighted under Open-List Proportional Representation? Harmonic Weights and Dirichlet Order Statistics
items.abstract: Candidates in open-list proportional representation systems are not equally prominent, and measurements that involve aggregation over candidates therefore require some form of weighting. We address the question of how those weights should be chosen. Since weights based on realized preference votes are unavailable in advance and endogenous to the electoral outcome, we seek a priori weights that depend on list position alone, and derive them as expected ordered vote shares under a probabilistic model of the division of the list vote among candidates. The natural starting point -- the uniform distribution on the simplex -- is unrealistic, as it prescribes the same degree of concentration of the vote for every list, and under it the leading candidates become more alike as lists lengthen. The other members of the symmetric Dirichlet family require a concentration parameter, which is unknown and which there is no reason to expect to be constant across countries, parties, and elections. Accordingly, we treat that parameter as random. We prove that under a scale-invariant prior restricted to lists with at least two effective candidates, the expected share of the $k$-th candidate decays as $1/k$, and we show that over the leading positions of a long list, up to one hundred of them, the resulting weights are within 1.4 to 3.4 percent, in total variation, of the harmonic weights $(k H_n)^{-1}$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number. No fixed value of the parameter yields similar weights. Moreover, under the uniform distribution itself, harmonic weights are exactly the normalized expected margins between consecutive candidates.

items.title: The Ionospheric Cut-off as a Potential Radio Technosignature
items.abstract: Radio emission generated on a planetary surface must cross the planet's ionosphere before escaping into space: below the local plasma frequency it is reflected back towards the surface. We investigate this process for broadband radio technosignatures (BRaTs) using a Chapman-layer description of photoionised atmospheres. The plasma frequency depends only weakly on stellar XUV irradiation, scaling as $Q_{\infty}^{1/4}$, implying turnover frequencies of 5-40 MHz for most terrestrial habitable-zone planets, potentially rising towards 100 MHz in extreme environments. The basic signature is simple: the continuum of a surface-origin BRaT should be strongly suppressed below a characteristic frequency that can be estimated from the XUV output of the host star, at every orbital phase and for any viewing geometry. Oblique propagation, magnetic fields, and collisional absorption broaden the cut-off into a smooth escape function, $f_{\mathrm{esc}}(ν,φ)$, where $φ$ is the orbital phase. Because the day-night ionisation pattern is anchored to the substellar point rather than to the rotating surface, disc integration adds a second, more discriminating signature: the half-escape frequency $ν_{1/2}$ varies predictably (by about 40-50 per cent over the orbit, depending on the angular emission pattern of the leakage) and remains locked to the orbital ephemeris. Finite atmospheric response times introduce modest phase lags but preserve the modulation. A low-frequency turnover alone is not unique to technology, but one that varies periodically with the orbital period would be difficult to reproduce through known astrophysical processes. Although observationally challenging, the ionospheric cut-off is a potential technosignature diagnostic and a novel probe of exoplanet ionospheres.

items.title: Particle physics science communication with grass-roots Instagram: a success story
items.abstract: Communicating science to the public is an integral part of the work of a research collaboration, not an afterthought. Institutional and collaboration-level social media accounts are often run by professional communicators rather than by practising scientists, and single-scientist ``influencer'' accounts are demanding to sustain. We describe {\em CMSatDESY}, a crowd-sourced Instagram account on which the CMS group at DESY tells its own stories, each member in their own voice. In the first half of 2026, the science communication activities through this reached 140k+ unique accounts and received 250k+ views, with an engagement rate of 7\%. We discuss experiences and best practices that can be used by other groups, and describe how the account doubles as a science communication playground for outreach training for a large particle physics group.

items.title: The Atmospheric Circulation of Cloudy Hot and Ultra-hot Jupiters: the Need for Dissipation of Large-scale Flows to Reduce the Nightside Brightness Temperatures of Ultra-hot Jupiters
items.abstract: We perform general circulation modeling of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters across equilibrium temperatures of T_eq=1600 to 2800 K, incorporating cloud formation and its feedback on atmospheric dynamics. This study specifically examines whether clouds explain the systematically low nightside brightness observed in Spitzer thermal phase curves of ultra-hot Jupiters. We found that clouds generally increase phase-curve amplitudes and reduce eastward offsets, and these effects are most pronounced at relatively low T_eq and gradually weaken as T_eq increases. We discussed two mechanisms responsible for reducing the phase-curve offsets by clouds: the dynamical and geometric effects. Without explicit dissipation of large-scale winds, strong equatorial jets develop, maintaining a hot equatorial region and clearing clouds near the nightside equator at T_eq >= 2200 K, with thick clouds instead forming mainly at mid-to-high latitudes. These patchy nightside clouds do not sustain low nightside fluxes as temperatures rise, suggesting that clouds alone cannot explain the observed nightside brightness for ultra-hot Jupiters. Strong dissipation, parameterized as magnetic drags, suppresses equatorial jets and promotes nightside cloud coverage. In both clear and cloudy models, drag weakens the dependence of Spitzer nightside brightness temperature on equilibrium temperature; clouds further lower the nightside brightness temperature with the same drag prescription. Clouds also dampen amplitudes of thermal spectra on the nightside and, under small-particle conditions, can even produce emission features. Due to limited dayside cloud cover, our models yield negligible Bond albedos. Finally, interpreting simulated thermal phase curves with energy balance models in near-IR and IR bands tends to overestimate the Bond albedos of ultra-hot Jupiters by an order of magnitude or more.

items.title: Dependence of Dust Growth on Magnetic field Strength in Protoplanetary Disks
items.abstract: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field. The dust size distribution is evolved taking into ac- count coagulation and fragmentation. For the magnetic field evolution, we considered both ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation. The MRI-driven turbulent viscosity was estimated self-consistently from the local magnetic field strength and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics diffusivities. We found that MRI-driven turbulence becomes stronger for smaller initial plasma beta, and the enhanced tur- bulence promotes dust growth in MRI-active regions. However, dust growth is ultimately limited by radial drift, and the dependence of dust size on the magnetic field strength is significant only in the outer regions of the disk. In other words, over most of the disk, radial drift remains the dominant factor controlling the maximum dust size, and the magnetic field strength plays only a minor role in determining the overall dust size distribution.

items.title: AI-Native Industrial Control Systems: An Agent Architecture for the Control System Lifecycle
items.abstract: Industrial control systems increasingly use AI for perception, control, and engineering, while available control functions and execution environments are typically established in advance. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control system in which collaborating agents determine the capabilities required by a task, construct the control application, and prepare its execution environment. System-level agents coordinate device-level agents within configured resource and permission constraints. A physical sorting workstation illustrates two forms of adaptation. In the first case, controller and robot agents construct a sorting application on a prescribed Raspberry Pi target. In the second, a camera agent adds inspection on an edge node, and the controller associates inspection results with downstream pickup decisions. A subsequent revision enables selective sorting using the same agents and deployment arrangement. The trials demonstrate the feasibility of task-driven construction and evolution on the workstation. Commissioning also reveals limitations in the traceability of design decisions, adherence to delegated responsibilities, diagnostic reasoning, and verification of physical behavior.

items.title: Linear and nonlinear characteristics of high-frequency electrostatic drift waves in absence of collisions
items.abstract: High-frequency electrostatic drift wave modes are shown as hybrid modes generated by the linear mixing of drift and cyclotron dynamics growing at the expense of cyclotron modes via a reactive mode-coupling instability. The fundamental role of the density gradient is to break the symmetry between the two cyclotron branches. A sufficiently steep gradient causes the drift-modified branch to overlap with the cyclotron branch leading to energy distribution. The analysis is carried out within a cold-ion fluid model without invoking collisional, non-adiabatic or finite Larmor radius effects. Laboratory observations of localized high-frequency drift wave signatures provide qualitative and parametric support for the density gradient threshold and high frequency scaling identified by this hybrid mode-coupling model. A second order nonlinear equation with variable coefficients has been derived to show the wave characteristics in various parameter ranges.

items.title: Correcting for the effects of the point spread function in intra-halo light measurements and application to deep Hyper Suprime-Cam data
items.abstract: The intra-halo light (IHL) is the diffuse stellar component that surrounds galaxies, groups, and clusters. Its formation is linked to the hierarchical assembly of the system, making it a key tracer of galaxy evolution. However, the low surface brightness of the IHL makes it challenging to detect and distinguish from the point spread function (PSF) effect of the telescope. In this paper, we present an innovative technique that corrects for PSF-scattering effects in astronomical images. We use this method to provide a statistically robust estimation of the IHL in galaxy groups and clusters by fitting an exponential model to this component using an MCMC optimiser algorithm. To test our methodology, we build 5440 mock observations of Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) groups using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program Public Data Release 3 (HSC-SSP PDR3). Each mock contains an IHL component with a flux fraction (fIHL) ranging from 0.01 to 0.5. Our results demonstrate the importance of properly removing the PSF-scattered light, especially at lower fIHL. The IHL effective radius is overestimated by ∼9.1 and ∼2 at fIHL = 0.01 and 0.5, respectively, while the IHL flux requires correction for fIHL < 0.4, with an overestimate of ∼84.4 at fIHL = 0.01. After applying our PSF correction, the recovered flux and effective radius are much closer to their true values. Finally, we apply our methodology to HSC-PDR3 UD real observations of the GAMA group G400138 in the g,r and i-bands, finding median IHL fractions of: fg, IHL ∼ 0.19$^{+0.09}_{-0.01}$, fr, IHL ∼ 0.08$^{+0.06}_{-0.02}$, and fi, IHL ∼ 0.06$^{+0.04}_{-0.02}$.

items.title: Probing dark matter interactions with stellar motion near Sagittarius A*
items.abstract: Stars orbiting Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) at the Milky Way’s center provide a unique laboratory to test gravity and dark matter (DM). We demonstrate that DM interactions in stellar interiors induce a novel momentum transfer force, altering orbits beyond gravitational effects. We derive the first astrophysical constraints on DM-nucleon scattering using S2’s 2000–2019 orbital data probing sub-GeV parameter space for specified DM distributions near Sgr A*. We further show that complementary orbital survival constraints and future observations of highly eccentric S stars extend the reach to DM profiles allowed by present gravitational measurements. Unlike bounds requiring DM capture and annihilation, our constraints apply broadly to scattering DM including asymmetric DM and extend to masses where methods based on capture can lose sensitivity. Stellar lifetime constraints over megayear timescales complement these, surpassing some direct detection and cosmological limits. This work establishes stellar dynamics as a novel probe of DM interactions.

items.title: Tightest constraints on tidal Love numbers of black holes from GW250114
items.abstract: Tidal Love numbers of black holes, zero in classical general relativity for Kerr black holes in vacuum, become non-vanishing in the presence of exotic matter or in alternative theories of gravity, making them a powerful probe of fundamental physics. The gravitational-wave event GW250114, observed with an unprecedented signal-to-noise ratio, provides a unique opportunity to test this prediction. By analyzing this event, we conclude that the data is consistent with the binary black hole hypothesis, and we place a 90\% upper limit on the effective tidal deformability of $\tildeΛ < 34.8$. These bounds imply that any environment surrounding the black holes must contribute less than $\sim 7\times 10^{-3}$ of their mass, and they rule out some models of boson stars. Our findings provide the strongest observational constraints yet on black hole tidal deformability and show that the data remain fully consistent with the Kerr black hole prediction of vanishing tidal Love numbers.

items.title: Gravitational self-interaction mitigates superluminal signalling
items.abstract: The Schrödinger-Newton equation aims at describing the dynamics of massive quantum systems subject to the gravitational self-interaction. As a deterministic nonlinear quantum wave equation, it is generally believed to conflict with the relativistic no-signalling principle. Here we undermine this viewpoint and show that it is of key importance to study the quantitative and operational character of the superluminal effects. To this end we employ a rigorous formalism of probability measures on spacetime and quantify the probability of a successful superluminal bit transfer via a (1+1)-dimensional analogue of the single-particle Schrödinger-Newton equation. We demonstrate that such a quantity decreases with the increasing size and mass of the system. Furthermore, we prove that the Einstein-Dirac system, which yields the Schrödinger-Newton equation in the non-relativistic limit, is perfectly compatible with the relativistic causal structure. Our study demonstrates that the Schrödinger-Newton equation, which is by construction non-relativistic, is in fact 'more compatible' with the no-signalling principle than the ordinary free Schrödinger equation.

items.title: High-precision mass measurements in the vicinity of 100 Sn: Signatures of enhanced N = 50 shell effects and constraints on x-ray burst nucleosynthesis
items.abstract: Using the ZeroDegree multi-reflection time-of-flight mass spectrograph of the CRISMASS project at RIKEN Radioactive Isotope Beam Factory, we performed high-precision mass measurements of proton-rich nuclei near the doubly magic nucleus 100Sn, achieving uncertainties on the order of 10 keV. The masses of 91Rh, 92Pd, and 96Cd were determined for the first time with high precision, and the accuracy of several additional masses was substantially improved. Incorporating the new data into X-ray burst simulations significantly reduces the abundance uncertainties in the $A$ = 90-100 region, shifting the reaction flow toward $A$ = 90 production and suppressing the synthesis of heavier nuclei. Further investigation of the $νp$-process indicates that 99Rh plays a significant role in the reaction flow within the mass region studied. These high-precision mass measurements refine the mass surface near 100Sn and provide critical constraints on models of proton-rich nucleosynthesis.

items.title: High-frequency thermal noise in Michelson interferometers
items.abstract: Thermal noise in optics constrains the precision of optical experiments, including Michelson interferometers, optical clocks, and optomechanical sensors. While high-power optical experiments such as gravitational-wave detectors are currently limited mainly by quantum noise, new experiments incorporating recent insights from quantum metrology are being developed that evade the quantum shot noise background. In particular, Michelson interferometers that use photon-counting readout will look for weak, high-frequency signals. Since shot noise is no longer the dominant noise source with these readout schemes, it is important to accurately model thermal noise to characterize signals and design more sensitive experiments. However, previous modeling uses approximations that are no longer valid in these frequency regimes. In the MHz band, the quasistatic approximation does not apply. We therefore develop more general models of substrate and coating mechanical (Brownian) noise, substrate and coating thermoelastic noise, and coating thermorefractive noise. We validate the models with comparisons to previous low-frequency modeling and high-frequency spectra from an experiment that has already taken data, the Holometer. We then apply the new models to GQuEST, an experiment under construction.

items.title: The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes
items.abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window (10 17 –10 23 g) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars. We develop the first global framework for the evolution of stars that capture PBHs, combining analytic calculations, stellar evolution models, 3D general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations, and Monte Carlo population synthesis. We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly. Capture is dominated by three-body interactions with planetary or stellar companions. For a solar-type host with a Jupiter analog, inspiral within a main-sequence lifetime requires M BH crit ≳ 1 0 22 g , while lighter PBHs generally require tighter companions. Once deposited at the center, the PBH grows through inefficient quasi-spherical Bondi accretion; if it reaches the angular-momentum threshold before consuming the host, the inflow circularizes into a disk. Our Monte Carlo calculations yield sizable quiet-consumption and explosive-disruption populations, with final PBH masses M BH ∼ 0.01–1 M ⊙ and disk-forming PBH spins a * ≈ 0.8. Disk formation is the point of no return: disk winds and relativistic jets of ∼10 45 –10 50 erg s −1 disrupt the star within minutes. The resulting transients may include a ∼day-long UV/blue signal, radio afterglow, and, if the jet escapes, an X-ray-flash (XRF)/low-luminosity gamma-ray-burst (llGRB) signal. For an O ( 1 ) PBH dark matter fraction and optimistic capture assumptions, the event rate can reach that of llGRBs. The low-mass, high-spin remnants offer a complementary PBH probe and possible source for subsolar black hole mergers.

items.title: Majorana fermions at self-generated interfaces
items.abstract: The Kitaev model describing a one-dimensional topological superconducting chain is known to support two Majorana fermions localized at the endpoints of the system when the parameters are tuned to the topological phase. In this work, we investigate the possibility that Majorana fermions may also emerge away from the physical boundaries of the chain. To this end, we generalize the Kitaev model by incorporating a local coupling between the electronic density and a classical elastic (lattice) field. This electron-lattice interaction can drive phase separation between superconducting regions characterized by distinct topological invariants, thereby generating internal interfaces that host Majorana bound states. Under these conditions, a dilute gas of Majorana fermions can emerge spontaneously in the bulk of the system, without the need for externally imposed interfaces.

items.title: Investigating black hole accretion and feedback self-regulation in Seyfert galaxies using the FIRE-3 cosmological hydrodynamic simulations
items.abstract: Observations of local Seyfert galaxies show an intriguing connection between AGN luminosity and a deficit of molecular gas on ∼50 pc scales compared to 200 pc, the plausible imprint of AGN feedback. Motivated by these findings, we investigate the interplay between supermassive black hole (BH) accretion, AGN feedback, and nuclear gas reservoirs using cosmological hydrodynamic simulations implementing FIRE-3 multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM) physics and multi-component BH accretion and feedback models. Focusing on the late-time evolution of four Milky Way-mass galaxies, we find recurrent cycles of increased gas inflow toward the accretion disc, enhanced BH accretion, feedback self-regulation, and suppressed gas inflow rate until the next fuelling event. AGN winds interact with the ISM and escape preferentially through low-density polar channels after opening central cavities on ∼10–500 pc scales, regulating BH growth and producing episodic behaviour on ∼10–100 Myr timescales. The simulations reproduce the observed diversity of nuclear morphologies, gas concentrations, and AGN luminosities in late-type Seyfert galaxies, but do not exhibit a clear anti-correlation between gas concentration and AGN luminosity. Higher-luminosity AGN (LX ∼ 1041.5 − 43 erg s−1) powered by the accretion disc reservoir can coexist with feedback-driven cavities, consistent with observations, but they are more common in simulated galaxies with centrally-peaked gas distributions. Although differences in sample selection, tracer choice, spatial resolution, and stochasticity in AGN fuelling may impact underlying concentration-luminosity trends, the apparent tension between simulations and observations points to the timing between gas inflow, accretion-disc depletion, and feedback-driven clearing on ∼50–200 pc scales as a key constraint on AGN self-regulation models.

items.title: Improving the Precision of Line-by-line Radial Velocities: A Data-driven Iterative Algorithm for Spectral Line Selection
items.abstract: Independent analysis of individual spectral lines, or line-by-line (LBL) analyses, can improve upon standard cross-correlation function (CCF) methods for measuring radial velocities (RVs) because they preserve critical information about individual line-shape changes that can be caused by stellar activity. In this work, we measure LBL RVs of 3830 spectral lines across 383 days of NEID solar observations. Our LBL approach achieves an RV rms of 2.012 m s −1 using all lines. Then, we describe several benchmark methods to select smaller line lists based on line properties such as depth and intrinsic RV scatter. Our primary finding is that a smaller line list can result in higher-quality and more stable RVs than standard RV extraction approaches. Motivated by these results, we present Filtering Lines for Accurate Radial-velocity Exoplanet Search (FLARES), an iterative line-selection algorithm. FLARES selects candidate spectral lines with extreme values of multiple line metrics and properties such as depth, signal-to-noise ratio, and detector position, and preferentially rejects lines whose removal produces the largest decrease in the weighted RV scatter. We find that FLARES-selected line lists can substantially reduce the RV rms with substantially fewer lines, outperforming the full line list and benchmark line-selection methods. Cross-validation tests demonstrate that FLARES is robust, yielding an RV rms of ≈1.3 m s −1 using just ≈25−100 lines. Comparisons to alternative line lists with properties similar to the best FLARES-selected lines demonstrate that FLARES successfully identifies line properties that lead to effective line lists for future extreme-precision radial velocity measurements.

items.title: Neutron stars with an agnostic dark sector: Core and halo configurations from a two-fluid approach
items.abstract: The study of dark matter admixed neutron stars has the potential to advance our understanding of dark matter particle candidates. However, the large parameter space of dark matter particle masses restricts a systematic, model-independent study. In this analysis, we employ agnostic hadronic and dark-matter equations of state to construct dark-matter-admixed neutron stars within a two-fluid formalism. Dark matter is characterized solely by its low-density equation of state and mass and is modeled as a Fermi gas, while hadronic matter is anchored at low and high densities by chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations. A speed-of-sound parametrization describes the intermediate- and high-density regimes of both hadronic and dark matter, enabling an agnostic treatment of the dark matter equation of state that is constrained only by thermodynamic consistency and does not favor softer or stiffer behavior. Within this agnostic framework, we find that dark matter does not generically compactify the star: light dark matter forms extended halos that raise the tidal deformability, while heavy dark matter forms compact cores that lower it. Consequently, the dominant observational constraint shifts from gravitational-wave tidal deformability for light, halo-dominated models to NICER mass-radius data for heavy, core-dominated models. Using current data at 1 σ , we constrain the dark matter fraction to f D M ≲ 0.11 for light dark matter. By treating the medium- and high-density dark matter equation of state agnostically within a fermionic framework, our approach yields conservative and broadly applicable bounds on the dark matter content of neutron stars. Neutron stars with similar masses but very different tidal deformabilities could be a smoking-gun signature of dark matter in Neutron stars.

items.title: Charting the expansion of the Universe from z∼0 to z∼14 with HII galaxies
items.abstract: We present an updated Hubble diagram of giant extragalactic H ii regions and H ii galaxies spanning the redshift interval z ∼ 0 to z ∼ 14, extending the use of the L(Hβ) − σ relation as an independent cosmological probe into the epoch of cosmic dawn. Our sample comprises 243 objects, including local anchor systems with primary distance measurements, previously published low- and intermediate-redshift H ii galaxies, recent JWST/NIRSpec observations, and a new subsample of extremely high-redshift H ii galaxies observed with JWST and, for the highest-redshift cases, with ALMA+JWST. We homogenise the measurements across the full sample, applying consistent corrections for instrumental and thermal broadening, extinction, and, where required, the transformation from [O III]-based to Balmer-line velocity dispersions. We model lensing effects of high redshift using a log-normal magnification formalism and infer cosmological parameters via a nested-sampling analysis, considering both spatially flat and non-flat versions of the ΛCDM, wCDM, and CPL models. The L − σ relation remains consistent over the full redshift range, showing no evidence for significant evolution even at the highest redshifts currently accessible. For the joint anchor+H ii galaxies sample, considering the spatially flat models, we obtain h = 0.725 ± 0.040 and $\Omega _m=0.308^{+0.043}_{-0.053}$ for ΛCDM. Allowing a constant dark-energy equation of state yields $w_0=-0.96^{+0.53}_{-0.21}$, while a CPL parametrisation gives $w_0=-0.92^{+0.57}_{-0.34}$ and $w_a=-0.48^{+0.60}_{-1.50}$, all consistent, within the uncertainties, with concordance cosmology. These results demonstrate that H ii galaxies offer a viable, fully independent tracer of the expansion history across almost the entire age of the Universe, opening a new avenue for testing ΛCDM and dark-energy evolution well beyond reionisation.

items.title: Primordial black holes and gravitational waves as multimessenger signals of first-order phase transitions
items.abstract: The collapse of false-vacuum domains during first-order phase transitions in the early Universe may lead to primordial black hole (PBH) formation whose signatures form a multimessenger complement to gravitational wave (GW) production. We focus on PBH formation through the gravitational collapse of false-vacuum domains, described using a junction condition formalism. This formalism develops the Schwarzschild collapse criterion dynamically, avoiding the usage of critical overdensity thresholds in a post-inflationary Universe, and is driven solely by the vacuum energy enclosed within shrinking false-vacuum domains without the assistance of particle or domain wall interactions in the false vacuum. We study the parameter space of phase transitions and identify regions producing observable GWs, observable PBHs, or both simultaneously. We investigate this phenomenology in polynomial and classically conformal scalar field potentials as model benchmarks. We find that the scalar fields with vacuum expectation values in the range of 1-100 MeV have the largest model parameter space available for these multi-messenger signals, which are testable with upcoming GW observatories, searches for Hawking radiation, and gravitational lensing surveys.

items.title: Monopoles, strings, walls, and gravitational waves
items.abstract: The gauge symmetry breaking S U ( 2 ) → U ( 1 ) → Z 2 → 1 successively produces monopoles, strings and domain walls bounded by strings (WBS), with the elementary monopole carrying a U ( 1 ) magnetic flux twice as large as the elementary string. The elementary strings and subsequently WBS emit gravitational waves, and during their decay, the WBS yield a network of composite strings that carry the same U ( 1 ) flux as the monopoles. Depending on the cosmological evolution, we provide the gravitational wave spectra generated by the elementary strings and WBS, in combination with the composite strings which are either effectively stable, quasistable, or metastable. These three scenarios are also realized in the symmetry breaking chain S U ( 3 ) → S O ( 3 ) → Z 2 → 1 . Both S U ( 2 ) and S U ( 3 ) have appeared in the literature as flavor gauge symmetries.

items.title: A Calibration Database Design for the Wide-field X-ray Telescope on Board the Einstein Probe
items.abstract: The wide-field X-ray telescope (WXT) is the primary payload of the Einstein Probe mission. Utilizing innovative lobster-eye micro-pore optics, it achieves an unprecedented combination of a large instantaneous field-of-view and high detection sensitivity. Precise scientific data analysis relies fundamentally on a standardized and robust calibration database (CALDB). In this paper, we present the design and implementation of the WXT CALDB. The database is designed to manage calibration data for 12 independent WXT modules and 48 complementary metal-oxide semiconductor sensors, incorporating both extensive on-ground calibration results and dynamic in-orbit updates. We detail the directory hierarchy, naming conventions, functionality, and the specific formats of key calibration products. The WXT CALDB is seamlessly integrated into the WXT data analysis pipeline, ensuring high data integrity and maximizing the scientific return of the mission.

items.title: Entropic Chaplygin-gas cosmology and late-universe tension diagnostics
items.abstract: We investigate an entropic generalized Chaplygin-gas (gCg) cosmology in which a single dark fluid accounts for both dark matter and dark energy. We constrain the model using DESI baryon acoustic oscillations, redshift-space-distortion measurements, compressed Planck 2018 distance and lensing information, and Type Ia supernova likelihoods with PantheonPlus+SH0ES (PPS) and DES–Dovekie. For Planck+DESI+RS D+PPS, the entropic gCg model yields $$H_{0}=68.64\pm 0.52,\mathrm{km,s^{-1},Mpc^{-1}}$$ H 0 = 68.64 ± 0.52 , km , s - 1 , Mpc - 1 and $$S_{8}=0.797\pm 0.021$$ S 8 = 0.797 ± 0.021 , compared with $$H_{0}=67.31\pm 0.28,\mathrm{km,s^{-1},Mpc^{-1}}$$ H 0 = 67.31 ± 0.28 , km , s - 1 , Mpc - 1 and $$S_{8}=0.809\pm 0.021$$ S 8 = 0.809 ± 0.021 in $$\Lambda $$ Λ CDM. The simultaneous upward shift in $$H_{0}$$ H 0 and downward shift in $$S_{8}$$ S 8 occurs in the directions required for a partial alleviation of both tensions. We also show that when PPS is replaced by DES–Dovekie, the parameter shifts are smaller, the best-fit improvement is negligible, and the Bayesian evidence favours $$\Lambda $$ Λ CDM. Thus, the entropic gCg model provides a potentially interesting simultaneous shift of $$H_{0}$$ H 0 and $$S_{8}$$ S 8 , but its statistical support depends on the adopted supernova likelihood.

items.title: An engineered nanobody inhibitor for molecular-to-circuit control of opioid receptors.
items.abstract: Opioid receptors (ORs) orchestrate pain relief, reward and dependence, yet their signaling across diverse cell types and subcellular compartments cannot be resolved by current pharmacological or genetic approaches. Single-domain antibodies, or nanobodies (Nbs), can probe receptor states, but their potential for controlling native receptor signaling at the systems level remains unexplored. Here we engineer high-affinity intracellular Nbs that bind active ORs through structure-guided evolution. Iterative functional optimization yields Nb64, an active-state-selective inhibitor that rapidly suppresses transducer engagement, receptor internalization and downstream signaling, including native μOR-driven G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium currents in ventral tegmental area neurons. Organelle targeting enables precise subcellular control of OR signaling, while bioreversible cell-penetrating peptide conjugation enables nongenetic cytosolic delivery. Cell-type-specific Nb64 expression in ventral tegmental area GABAergic neurons attenuates fentanyl-evoked dopamine release and behavioral responses in mice. Nb64 provides a versatile strategy for dissecting OR biology and establishes a generalizable framework for precision inhibition of native G protein-coupled-receptor signaling in vivo.

items.title: Brain extracellular matrix remodelling in health and neuropsychiatric disorders.
items.abstract: The neural extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as an active regulator of brain function and an important contributor to the pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric disorders. This Review examines ECM organization, function and adaptive remodelling in the healthy brain and synthesizes evidence for its pathophysiological alterations in schizophrenia, major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder. Based on findings from human studies and animal models, we propose an ECM-extended conceptual framework of major psychiatric diseases in which polygenic liability, stress exposure and neuroinflammatory signalling converge to remodel the ECM in circuits supporting reward processing, emotion regulation, cognitive control and social cognition. In this model, an early phase of protease-dominant ECM loosening destabilizes microcircuits composed of parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons and principal cells whereas later reactive ECM rebuilding stabilizes dysfunctional network states and contributes to disease persistence, relapse and treatment resistance. This framework positions the ECM as a central hub of genetic, glial, synaptic and systems-level pathogenesis and suggests avenues for the development of ECM-sensitive biomarkers and ECM-directed interventions that may improve the treatment of these disorders.

items.title: Dosage compensation is regulated by segregated chromatin modules during development in Drosophila.
items.abstract: Dosage compensation (DC) restores the expression balance between the X chromosome and autosomes in males. How this chromosome-wide regulation is precisely regulated to accommodate the heterogeneous functions and dosage-sensitivity among X-linked genes is unclear. To address this, we analyse the epigenomic and 3D genome data of mostly sexed samples from embryos to adults of Drosophila melanogaster, whose DC is known to be mediated by three classes of X-enriched sequence elements of HAS/CES, PionX and 1.688 3F satellites. We find that about 30% of the X-linked genes are compensated specifically in one or a few male stages or tissues, indicated by their significant bindings of the DC-associated protein or H4K16ac histone modification. These specifically (SDC) or facultatively (FDC) compensated genes are more likely to have a developmentally regulated expression and a highly relevant function with the stage or tissue where they are compensated. They show a higher level of co-binding of facultative heterochromatin hallmark H3K27me3 than the constitutively (CDC) compensated housekeeping genes. CDC genes preferentially harbor constitutive long-range (>1Mb) contacts (LRCs) with other CDC genes and the HAS elements, which form by the onset of DC in embryos. While SDC and FDC genes show developmentally increased LRCs with the respective type of genes and the PionX elements and 1.688 3F satellites. The CDC genes and their interacting partners more often coincide with the constitutive boundaries of topologically associated domains, while the other DC genes tend to coincide with the developmentally regulated boundaries. Our results uncover that the Drosophila DC is regulated through separate chromatin modules between housekeeping vs. developmental genes involving different combinations of regulatory sequence elements and 3D genome contacts. This provides broad implications for the hierarchical regulation of DC against different developmental and gene backgrounds among other organisms.

items.title: Cortical Hypoperfusion in Acute Anorexia Nervosa Is Graded Along the Sensorimotor-Association Hierarchy.
items.abstract: Objective Cortical gray-matter changes in anorexia nervosa (AN) are among the largest reported in psychiatry, but the functional-metabolic state of that tissue is largely unknown. Because cortical energy use is highest in transmodal association cortex (prefrontal, parietal, and temporal regions of the default-mode and frontoparietal networks), a reduced energy supply predicts a graded rather than uniform reduction in perfusion (blood delivery to tissue). Method A total of 44 acutely underweight women with AN and 45 healthy women underwent 3 T pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling with partial-volume correction. Cerebral blood flow was compared between groups across the Schaefer 100 regions 7 networks atlas, age-adjusted and false-discovery-rate-corrected, and the case-control map was compared with the principal functional gradient (the axis running from sensorimotor to transmodal cortex), with cortical thickness in the same participants, and with 18 PET and SPECT receptor maps. Results Perfusion was lower in AN in 97 of 100 regions and maximal in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex (composite d = -0.56). The deficit scaled with position along the principal functional gradient (ρ = -0.56), an axis unrelated to perfusion in health, and was recoverable in individual brains (d = -0.53). Thinning was widespread but unrelated to gradient position, and the two effect maps did not correspond. Hypoperfusion was greater where D1, CB1, mGluR5, M1, 5-HT2A, and μ-opioid systems are dense, the dopaminergic, cannabinoid, glutamatergic, and muscarinic ones persisting after gradient adjustment. Discussion Cortical perfusion in acute AN is not uniformly reduced but organized along the cortex's principal functional axis, dissociable from cortical thinning and aligned with reward-related neurochemistry.

items.title: International Expert Consensus Statement on Contemporary Prevention and Management of Postoperative Delirium in Cardiac Surgery.
items.abstract: Background Postoperative delirium is among the most frequent neurocognitive complications of cardiac surgery, with reported incidence ranging from 14% to more than 50% depending on patient population and operative complexity. It is independently associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, extended intensive care unit and hospital stay, long-term cognitive decline, and increased mortality. Despite this burden, prevention and management strategies remain inconsistent across institutions worldwide. Methods An international multidisciplinary expert panel applied a structured PICOT (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Timing) framework to predefined clinical questions spanning four perioperative phases: preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative and intensive care, and recovery after intensive care. Designated expert groups synthesized available evidence through structured literature reviews, and consensus recommendations were developed using a modified Delphi methodology. Results The panel developed 14 consensus statements. Preoperatively, routine screening with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Clinical Frailty Scale, and multicomponent optimization are recommended. Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia is recommended, whereas perioperative dexmedetomidine in place of benzodiazepines, cerebral oximetry, processed electroencephalography-guided anesthesia depth monitoring, and optimized oxygen delivery may be considered. In intensive care, validated delirium screening paired with sedation assessment, daily awakening and breathing trials, structured multicomponent care bundles, correction of reversible precipitants, and circadian-supportive environments are central. After transfer from intensive care, continued ward screening and structured post-discharge cognitive follow-up are recommended. Conclusions These statements provide a framework for preventing and managing postoperative delirium after cardiac surgery and advocate a coordinated multimodal approach. Standardizing screening, prevention bundles, and long-term follow-up within routine clinical pathways is recommended as a core institutional priority.

items.title: Synaptic injury and neurodegeneration: recent advances in mechanisms of SGN injury in ARHL.
items.abstract: Age-related hearing loss (ARHL) is a common chronic sensory disorder among the elderly. It causes communication difficulties and is closely associated with cognitive decline and depression. The degeneration of cochlear spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) and early damage to ribbon synapses are crucial processes in ARHL. Since synaptic dysfunction often occurs before hair cell loss and threshold elevations, it contributes to hidden hearing loss and adversely affects the efficacy of cochlear implantation. However, the mechanisms by which synaptic injury drives SGN aging are not yet fully understood. This review systematically overviews the degeneration of ribbon synapses and SGN in ARHL, including the molecular and functional heterogeneity of SGN subtypes, the spatial and temporal patterns of ribbon synapses, the pathological mechanisms and the cell death pathways of SGN damage during aging. This review also identifies future research directions and emphasizes early intervention targets in ARHL, aiming to provide a systematic theoretical framework for the early prevention and clinical management of ARHL.

items.title: Where could the brain keep a symbol?
items.abstract: Neuroscience routinely describes memories as stored neural symbols, yet durable memory and successful retrieval do not establish a separately accessible symbolic vehicle. I distinguish retention, the claim that a physical change persists and later influences behavior, from symbolic storage, the stronger computational claim that a description can be accessed independently of the operation it specifies. The criterion is functional and system-relative and does not rule out neural activity as access. It requires specifying, before testing, the candidate vehicle, its proposed use, the system boundary, and an endogenous route reaching the vehicle without using it. DNA meets the criterion: replication preserves nucleotide sequence without producing the encoded gene product. Evidence from synapses and circuits establishes persistent, functionally useful organization but has not shown this separation for any neural memory vehicle; in these states, identified reads are executions that modify what they read. Hippocampal replay, neuromodulation, and artificial-network checkpoints show that the verdict depends on the vehicle and operations compared. I agree with Gallistel that intracellular nucleic acid mechanisms could provide a genuine store, but disagree that behavioral precision alone requires one. Maintained coupling, in which memory is sustained by continual recalibration rather than read from a store, offers an alternative whose predictions depend on error source: drift can be corrected where a reference signal remains, but a unique, never-revisited episode offers none. Current evidence favors retention without symbolic storage in synapses and circuits; I propose operational tests that could overturn this verdict. Either way, retention and use remain memory.

items.title: Mismatch Negativity and General Cognitive Ability - A Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Intelligence or general cognitive ability (GCA) is fundamental to human behavior and cognition. It impacts important life outcomes like educational success, and even health and longevity have been related to differences in GCA. Understanding the biological basis of such individual variations presents a crucial goal of neuroscience. The mismatch negativity (MMN) is an event-related brain potential that can be measured when-within a series of frequent standard stimuli, rare deviants are presented-and is suggested to reflect conscious (active) or unconscious (passive) detection processes of the brain. Importantly, variations in MMN amplitude and latency have been linked to differences in GCA. Yet findings vary considerably. This preregistered meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the current state of research. Following the study selection process in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, and the rating of study design quality with the Study Design and Implementation Assessment Device for Individual Difference Research (DIAD-ID), the association between GCA and MMN amplitude and latency was examined in 645 healthy adults across 12 included studies. The estimated across-sample associations between MMN and GCA were small, but significant (MMN amplitude-GCA: r = -0.09, MMN latency-GCA: r = -0.16; p < 0.01) and moderators were identified. Between-sample heterogeneity was moderate, with no evidence of publication bias. Our findings suggest that higher cognitive ability is associated with slightly stronger and faster MMN responses. However, the low estimated across-sample effect sizes and the small number of included studies also highlight the need for more research.

items.title: Single cell RNA-Seq in crim1<sup>-/-</sup> eyes in zebrafish shows dysregulation of β-actin and genes involved in cell adhesion and motility.
items.abstract: Purpose Cysteine-Rich Motor Neuron Protein 1 (CRIM1) haploinsufficiency is associated with eye defects, including coloboma, in humans. We previously generated a zebrafish model of reduced crim1 function that had smaller and malformed lenses and an abnormal retinal ganglion cell (RGC) layer, but our understanding of the gene dysregulation causing these ocular findings is limited. Methods To address this knowledge gap, we performed scRNA-Seq in dissected eyes from the crim1 -/- mutants and controls at 48 hours post fertilization and focused our analysis on cell types with differential expression of crim1. We used Comprehensive Multi-omics Platform for Biological InterpretatiOn (CompBio) to identify enriched biological themes. Results We identified a 31-cluster model that provided clear separation of ocular cell types and tissues. Lectin, galactoside-binding, soluble (lgals2b), orthologous to LGALS2 that was shown to bind β 1 -integrin in T cells, was the most upregulated gene in the Lens cluster. We found significant downregulation of integrin 1b.1 (itgb1b.1) and integrin 1b.2 (itgb1b.2) in the Corneal cluster of the crim1 -/- mutants. In the RGC clusters, serpin family E member 3 (serpine3) that is associated with retinal layering and sidekick cell adhesion molecule 1b (sdk1b) that encodes a protein involved in cell adhesion were upregulated, whereas glycoprotein M6A (gpm6a) was downregulated. CompBio identified numerous themes, including actin cytoskeleton remodeling, Wnt signaling, apoptosis and cell cycle regulation, and extracellular matrix organization. We found that β-actin expression was absent from the outer plexiform layer of the crim1 -/- mutants. Conclusions Our results support the known function of crim1 in integrin binding, cell adhesion, and apoptosis, but also uncover novel differentially expressed genes, including β-actin, lgals2b, serpine3, sdk1b, and gpm6a.

items.title: The neural mechanisms of fast versus slow decision-making.
items.abstract: One hallmark of intelligent behavior is the ability to optimize how much time is devoted to decisions. Yet the principles governing decision timing remain unclear. Here, we developed a novel paradigm for directly comparing decision-making between mice and humans. This approach allowed us to combine widefield and 2-photon imaging in the mouse frontal cortex with optogenetic inhibition to examine the underlying mechanisms. We found that history-dependent refinement of sequences in the medial frontal cortex (MFC), versus a thresholding mechanism in the lateral frontal cortex (LFC), provides a unified logic for decision strategy on a trial-by-trial basis. Notably, behavioral performance and strategy were profoundly disrupted by optogenetic inhibition of the MFC compared with that of the LFC, revealing a dominant cognitive role for MFC in decision selection and timing. These dynamics reflect reinforcement-learning updates that explain timing variability better than sensory evidence. Our findings provide a computational framework that unifies voluntary decision-making across species.

items.title: Sir Roger Bannister (1929-2018): beyond the track, documenting his influence in the field of autonomic neurology.
items.abstract: Sir Roger Bannister, best known for running the sub-four-minute mile, was influential in establishing the field of autonomic neurology. His early experiences studying exercise physiology, spinal cord injury, and thermoregulation shaped his interest in the mechanisms underlying autonomic regulation. The development of therapeutic approaches such as droxidopa to treat dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency could not have been accomplished without Bannister's dedication and contributions. Through his research, collaborations, and leadership in establishing the Clinical Autonomic Research Society, Bannister helped transform a field that was once dismissed as 'no more than an overture' into a lasting discipline in the field of neurology.

items.title: Differential Impacts of Acoustic Challenge on Three Language-Related Event-Related Brain Potential Components During Speech Processing: Evidence From the N400, the P600, and a Late Frontal Response.
items.abstract: When listening to acoustically challenging speech, listeners may strategically shift neural resources across multiple language-related cognitive processes in order to compensate for the additional demands. In the current study, we examined the impact of acoustic challenge (via speech-shaped background noise) on three language-related event-related brain potentials (ERPs): the N400 and two late positivities following the N400-a posterior P600 to syntactic violations and a late frontal effect sensitive to word expectancy. Young, normal-hearing adults (N = 48) listened in quiet and in noise (+3 dB SNR speech-shaped stationary noise) to contextually constraining sentences that ended in an expected word, an unexpected word, or a morphosyntactic violation of the expected word, while electroencephalography data were collected. Replicating prior work, we showed that an N400 expectancy effect was both reduced in amplitude and delayed in onset latency in noise. Providing novel insights into late ERP components, we found that a P600 syntax effect was reduced in amplitude by the presence of background noise. We additionally observed that the P600 response was only present for trials in which the listener successfully identified syntactic violations (irrespective of noise). In contrast to the reductions in the N400 and P600, the late frontal response was not reduced in noise. Collectively, this suggests that, while semantic retrieval and syntactic integration may be impaired by acoustic challenge, young, normal-hearing listeners may still prioritize neural resources toward prediction-related processes to help compensate for increased perceptual demands.

items.title: A "Basin of Attraction" Theory of Speech Initiation and Stuttering.
items.abstract: Recent work in motor neuroscience suggests that well-learned actions are implemented as stable, stereotyped trajectories in neural state space. The purpose of this article was to propose a theory of the neural basis of speech initiation that extends this idea to speech production and identifies a specific disruption that may underlie speech dysfluencies in stuttering. We advance a conceptual framework in which the motor program for a familiar word corresponds to a stable neural trajectory with an associated basin of attraction. We integrate findings from primate motor control, human speech neuroscience, and basal ganglia physiology to specify the role of the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical (BGTC) circuit in initiating these trajectories. We propose that fluent speech depends on the ability of the BGTC circuit to steer the distributed speech motor network into the basin of attraction of the upcoming word's motor program. Stuttering arises when this process is unreliable or poorly coordinated, preventing the motor program from being executed until the neural state is corrected or the effective basin of attraction is broadened through compensatory mechanisms. The basin of attraction framework provides a mechanistic description of the proximal neural processes responsible for stuttering events that can account for a wide range of behavioral and neurophysiological findings in stuttering. It also aligns stuttering theory with contemporary dynamical systems approaches to motor control and generates testable predictions for future neurophysiological and neuroimaging studies.

items.title: Deep Clustering of fMRI with Global-Local Feature Extraction for Functional Brain Activity Analysis.
items.abstract: Clustering is essential for identifying patterns in data. In neuroscience, it is widely used on functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data to uncover brain activity patterns during cognitive tasks and rest. However, traditional methods like K-means struggle with the high dimensionality and temporal complexity of fMRI data, and often fail to capture spatial or contextual structures in image data, limiting their effectiveness. To address these challenges, we propose a deep clustering model that leverages the complementary strengths of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and Masked Autoencoder (MAE) for comprehensive feature extraction. The SAE captures global features and reduces data dimensionality while preserving overall structure. In parallel, the MAE reconstructs masked input patches to learn local contextual features-temporal for sequential data like fMRI, and spatial for imagedata. The combination of global and local features yields a more informative representation of the data. These fused features are then fed into a Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC) module, which iteratively refines cluster centers and feature representations using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss, improving clustering accuracy and robust ness. Experimental results show that our model effectively identifies functional brain activity patterns in task based fMRI and differentiates hippocampal subregions in resting-state fMRI. Overall, our approach offers a unified and versatile deep clustering framework capable of handling various data modalities, enabling more accurate and interpretable analysis in both neuroimaging and general high-dimensional data applications. The proposed framework explicitly decomposes global and local feature learning, overcoming limitations of single path deep clustering methods and providing physiologically meaningful clustering patterns.

items.title: Reinforced hippocampus-accumbens pathway marks a shift toward cognitive decline in aging.
items.abstract: Aging triggers early functional alterations in brain circuits preceding cognitive impairment, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unaddressed. Spatial navigation and memory, among the earliest affected, depend on the hippocampus and downstream targets such as the nucleus accumbens (NAc), which integrates spatial and motivational information to guide goal-directed behaviors. Here we identify age-related, sex-dependent changes in the dorsal hippocampus-NAc (dHPC→NAc) pathway. Combining optogenetics with electrophysiology, chemogenetics, and behavioral analyses in mice, we show that aging shifts the excitation-inhibition balance in dorsal CA1 toward pyramidal neuron hyperactivity, strengthening hippocampal outputs. This selectively enhances synaptic drive onto D1 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons and involves a previously unrecognized long-range parvalbumin-expressing projection. Chemogenetically reducing the dHPC→NAc activity improves memory in aged mice. In humans, fMRI reveals heightened posterior hippocampal activity and stronger posterior HPC-NAc coupling during navigation. Together, we uncover a targetable pathway acting in an intervention-sensitive window of aging to correct negative cognitive trajectories.

items.title: Racial trauma and criterion a: On the nature of discrimination, threat, and danger.
items.abstract: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision, Criterion A for posttraumatic stress disorder describes potential traumatic events as actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. On its face, racial discrimination, particularly when individual discriminatory experiences, does not meet conventional trauma criteria. This commentary considers whether racial discrimination could be a source of perceived threat and considers how this might be relevant regarding the trauma diagnosis. Drawing on research in psychoneuroimmunology, neuroscience, and social rejection, this commentary examines the physiological mechanisms through which perceived discrimination activates the body's threat-response systems. Evidence suggests that racial discrimination activates neurobiological threat pathways involving the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and inflammatory response system. Studies have linked perceived discrimination to elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, as well as adverse cardiovascular, metabolic, and reproductive outcomes. Research on social rejection provides a theoretical framework for understanding why seemingly minor discriminatory experiences may cumulatively signal danger and activate physiological defense mechanisms. Racial discrimination can function as a biologically meaningful threat even when individual experiences fall outside current Criterion A definitions. Incorporating evidence of physiological threat activation into trauma research and reconsidering how subjective and cumulative threats are addressed in posttraumatic stress disorder diagnostic criteria may provide a more comprehensive understanding of racial trauma and its health consequences. items.title: Clean sport in childhood: a paediatric call for doping prevention and early clinical recognition.
items.abstract: Physical activity is essential to child health, yet its potential adverse aspects, particularly doping, remain largely overlooked in paediatric populations. Emerging data indicate that doping behaviours are not anecdotal among youth in a context of increasingly intensive and widespread competitive youth sports. Children and adolescents represent a uniquely vulnerable population due to neurological, endocrine and musculoskeletal immaturity, identity construction, and strong social influences, including those from elite sports, peers, parents, and coaches. These factors may favour risk-taking behaviours and the normalisation of doping, with potentially serious and multisystem health consequences. Despite this, doping remains a blind spot in paediatric clinical practice. This narrative review aims to raise awareness of this underestimated issue, highlight key mechanisms of vulnerability, and emphasise the critical role paediatricians can play in early identification and prevention. Promoting proactive education, identification and multidisciplinary care is essential to safeguard young athletes in the evolving sporting environment. • Doping may cause significant physical and psychological harm during growth and development, yet it remains under-recognised in paediatric practice. • This narrative review highlights the specific vulnerability of children and adolescents to doping, summarises key warning signs for early clinical recognition, and proposes a practical prevention framework for paediatricians, emphasising their central role in prevention in line with international recommendations.
